He became the first ruler of both kingdoms since Alfonso VII died in 1157.

A succession crisis in the Almohad Caliphate after 1224 gave Ferdinand his opening. In 1228 the last Almohad forces left Spain for Morocco, and al-Andalus fell into the hands of local strongmen. From then until 1248 he took Úbeda in 1233, Córdoba in 1236, Jaén in 1246 and, on 22 December 1248, Seville, and Murcia came by the pact of Alcaraz in 1243. Only the Emirate of Granada remained unconquered, and in 1238 he extracted a tributary arrangement from it. He divided the conquered land among the military orders, the Church and the nobility, and Pope Gregory IX called him athleta Christi, champion of Christ.

Ferdinand strengthened the University of Salamanca, erected the present Cathedral of Burgos and founded houses of friars of the Dominican, Franciscan, Trinitarian and Mercedarian orders throughout Andalusia. He died on 30 May 1252 after a dropsy contracted in the winter of 1251 and was buried in the Cathedral of Seville. He left his son Alfonso X a greatly enlarged kingdom, whose boundaries stayed nearly unchanged until the late 15th century. Pope Clement X canonised him in 1671.
ferdinand-lassalle: Ferdinand Lassal, who later adopted the French spelling Lassalle, was born in Breslau, now Wrocław, on 11 April 1825. His Jewish family had moved to Prussian Silesia from Poland in the late 18th century, and his father, Heymann Lassal, a prosperous wholesale silk merchant, had trained for a rabbinical career. A diary he kept as a boy shows a quick-witted, ambitious youth, sensitive about his Jewishness and his provincial background. After passing his matriculation examination in 1843 he studied at the universities of Breslau and Berlin, where he discovered Hegel, whose philosophy he later described as a second birth.

In 1846 Lassalle met Countess Sophie von Hatzfeldt, unhappily married to Count Edmund von Hatzfeldt-Kinsweiler, and spent the next eight years almost entirely on her legal claims against her husband. The case brought him public renown and, in 1848, a sentence of two months for criminal libel; arrested for complicity in the theft of documents, he was acquitted at Cologne in August 1848. There he met Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels. Engels disliked his ostentation, while Marx was more tolerant, though a report of 1855 left him mistrustful. Lassalle also wrote Heraclitus the Obscure (1857) and The System of Acquired Rights (1861).

In April 1862 he gave two lectures in Berlin arguing that a constitution is the factual power relationship in a society written down, and that the working class should form its own party. In 1863 he founded the General German Workers' Association, whose platform called for socialism through state-aided producers' co-operatives won by universal suffrage. He negotiated secretly with Otto von Bismarck, hoping to ally the workers' movement with the conservative state against the liberal bourgeoisie.

In the summer of 1864 Lassalle became engaged to Helene von Dönniges, daughter of a Bavarian diplomat. Her family opposed the match because of his Jewish origins and political notoriety, and she was pressured into renouncing him for a previous suitor, Yanko von Rakowitza. Lassalle challenged her father to a duel; he declined, and Rakowitza accepted in his place. Lassalle was killed in a duel on 31 August 1864, aged 39.

The association then had only a few thousand members, but under Johann Baptist von Schweitzer it kept Lassalle's centralised organisation and pro-governmental tactics. In 1875 it merged with the Social Democratic Workers' Party at the Gotha Congress to form what became the Social Democratic Party of Germany, whose programme drew on his demand for state-aided co-operatives. Marx thought his state socialism a misunderstanding of his own theories.
ferdinand-magellan: Magellan was born in northern Portugal, possibly around 1480. His father, Pedro de Magalhães, was a minor member of the Portuguese nobility and mayor of the town, and his mother was Alda de Mezquita. He was brought up as a page of Queen Eleanor, consort of King John II, and in 1495 he entered the service of Manuel I.

In March 1505 he enlisted in the fleet sent to host Francisco de Almeida as the first viceroy of Portuguese India, and he remained there eight years. He took part in the battle of Cannanore in 1506, where he was wounded, and the Battle of Diu in 1509. In 1511, under Afonso de Albuquerque, he and his friend Francisco Serrão took part in the conquest of Malacca. Serrão went on to the Moluccas, and his letters to Magellan later gave decisive information about the spice-producing territories.

King Manuel I repeatedly rejected Magellan's proposals for expeditions to the Spice Islands. Magellan then offered the project to Charles I of Spain, who approved it. Under the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494 Portugal was to control the eastern routes around the Cape of Good Hope, so Magellan proposed a southwestern passage around South America. He was given command of the five-ship Armada of Molucca and sailed in August 1519 with about 270 men. King Manuel did all he could to disrupt the preparations, and a Portuguese fleet sent after him failed to capture him.

The fleet crossed the Atlantic and went south to Patagonia. Despite storms and mutinies, it passed through the Strait of Magellan into the sea Magellan renamed the Mar Pacifico, landed at Guam and reached the Philippines. Magellan converted as many as 2,200 locals to Christianity, including Rajah Humabon of Cebu, but Lapulapu, the leader of Mactan, resisted. On the morning of 27 April 1521 Magellan sailed to Mactan with a small force and was killed in the battle that followed.

Antonio Pigafetta and Ginés de Mafra left accounts of the death. Lapulapu refused a ransom of copper and iron for the body. Under Juan Sebastián Elcano the expedition reached the Spice Islands, and the ship Elcano commanded returned to Spain in September 1522, completing the first circumnavigation of Earth. In the aftermath Magellan was widely discredited in Spain and Portugal. Some in Portugal regarded him as a traitor for having sailed for Spain.
ferdinand-marcos: Ferdinand Marcos was born in Sarrat, Ilocos Norte, on 11 September 1917. His father, Mariano Marcos, was a lawyer who represented Ilocos Norte in the House of Representatives from 1925 to 1931. Marcos studied law at the University of the Philippines, where he was a national rifle champion. In 1935 Julio Nalundasan, who had defeated Mariano Marcos in two elections, was shot dead at his home. Ferdinand and his uncle were convicted of the murder, but the conviction was overturned on appeal. He fought the Japanese after joining the United States Army in 1941. Researchers later found that most stories about his military service were inaccurate or untrue.

Marcos won his father's former seat in 1949, sat in the House of Representatives until 1959, in the Senate from 1959 to 1965, and was Senate president from 1963 to 1965. He was elected president in 1965 and re-elected in 1969. His early policies centred on massive infrastructure construction, funded by foreign lending. A balance of payments crisis in 1969 and growing Philippine involvement in the Vietnam War then triggered social unrest.

On 23 September 1972 Marcos declared martial law, extending his rule beyond the two-term constitutional limit. A 1973 plebiscite, overseen by the military, ratified his rule; media outlets and opposition politicians were silenced. He lifted martial law on 17 January 1981 and won a third term. The assassination of Ninoy Aquino in 1983 and an economic collapse damaged his standing. He called snap elections in 1986 against Aquino's widow, Corazon Aquino, and allegations of mass electoral fraud led to the People Power Revolution of February 1986.

On 25 February 1986 Marcos and his family left Malacañang by helicopter for Clark Air Base and flew on to Hawaii. He died there on 28 September 1989. The regime committed documented human rights abuses, especially after 1972, against students, farmers, journalists, priests and nuns and political opponents. Estimates generally include about 1,500 to 4,000 extrajudicial killings or disappearances, and tens of thousands imprisoned or tortured. The Marcos family denies responsibility for these violations.
ferdinand-vii-of-spain: Ferdinand was born on 14 October 1784 at El Escorial, the eldest surviving son of Charles IV and Maria Luisa of Parma. As heir he was excluded from government by his parents and their favourite, the Prime Minister Manuel Godoy. In October 1807 he was arrested for his part in the El Escorial Conspiracy, which sought support from Napoleon, and submitted to his parents. After a popular riot at Aranjuez, Charles IV abdicated in March 1808 and Ferdinand took the throne. He abdicated on 6 May 1808, and Napoleon kept him under guard in France for six years at the Château de Valençay.

The Spanish people rejected Napoleon's choice of Joseph Bonaparte as king, and the Peninsular War began. After the Battle of Bailén the Council of Castile declared the abdications of Bayonne void on 11 August 1808, and Ferdinand was proclaimed king on 24 August. Napoleon recognised him in the Treaty of Valençay of 11 December 1813. Ferdinand returned to a country governed under the liberal Constitution of 1812. On 4 May 1814 he ordered its abolition, and on 10 May he had its liberal authors arrested. He argued that the Cortes had been illegally assembled in his absence, and he never convened a traditional one.

His restored government was guided by a small circle of favourites, and he changed ministers every few months. He reinstated the Inquisition and the Jesuits and suppressed Freemasonry. Several military pronunciamientos followed. The most successful, led by Rafael del Riego in 1820, forced him to accept the constitution and began the Liberal Triennium. In 1823 the Congress of Verona authorised a French intervention that restored him to absolute power, and reprisals followed. Meanwhile wars of independence had broken out in the Americas. After the Treaty of Córdoba of 1821 he refused the Mexican crown and declared the Mexican constitution void.

In May 1830 Ferdinand published the Pragmatic Sanction, which allowed daughters to succeed. His daughter Isabella was born on 10 October 1830 and displaced his brother, Infante Carlos María Isidro, in the line of succession. Ferdinand died in late September 1833. Carlos claimed to be the legitimate king, and Maria Christina, regent for her daughter, turned to the liberals for support, which led to the Carlist Wars. Historians typically criticise his reign. Stanley G. Payne called him in many ways the basest king in Spanish history.
ferdinand-von-zeppelin: Ferdinand von Zeppelin was born on 8 July 1838 into a noble family. He spent his childhood with his sister and brother at the Girsberg manor near Konstanz, educated by private tutors. He became a cadet at the military school at Ludwigsburg in 1855 and began his career as an officer in the Württemberg army.

In 1863 he went to Virginia as an observer for the Union's Army of the Potomac in the American Civil War. At Saint Paul, Minnesota, he made his first aerial ascent with the German-born balloonist John Steiner on 19 August, which he later credited with starting his thinking about dirigibles. A reconnaissance mission behind enemy lines in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 made him known to many Germans.

Zeppelin first set out his idea for a large airship in a diary entry of 25 March 1874: a rigidly framed outer envelope containing a number of separate gasbags. After leaving the army, where his handling of a cavalry brigade at the manoeuvres of 1890 had been severely criticised, he devoted himself to airships. The engineer Theodor Kober refined the design, the Prussian Airship Service rejected it in 1895, and Zeppelin received a patent in August of that year. In 1898 a joint stock company was formed, and he invested 441,000 marks, over half its capital.

On 2 July 1900 the LZ 1 made the first flight over Lake Constance near Friedrichshafen and stayed up for 20 minutes. It was not judged successful enough to justify government investment, and Zeppelin, his funds exhausted, suspended work. The LZ 2 flew only once, in January 1906, and was wrecked by wind. The LZ 3 flew successfully, and the Reichstag voted him 500,000 marks.

The LZ 4 was destroyed by fire at Echterdingen in 1908, but public enthusiasm raised over 6 million marks, which created Luftschiffbau Zeppelin GmbH and the Zeppelin Foundation. The government accepted LZ 3 in November 1908. Until 1914 the German Aviation Association carried 37,250 passengers without incident, and in the First World War the German empire used Zeppelins as long-distance bombers against Belgium, France and the United Kingdom.

Zeppelin died on 8 March 1917, before the end of the First World War. The Treaty of Versailles later halted the Zeppelin project for a time, and his successor Hugo Eckener led its resurgence. The airship LZ 127 Graf Zeppelin, which circled the world, was named after him, as was the unfinished German aircraft carrier Graf Zeppelin.
ferentino: Ferentino is a town and comune in the province of Frosinone in Lazio, 65 kilometres south-east of Rome. It lies on a hill 400 metres above sea level, in the Monti Ernici area. In antiquity it was the town of the Hernici of Ferentinum. It stood just above the Via Latina and, being a strong place, served for the detention of hostages.

Ferentinum took no part in the rising of 306 BCE. Its inhabitants became Roman citizens after 195 BCE, and the place later became a municipium. From 1198 to 1557 Ferentino was the seat of the papal rectorate of Campagna and Marittima province. The town was strong in textiles, linen and embroidery, and in handicraft such as clay bricks, and after World War II it saw heavy industrial growth, mainly in pharmaceuticals.

The town keeps remains of ancient fortifications. The lower part of the outer walls is built of roughly hewn blocks of limestone, with rectangular blocks of tuff above in places. Two gates survive, the Porta Maggiore, a double gate built wholly of tuff blocks, and the Porta Sanguinaria. The acropolis, dating from the 2nd to 1st centuries BCE, has massive retaining walls like those of the lower town, and a building of travertine blocks whose cornice carries two inscriptions of the period of Sulla recording its construction by two censors.

The Cathedral of Sts John and Paul stands on part of the ancient acropolis, rebuilt in 1099 to 1118 on the site of an older church. It contains a Cosmatesque ciborium and a 12th-century mosaic pavement. The Gothic church of Santa Maria Maggiore dates from the 13th and 14th centuries. The Romanesque monastery of Sant'Antonio Abate housed the remains of Pope Celestine V until 1327.
fergana-valley: The Fergana Valley is an intermountain depression between the Tien Shan in the north and the Alay in the south. It is about 300 km long and up to 70 km wide, covering about 22,000 square kilometres, and it crosses eastern Uzbekistan, southern Kyrgyzstan and northern Tajikistan. Its fertility comes from the Naryn and the Kara Darya, which join near Namangan to form the Syr Darya. The climate is dry and continental, with hot summers and frost in December and January. The name Fergana is of Persian origin.

As early as 500 BCE the western part of the valley formed part of Sogdiana, which owed allegiance to the Achaemenid Empire under Darius the Great. In 329 BCE Alexander the Great founded Alexandria Eschate, the Furthest, in the south-west of the valley, at the site of the modern city of Khujand. Chinese chroniclers, drawing on the travels of Zhang Qian and published around 126 BCE, present the region as the country of the Dayuan, possibly descendants of Greek colonists, known for its Heavenly Horses. The Chinese waged war against the Dayuan in 104 BCE to obtain them. The Kushan Empire later ruled the area until the 3rd century CE, when the Sassanid Empire invaded.

Fergana then passed between the Sassanid Empire, the Hephthalite Empire and, from the mid-6th century, the Turkic Khaganates. In the 8th century it was a field of rivalry between Tang China and the expanding Muslim power. The Abbasid victory at the Battle of Talas in 751 led to the disengagement of China from Central Asia. In 819 Ahmad ibn Asad was granted authority over the city of Fergana, a step in the rise of the Samanid Empire. Genghis Khan invaded Transoxiana and Fergana in 1219, and the valley later became part of the Chagatai Khanate. The Babur who founded the Mughal dynasty came from the valley.

The Russian Empire conquered the valley at the end of the 19th century, forming the province of Fergana in 1876 out of the former khanate of Kokand. It became part of the Soviet Union in the 1920s, and the three republics that share it became independent in 1991. The valley is ethnically diverse, populated largely by Uzbek, Tajik and Kyrgyz people. Cotton cultivation, begun by the Soviets, is joined by grains, fruits and vegetables, stock breeding and mining of coal, iron and other minerals.
ferhat-abbas: Ferhat Abbas was born on 24 August 1899 in the village of Taher, Algeria, the son of a caid who had been awarded the rosette of a commander of the Legion of Honor. He was educated at Phillipeville and Constantine, served in the French army medical corps, reaching the rank of sergeant, and studied at the pharmacy school of the University of Algiers.

He then worked as a pharmacist in Sétif, where he entered politics and was elected to the municipal council and to the general council of Constantine. In an article of 1936 he wrote, "I am France", but in 1938 he grew disillusioned as his hopes of equality came to nothing.

In 1938 he organised the Algerian Popular Union, which promoted equal rights for French and Algerians while keeping Algerian culture and language as primary values. After General Giraud refused to let Muslims enlist as equals, he turned to nationalism and issued the Manifesto of the Algerian People on 10 February 1943, condemning French colonial rule and demanding self-determination. The governor general rejected it. With Messali Hadj he formed the Amis du Manifeste et de la Liberté, and he was imprisoned for a year. In 1946 he founded the Union Démocratique du Manifeste Algérien, a moderate party, and was elected to the French Constituent Assembly.

After arrests and the failure of moderate nationalism he fled to Cairo in 1956 and joined the Front de Libération Nationale as the war intensified. He became its delegate to the United Nations in 1957 and on 18 September 1958 president of the Provisional Government of the Algerian Republic, a largely diplomatic post. Talks with Charles de Gaulle failed to end the war, and in 1960 he visited China and the Soviet Union. He resigned on 27 August 1961 and was succeeded by Benyoucef Ben Khedda.

Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962. Abbas was president of the constituent assembly from 25 September 1962 to 15 September 1963, but Ahmed Ben Bella sidelined it, and Abbas resigned in protest. He was expelled from the FLN and held under house arrest from 1964 to 1965. He received the Medal of Resistance on 30 October 1984 and died on 24 December 1985, and he is buried at El Alia Cemetery. His books include La nuit coloniale (1962), Autopsie d'une guerre (1980) and L'indépendance confisquée (1984).
fernand-braudel: Fernand Braudel was born on 24 August 1902 in Luméville-en-Ornois, in the Meuse, and joined his father, a mathematics teacher, in Paris at the age of seven. He studied at the Sorbonne and gained his agrégation in history in 1923, then taught in Algeria until 1932. There he became fascinated by the Mediterranean and began a doctoral thesis on the foreign policy of Philip II of Spain, working in archives at Simancas, Venice and Dubrovnik. In 1935 he went to Brazil to help build the University of São Paulo. On the voyage home in 1937 he travelled with Lucien Febvre, co-founder of the journal Annales, and came under the influence of the Annales School.

Called up in 1939, Braudel was taken prisoner on 29 June 1940 and held at Mainz, where he became rector of the camp university, and from June 1942 near Lübeck. He drafted his work on the Mediterranean in captivity, without his own books and notes, sending copy books to Febvre in Paris. After 1945 he led the second generation of Annales historians, defended his thesis in 1947 and was elected to the Collège de France in 1949. He headed the Sixième section of the École pratique des hautes études from 1956 and edited the Annales from 1957. He directed the Fondation Maison des Sciences de l'Homme from 1970 until his death and was elected to the Académie française in 1984.

The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II (1949) was his most influential book. For Braudel there is no single Mediterranean but many seas, bound to the plains, mountains and desert around them. He divided time into three levels: the slow time of geography, the social and economic history of two or three centuries, and the history of events, which he called the time of surfaces.

Civilization and Capitalism, 15th–18th Century (1967–1979) follows how ordinary people made economies work, and traces centres of capitalism in turn: Venice, Antwerp and Genoa, Amsterdam and London. He argued that capitalists were typically monopolists, not entrepreneurs in competitive markets. His last book, The Identity of France, was unfinished at his death on 27 November 1985. He stressed constraints on human action and the lives of slaves, serfs, peasants and the urban poor, and is regarded as a precursor of world-systems theory.
fezzan: Fezzan is the southwestern region of modern Libya. It is largely desert, broken by mountains, uplands and dry river valleys, or wadis, in the north, where oases allow ancient towns and villages to survive in the Sahara. Only the ash-Shati Valley, the Wadi Irawan, parts of the Tibesti Mountains and a few remote oases can support settled populations, while the dune seas of the Idehan Ubari and the Idehan Murzuq cover most of the rest. In Berber languages the name means rough rocks, and it may also derive from the Greek Phazania, which may mean the country of the pheasants.

From the 5th century BCE to the 5th century CE Fezzan was the home of the Garamantes, who operated the trans-Saharan trade routes between Carthage and later the Roman Empire in North Africa and the Sahelian states of west and central Africa. The Roman generals Septimus Flaccus in 19 BCE and Suetonius Paulinus in 50 CE led small expeditions into the northern Sahara. After the Roman Empire ended, a commercial crisis cut its importance, and desertification greatly reduced the population.

In the 13th and 14th centuries Fezzan was part of the Kanem Empire. Wars against Kanem-Bornu in the early sixteenth century led to the Awlad Muhammad dynasty, with Murzuk as its capital. In 1574 Ottoman Tripolitania invaded and occupied it, though the Turks refrained from exercising much influence. Italy occupied it from 1911 and met resistance from the Sanusiyya Sufi order. Free French troops occupied Murzuk on 16 January 1943 and ran Fezzan from Sabha as the Fezzan-Ghadames Military Territory. When French control ceased in 1951, Fezzan became part of the Kingdom of Libya.

After the formation of Libya in 1934, Fezzan was designated one of the country's three primary provinces, with Tripolitania to the north and Cyrenaica to the northeast. Murzuk and Sabha are its chief towns.
fiat: On 11 July 1899 Giovanni Agnelli was among the founding members of FIAT, Fabbrica Italiana Automobili Torino. The first plant opened in 1900 with 35 staff making 24 cars. The first car, the 3½ HP, was based on a design bought from Ceirano GB & C and had a 697 cc boxer twin engine; only 24 were built. The company was known from the beginning for the talent of its engineers. By 1903 it made a small profit and produced 135 cars.

By 1910 FIAT was the largest automotive company in Italy, and the American FIAT Automobile Company opened a plant at Poughkeepsie, which closed when the United States entered the First World War in 1917. During that war FIAT devoted all its factories to supplying the Allies with aircraft, engines, machine guns, trucks and ambulances. By the early 1920s it held 80 per cent of the Italian market. In 1921 workers seized its plants and hoisted the red flag, and Agnelli quit the company until the occupation ended. The Lingotto factory, the first FIAT plant to use assembly lines, was then the largest in Europe, and by 1925 FIAT held 87 per cent of the Italian car market.

In the Second World War FIAT made vehicles and aircraft, among them the CR.42 Falco, for the Army and the Regia Aeronautica and later for the Germans. After Benito Mussolini was overthrown, the National Liberation Committee removed the Agnelli family from leadership because of its ties to his government. They returned in 1963, when Giovanni's grandson Gianni became general manager, and he was chairman from 1966 to 1996. In 1970 FIAT employed more than 100,000 people in Italy and production there reached 1.4 million cars.

FIAT Automobiles was formed in January 2007 from the group's reorganised car business. FIAT merged with Chrysler in 2014 as Fiat-Chrysler Automobiles, and in 2021 it became a subsidiary of Stellantis after the merger with Peugeot SA's PSA Group. It is the largest car maker in Italy and for over twenty years was the largest in Europe and third in the world, until the car industry crisis of the late 1980s.

Outside Italy, Brazil is the largest country of production; FIAT built its first Brazilian plant at Betim in 1973. Nine FIAT Automobiles models have won the European Car of the Year award, from the 124 in 1967 to the 500 in 2008.
fidel-castro: Fidel Alejandro Castro Ruz was born out of wedlock at his father's farm in Birán on 13 August 1926. His father, Ángel Castro y Argiz, was a migrant from Galicia in north-west Spain who took his household servant, Lina Ruz González, as his mistress and later second wife; they had seven children. At six Castro was sent to live with his teacher in Santiago de Cuba, and he later attended the Jesuit-run Dolores School there and, from 1942, El Colegio de Belén in Havana. In 1945 he began studying law at the University of Havana, where he took up anti-imperialist ideas and became involved in student activism. In 1947 he joined the Party of the Cuban People, founded by Eduardo Chibás.

In 1952 Castro formed a group called The Movement, which ran on a clandestine cell system and gained about 1,200 members in a year, most from Havana's poorer districts. He planned an attack on the Moncada Barracks, a garrison outside Santiago de Cuba, to be launched on 25 July 1953; it failed. After a year's imprisonment he went to Mexico and formed the 26th of July Movement with his brother Raúl Castro and Ernesto Che Guevara. Returning to Cuba, he led a guerrilla war against the forces of Fulgencio Batista from the Sierra Maestra. After Batista's overthrow in 1959 Castro assumed military and political power as prime minister.

The United States came to oppose his government and tried to remove it by assassination attempts, an economic embargo and counter-revolution, including the Bay of Pigs Invasion of 1961. Castro aligned Cuba with the Soviet Union and allowed Soviet nuclear weapons to be placed there, which led to the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962. He declared himself a Marxist–Leninist from December 1961, and Cuba became a one-party state under Communist Party rule. A new constitution in 1976, based on the Soviet Constitution of 1936, ended 16 years of rule by decree, and Castro became president.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991 Castro led Cuba through the economic downturn known as the Special Period. On 31 July 2006, after surgery for intestinal bleeding, he delegated his duties to Raúl Castro, who was elected president by the National Assembly on 24 February 2008. Fidel stepped down as first secretary of the Communist Party in 2011 and died on 25 November 2016, aged 90, of natural causes.

He was the longest-serving non-royal head of state of the 20th and 21st centuries. His supporters regard him as a champion of socialism and anti-imperialism whose government advanced economic and social justice and secured Cuba's independence from American domination. His critics regard him as a dictator whose administration oversaw human rights abuses, the exodus of many Cubans and the impoverishment of the economy.
fidesz: Fidesz was founded in the spring of 1988 as Fiatal Demokraták Szövetsége, the Alliance of Young Democrats, an underground liberal student movement opposed to the ruling Hungarian Socialist Workers' Party. Founding such a movement was semi-illegal at the time, so its founders risked their careers. Membership had an upper age limit of 35 years, abolished at the 1993 congress. In 1989 the movement won the Thorolf Rafto Memorial Prize, received by one of its leaders, Péter Molnár. During the transition to multiparty democracy in 1989 and 1990 it became a political party, and in the 1990 election it entered the National Assembly with about 6 percent of the vote, with Viktor Orbán at its head.

In 1992 Fidesz joined the Liberal International. At its 1993 congress it redefined itself from liberal to civic-centrist, which split the membership: Péter Molnár, Gábor Fodor and Klára Ungár left for the liberal Alliance of Free Democrats, and Orbán was elected chairman. After a disappointing result in 1994 the party grew more conservative, and in 1995 it renamed itself the Hungarian Civic Party and sought links with the national-conservative Hungarian Democratic Forum.

Fidesz first took power at the 1998 election, with Orbán as prime minister, in coalition with the Hungarian Democratic Forum and the Independent Smallholders' Party. In 2000 it left the Liberal International and joined the European People's Party. It narrowly lost the 2002 election to the Hungarian Socialist Party, with 41.07 percent against 42.05 percent, and accused its opponents of electoral fraud. In 2003 it took the name Fidesz – Hungarian Civic Union. In 2004 it won 47.4 percent of the vote in the European Parliament elections and 12 seats. Its nominee László Sólyom was elected President of Hungary in 2005. During its years in opposition between 2002 and 2010 it formed an electoral alliance with the Christian Democratic People's Party.

Fidesz's position has shifted over time. It began on the centre-left, strongly committed to anti-clerical and secular policies, moved to the right from 1994, and by 1998 was the most prominent liberal-conservative force in Hungary, adopting nationalism and Christian democracy in the early 2000s. After winning a parliamentary supermajority in the 2010 election it promulgated a new constitution, the Fundamental Law, in 2011, and it won supermajorities again in 2014, 2018 and 2022.
fief: In ancient Rome a benefice, from the Latin beneficium, was a gift of land for life as a reward for services to the state, and medieval Latin documents continued to call a land grant in exchange for service a beneficium. Later the term feudum, or feodum, replaced it, first attested in 984 although more primitive forms appear up to a century earlier. Why it replaced beneficium is not well established. The most widely held theory, from Marc Bloch, links it to a Frankish word meaning movable goods, so that when land replaced currency as the main store of value the Germanic word displaced the Latin one.

A fief gave the vassal the use of the land and its income, while the granting lord kept ultimate ownership and could in principle recover it in case of disloyalty or death. Originally vassalage did not imply a landholding, but by the 8th century the grant of land was becoming standard. In Francia Charles Martel was the first to make large-scale, systematic use of granting the usufruct of lands to vassals for life, sometimes passing to the second or third generation. By the middle of the 10th century fees had largely become hereditary, and the eldest son had first to do homage and fealty and pay a relief. There never existed a standard feudal system or one type of fief, and customs varied by region.

In the 13th century the term feodum described a dependent tenure held in return for a specified amount of knight service and occasional payments. Knight service in war was far less common than castle-guard, suit in court, attendance in the lord's entourage and hospitality. In northern France in the 12th and 13th centuries a knight's service on offensive campaigns was limited to 40 days. A lord in late 12th-century England and France could also claim wardship and marriage, aids, and escheat, the reversion of the fief when there was no heir. By the 12th century English and French kings and barons began to commute military service for cash payments called scutages, with which they could hire mercenaries.

In England Henry II turned fiefs into important sources of royal income and patronage. The discontent of barons at the arbitrary reliefs claimed under his son King John resulted in Magna Carta of 1215.
fiesole: Fiesole is a town and comune of the Metropolitan City of Florence in Tuscany, on a height above Florence, about 5 km north-east of that city. Its Latin name was Faesulae, from the Etruscan Viesul, Viśl or Vipsul. It was an important member of the Etruscan confederacy, and the remains of its ancient walls and buildings have been preserved, with an archaeological museum in the town.

The earliest recorded mention dates to 283 BCE, when the Romans conquered the Etruscan town. In Roman times it was the seat of a school of augurs, to which twelve young men were sent each year from Rome to study divination. The old town was destroyed either in the Social War or by Sulla in 80 BCE, in reprisal for supporting the populares, and Sulla colonised it with veterans, who later supported Catilina under Gaius Mallius. In 406 the general Stilicho won a victory near Fiesole over the Vandals and Suebi under Radagaisus. In the Gothic War the town was besieged several times, and in 539 the Byzantine general Justin captured it and razed its fortifications.

For several centuries in the early Middle Ages Fiesole was independent and no less powerful than Florence in the valley below, and wars arose between them. The Florentines sacked it in 1010 and 1025 and conquered it in 1125, obliging its leading families to live in Florence. Dante reflects the rivalry in the Divine Comedy by referring to the beasts of Fiesole. From the 14th century wealthy Florentines had villas in the hills, and one is the setting of the frame story of Boccaccio's Decameron. The Medici built a villa there in the fifteenth century.

The Roman theatre, below the cathedral, has 19 tiers of stone seats and is 34 metres in diameter, and there are remains of Roman baths and of Etruscan walls. The cathedral holds the shrine of Saint Romulus, according to legend the first bishop, and an altarpiece by Pietro Perugino. The Badia, the old cathedral, was built in 1028. The European University Institute is based in the town, in historic buildings such as the Badia Faesolina and the Villa Schifanoia, and several American universities maintain campuses there.
fifa-world-cup: The first international football match was a challenge match played in Glasgow in 1872 between Scotland and England, and the first tournament for nations, the British Home Championship, took place in 1884. Football was a demonstration sport at the Olympic Games of 1900 and 1904, and FIFA, founded in 1904, tried to arrange its own tournament in Switzerland in 1906, which its official history describes as unsuccessful.

After the success of the Olympic football tournaments, FIFA, with its president Jules Rimet as the driving force, looked again at staging a competition outside the Olympics. On 28 May 1928 the FIFA Congress in Amsterdam decided to stage a world championship, and Uruguay, celebrating the centenary of its independence in 1930, was named host of the first tournament.

Early hosts were chosen at meetings of FIFA's congress, and the choices were controversial because travel between South America and Europe took three weeks by boat. Holding the first tournament in Uruguay reduced the European entries to four. The next two were both held in Europe, and Argentina and Uruguay boycotted the 1938 tournament in France, as the South American countries had assumed that the location would alternate between the continents.

The 1950 World Cup in Brazil was the first to include the British football associations, which had withdrawn from FIFA in 1920 and rejoined in 1946. Uruguay, who had boycotted the two previous tournaments, won it by defeating the host nation in the match called the Maracanazo. The tournament was expanded to 24 teams in 1982 and to 32 in 1998, which allowed more teams from Africa, Asia and North America to take part; South Korea finished fourth in 2002 and Morocco fourth in 2022. European and South American teams still dominate, and the finalists of every tournament have come from those two continents.

Since the second World Cup in 1934 qualifying tournaments have been held within the continental zones under their confederations, and the finals are played within a host nation or nations over about a month, first in groups and then in knockout rounds. The trophy has been won by eight national teams, and Brazil are the only team to have played in every tournament.

From 1930 to 1970 the winners received the Jules Rimet Trophy, named in 1946 after the FIFA president who set up the first tournament. Brazil's third victory in 1970 entitled them to keep it, but it was stolen in 1983 and has never been recovered, apparently melted down. A new trophy of solid 18 carat gold, designed by the Italian Silvio Gazzaniga, has been awarded since then. The World Cup was first televised in 1954, and the 2018 tournament was watched by an estimated 3.5 billion people.
fife: Fife is a natural peninsula in eastern Scotland, bordered by the Firth of Tay to the north, the North Sea to the east and the Firth of Forth to the south. The Ochil Hills partly block the route to the west. The coast has small harbours, from the docks at Burntisland and Rosyth to the fishing villages of the East Neuk such as Anstruther and Pittenweem, with their stepped gables.

The Pictish king list and the Poppleton manuscript mention a division of the Pictish realm into seven sub-kingdoms, one of them Fife, recorded as Fib in 1150. The hill-fort of Clatchard Craig near Newburgh was an important Pictish stronghold between the sixth and eighth centuries. The epithet Kingdom of Fife is first recorded only in 1678, and may derive from the quasi-regal privileges of the Earl of Fife. Until the 15th century the earl was considered the principal peer of the Scottish realm and had the right to crown the nation's monarchs.

Fife became an important royal centre from the reign of King Malcolm III, who had his principal home at Dunfermline. Dunfermline Abbey replaced Iona as the burial place of Scotland's royal elite, and Robert I is buried there. The House of Stuart built a palace at Falkland, favouring Fife for its hunting grounds. James VI called the county a beggar's mantle fringed wi gowd, the fringe being a coast of small ports trading wool, linen, coal and salt with the Low Countries.

Fife became a centre of heavy industry in the 19th century. Coal had been mined since at least the 12th century, and the number of pits increased ten-fold in the Victorian period. The Forth and Tay rail bridges linked it with Edinburgh and Dundee, and Kirkcaldy became the world centre of linoleum production. After the Second World War Glenrothes became Scotland's second new town. The county was governed by a county council from 1890 until 1975, when Fife region was created, and Fife Council became a unitary authority in 1996.

Fife is a council area with 373,990 residents in 2025, administered from Glenrothes. Its largest settlement is Dunfermline, which was awarded city status in 2022, and its largest town on the north-east coast is St Andrews. The University of St Andrews is the oldest of the ancient universities of Scotland, and the Old Course there is the world's oldest golf course. Fife has 4,961 listed buildings, among them Falkland Palace, Culross Palace, Dunfermline Abbey and St Andrews Cathedral.
fifth-crusade: Pope Innocent III, disappointed by the Fourth Crusade's failure to recover Jerusalem, issued the bull Quia maior in April 1213 calling all of Christendom to a new crusade, and the decree Ad Liberandam followed in 1215. Few Frenchmen took part in the expedition of 1217, unwilling to go in the company of Germans and Hungarians. Most of the men came from Germany and other lands of the Holy Roman Empire. Emperor Frederick II had taken the cross in 1215 but did not take part in person as promised.

The Ayyubid Sultanate in Egypt was ruled by al-Adil, Saladin's brother, who preferred truces and concessions to war and whose chief concern was Egypt itself. The crusaders therefore chose Egypt as their first target, viewing it as the key to Jerusalem.

Andrew II of Hungary, who had mortgaged his estates to pay for the expedition, reached Acre in autumn 1217. A campaign in Syria that year was inconclusive. The crusaders then turned to Egypt, and the first of their fleet reached Damietta on 27 May 1218. The siege began on 23 June. After a first assault failed, Oliver of Paderborn built a siege engine with a revolving ladder, and the day after the renewed assault began on 24 August 1218 the chain tower that guarded the river was taken.

The cardinal Pelagius Galvani arrived as papal legate and considered himself supreme commander. On 5 November 1219 the crusaders entered Damietta and found it abandoned, filled with the dead and with most of the remaining citizens ill. Al-Kamil offered peace terms that included the return of Jerusalem, but Pelagius rebuked the sultan's envoys, and in July 1221 the army marched south towards Cairo. Defeated at the battle of Mansurah, it was forced to surrender.

The terms of surrender required the crusaders to leave Damietta and Egypt altogether and accepted an eight-year truce. The Crusade ended with nothing gained for the West and much loss of life, resources and reputations. Many had opposed the treaty, bitter that operations had begun before the emperor's forces arrived. John of Brienne was censured for leaving Damietta around Easter 1220 to press his claim to Cilicia, and Pelagius was accused of ineffectual leadership and of rejecting the sultan's offer. The sharpest criticism fell on Frederick II, whose ambition lay in Europe rather than the Holy Land.
fiji: Fiji is an archipelago of 332 islands, of which 106 are inhabited, and 522 smaller islets, in the South Pacific about 2,000 km north-northeast of New Zealand. Only around 10% of its area of some 194,000 square kilometres is land. The two largest islands, Viti Levu and Vanua Levu, account for about three-quarters of the land area. The islands are mountainous, with peaks up to 1,324 metres, and covered with thick tropical forest. Most were formed by volcanic activity beginning around 150 million years ago. The 180° meridian runs through Taveuni, but the International Date Line is bent so that the whole group keeps one time.

Pottery shows that Austronesian peoples had settled Fiji by at least 3500 to 1000 BCE, with Melanesians following about a thousand years later. It is believed that either the Lapita people or the ancestors of the Polynesians settled first, though not much is known of what became of them. Archaeological evidence shows settlement on Moturiki Island from at least 600 BCE and possibly 900 BCE, and some migrants moved on to Samoa, Tonga and even Hawai'i. Trade with neighbouring archipelagos began long before European contact. In the 10th century the Tu'i Tonga Empire was established in Tonga and Fiji came within its sphere of influence, bringing Polynesian customs and language; that empire began to decline in the 13th century.

Europeans first visited in the 17th century. The name Fiji comes from the Tongan pronunciation, Fisi, of the Fijian name Viti, and was first promulgated by Captain James Cook; accounts written until the late 19th century spelled it Feejee. After a brief period as an independent kingdom, the British established the Colony of Fiji in 1874. It was a Crown colony until it gained independence in 1970 as the Dominion of Fiji. After a series of coups, the military government declared a republic in 1987.

Fiji is a parliamentary republic with its capital at Suva on Viti Levu, home to nearly three-quarters of the population. About 54.3% of the people are native Fijians, who are Melanesians with Polynesian ancestry in many cases, and 38.1% are Indo-Fijians, descendants of Indian contract labourers brought by the British in the 19th century. Rotuma, with a culture closer to Tonga and Samoa, has a special administrative status. Rugby sevens is the national sport.
filippo-brunelleschi: Brunelleschi was born in Florence in 1377, the son of Brunellesco di Lippo Lapi, a notary and civil servant, and Giuliana Spini. He received a literary and mathematical education, but being artistically inclined he was apprenticed at 15 as a goldsmith and sculptor in cast bronze, and in December 1398 he became a master.

In 1401 he was one of seven competitors for the second pair of bronze doors of the Florence Baptistery, each making a panel of the Sacrifice of Isaac. The jury could not choose between his panel and that of Lorenzo Ghiberti and proposed that the two collaborate. Brunelleschi refused to give up total control and preferred that the work go to Ghiberti. He later gave up sculpture for architecture and optics.

His first architectural commission was the Ospedale degli Innocenti, a foundling hospital begun in 1419 and opened on 25 January 1445, whose loggia drew clearly on classical forms and became a model across Europe. He also designed the Old Sacristy and the nave of the Basilica of San Lorenzo for the Medici family.

In 1418 he won the competition to build the dome of Florence Cathedral, helped by a brick model made by his friend Donatello. His later works included the Pazzi Chapel, the Basilica of Santo Spirito and Santa Maria degli Angeli, an octagonal church whose funds the government seized in 1437 for a war against Lucca.

The dome was built from 1420 to 1436 with two shells, one within the other, and more than four million bricks. Brunelleschi left no plans of it, and he invented a new hoisting machine and chains of wood and sandstone that act as tension rings. His early biographer Antonio Manetti says that between 1415 and 1420 he made perspective paintings of the Baptistery and the Palazzo Vecchio, and he is credited as the first to describe a precise system of linear perspective. In 1421 he received what is thought to be one of the first modern patents, for a boat to carry goods on the Arno. He died on 15 April 1446 and was buried in the crypt of the cathedral.
finistere: Finistère lies in the extreme west of Brittany. Its prefecture is Quimper, and its largest city is Brest. Other large towns include Concarneau, Morlaix, Carhaix, Quimperlé and Douarnenez, and the department includes the island of Ushant, called Eusa in Breton and Ouessant in French. It is the westernmost department of metropolitan France and has a claim to being the most coastal: 117 of its 277 communes lie on the coast, and its coastline of about 1,250 km makes up almost a quarter of that of Brittany.

The abers, rugged fjord-like inlets, are a notable feature of the north coast. The Pointe de Corsen, at the north-western tip of the department, is the westernmost point of continental France. About 40 kilometres to the south lies the rugged and isolated headland of the Pointe du Raz.

The present department consists of the historical region of Léon and parts of Cornouaille and Trégor, all of them parts of Brittany before the Revolution. Its name comes from the Latin Finis Terræ, meaning the end of the earth. The Breton name, Penn ar Bed, means head or end of the world and resembles the Cornish name of Land's End, Pedn an Wlas. It should not be confused with Fisterra in Galicia, Spain, which has the same origin.

Agriculture, fisheries and food processing occupy an important place in the economy. A military presence, including the Île Longue submarine base and the naval air base at Lanvéoc-Poulmic, together with related industries, employs a significant part of the population. The port of Roscoff has ferry links with Ireland and Great Britain.

Finistère is the area where Breton survives most strongly as a spoken language, and its Breton-speaking schools are called Diwan, Divyezh and Dihun. The Festival de Cornouaille in Quimper celebrates Breton music and traditions. The sculptor Roland Doré made many of the calvaries that stand in the department.
finland: Finland lies approximately between latitudes 60° and 70° N, and only Reykjavík lies further north among world capitals than Helsinki. Its land is predominantly covered by boreal forest, and it has about 168,000 lakes and 179,000 islands; the largest lake, Saimaa, is the fourth largest in Europe. Much of the landscape is a result of the Ice Age, and the terrain is rising by about 1 centimetre a year around the Gulf of Bothnia because of post-glacial rebound, so that the surface area of the country expands by about 7 square kilometres annually. Halti, at 1,324 metres, is the highest point.

The area was settled around 8500 BCE towards the end of the last glacial period, by hunter-gatherers using stone tools. The first pottery appeared in 5200 BCE with the Comb Ceramic culture, and the Corded Ware culture arrived in the south of coastal Finland between 3000 and 2500 BCE and may have coincided with the start of agriculture. In the Iron Age, Finland Proper was the most densely populated area, and main exports were furs, slaves, castoreum and falcons to European courts. At the end of the ninth century, local artefacts had more common features than ever before, which has been interpreted as expressing a common Finnish identity.

From the middle of the 13th century Finland became part of Sweden during the Northern Crusades. In 1809, as a result of the Finnish War, it was captured from Sweden and became an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire, and an independence movement gradually developed. Finland declared its independence after the Russian Revolution of 1917, and a civil war the following year ended in victory for the anticommunist Whites. During World War II Finland fought the Soviet Union in the Winter War and the Continuation War and Nazi Germany in the Lapland War, losing parts of its territory but retaining its independence and democracy.

Finland has a population of 5.7 million, and Helsinki is the capital and largest city. The official languages are Finnish and Swedish, the mother tongues of 83.5 percent and 5.0 percent of the population. It became the first country in Europe to grant universal suffrage in 1906. A new constitution enacted in 2000 made the presidency primarily a ceremonial office, and Finland is now considered a parliamentary republic. It joined the European Union in 1995 and the Eurozone in 1999, and NATO in 2023. National minorities include the Sámi, Roma, Jews and Tatars.
finnish-civil-war: Finland had been a grand duchy of the Russian Empire since 1809. Its population grew from 860,000 in 1810 to 3,130,000 in 1917, industry and a labour movement developed, and tension rose over the autocratic rule of the tsar and the undemocratic system of estates inherited from Swedish rule. The main cause of the war was the crisis of the First World War. After the February Revolution of 1917 the Russian Provisional Government restored Finland's autonomy, and after the October Revolution both conservatives and socialists came to support independence, though they disagreed about who should lead the nation.

The final escalation began in early January 1918, when each action by one side drew a counteraction from the other. The Red Guards, led by a section of the Social Democratic Party, held the south, including nearly all the major towns and industrial centres. The Whites, led by General Mannerheim and built around the Jägers trained in Germany and volunteer Civil Guards, held the agrarian centre and north. The Reds' general offensive in February failed.

Mannerheim chose to strike first at Tampere, the main industrial town of the south-west, which held nearly 15,000 heavily armed Red Guards. His assault began on 16 March, and the Whites besieged the town. After German troops landed in April, the Reds' leaders withdrew from Helsinki to Viipuri and then to Petrograd. Thousands of Reds tried to flee to Russia, but most were encircled, and those in the Lahti area surrendered on 1 and 2 May. The war ended on 15 May with the capture of Fort Ino. Both sides carried out executions, known as the White Terror and the Red Terror.

The Whites and German troops captured around 80,000 Red prisoners, including 5,000 women and 1,500 children, and held them in camps such as Suomenlinna and Hämeenlinna. Most of the deaths in the war occurred outside the battlefields, in the camps and the terror. Treason courts examined 76,000 cases and convicted 68,000 Reds, and of 555 death sentences 113 were carried out. About 15,000 children were left orphaned, and many moderate Finns came to think of themselves as citizens of two nations.

A plan for a German-led Finnish monarchy collapsed with Germany's surrender in November 1918, and Finland became an independent republic, confirmed by the Constitution Act of 17 July 1919. The war has several names, among them Civil War, Class War, War of Independence and Red Rebellion, each tied to a political viewpoint.
finnish-war: After concluding the Treaty of Tilsit with Napoleon in 1807, Emperor Alexander I of Russia wrote on 24 September 1807 to King Gustav IV Adolf of Sweden that peace between them depended on Sweden accepting the treaty's limits, which in practice meant cutting off trade with Britain. The king, who viewed Napoleon as the Antichrist, secured an alliance with Britain on 8 February 1808. In Saint Petersburg his stubbornness was seen as a convenient pretext for occupying Finland. Swedish plans assumed that war in winter was impossible, while Russian planners chose a winter offensive, when frozen seas would isolate Finland.

On 21 February 1808, 24,000 Russian troops under Friedrich Wilhelm von Buxhoeveden crossed the border and took Loviisa; war was not declared until April. Helsinki fell on 2 March and Turku on 21 March, as the Swedish army under General Wilhelm Mauritz Klingspor withdrew northwards. Sveaborg, with a garrison of 6,000 men and over 700 cannons, surrendered on 6 May 1808 after prolonged negotiations, its commander Admiral Carl Olof Cronstedt believing resistance futile, and the Russians gained most of the Swedish archipelago fleet intact. Swedish counter-attacks at Siikajoki and Revolax halted the offensive for a time, and Finns rose in guerrilla fighting.

Reinforced to 55,000 men against an estimated 36,000, the Russians attacked again in August, and Count Nikolay Kamensky won the most important victory at Oravais on 14 September. By November 1808 Russian forces had overrun all of Finland, and the Convention of Olkijoki of 19 November obliged the Swedish army to leave. In March 1809 Russian columns crossed the frozen Gulf of Bothnia, occupying the Åland Islands and entering Umeå on 24 March. King Gustav IV, blamed for the loss of Finland, was dethroned by a coup in Stockholm on 13 March, and his uncle became Charles XIII of Sweden.

By the Treaty of Fredrikshamn of 17 September 1809 Sweden also gave up its domains east of the Torne river. The Grand Duchy of Finland kept the Gustavian constitution of 1772 with only slight modifications until 1919, and in 1812 Russia attached to it the areas it had gained from Sweden in the 18th century, known as Old Finland. In Sweden the war was followed by a new constitution and, in 1818, by the establishment of the House of Bernadotte. Two studies of 2015 by the political scientists Jan Teorell and Bo Rothstein argue that the defeat moved Swedish elites to reform the bureaucracy.
first-balkan-war: Serbia and Montenegro had secured their independence by 1867, confirmed by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878. Between 1878 and 1912 Greece, Bulgaria and Serbia sponsored insurgent groups in Ottoman Macedonia that fought the government and each other in the Macedonian Struggle. The Young Turk Revolution of July 1908 revived the question of whether Ottoman rule could last. By 1912 the Ottoman Empire, known as the sick man of Europe, was still fighting Italy in Libya and the Dodecanese, and peace came only on 15 October 1912, days after the Balkan war began. Bulgaria was the strongest of the four states of the Balkan League, with some 600,000 men mobilised, while Greece, thought the weakest, was the only member with a meaningful navy.

Montenegro declared war on 8 October 1912. In Thrace the Ottoman command had wrongly expected the main Bulgarian army to go to Macedonia, and the Bulgarians defeated the Ottoman East Army on the Edirne-Kırklareli line. In Macedonia the Greek Army of Thessaly seized Thessaloniki, and the Serbs and Bulgarians won great victories at Kirkkilise, Lüleburgaz, Kumanovo and Monastir. The Greek fleet took Lemnos and kept the Ottoman fleet in the Dardanelles.

Adrianople fell on 11 March 1913 after a two-week bombardment and a final assault by the Bulgarian Second Army and two Serbian divisions. Ottoman casualties in the whole Adrianople campaign reached 23,000 dead, and the Ottoman command lost all hope of regaining the initiative. On 23 April 1913 the garrison of Shkodër surrendered, starved, to the Montenegrins. The Ottoman government had declared war with its mobilisation only partly complete, and 580,000 Ottoman soldiers in the Balkans faced 912,000 of the League.

The Treaty of London ended the war on 30 May 1913. All Ottoman territory west of the Enez-Kıyıköy line passed to the Balkan League, and Albania was declared independent. The Ottomans lost 83 per cent of their European territories and 69 per cent of their European population. Many civilians were killed or driven from their homes, and both sides committed war crimes. Serbia and Greece, which occupied most of the territory meant for Albania, withdrew only reluctantly. Greece and Serbia signed a military alliance against Bulgaria on 1 May 1913, and Bulgaria, disputing the division of Macedonia, attacked its former allies on 16 June 1913, beginning the Second Balkan War.
first-battle-of-the-marne: Germany declared war on France on 3 August 1914. Under the Schlieffen Plan, as revised by Helmuth von Moltke, the German armies were to sweep through Belgium and into France, capture Paris and destroy the French army within about six weeks, so that Germany could then turn on Russia. August brought bloody battles that the Germans mostly won, and the French and British retreated southward for more than 250 km in what is called the Great Retreat. The French commander, Joseph Joffre, kept his army in order and reinforced it with troops from his eastern flank and with reserve units.

By early September the German armies were exhausted and had outrun their supplies. Kluck's 1st Army turned south-east and crossed the Marne on 3 September, unaware that a new French army, the 6th, was guarding Paris to his west. Joseph Gallieni, the military governor of Paris, saw that the German right flank was vulnerable, and on 4 September Joffre ordered a counter-offensive. The battle was fought from 5 to 12 September along a front of 230 km between Paris and Verdun.

On 5 September part of the French 6th Army met a German reserve corps near the Ourcq river, which held it for 24 hours and warned Kluck. He turned his army west to face the threat, which opened a gap of 50 km between his army and Bülow's 2nd Army. French aerial reconnaissance found the gap, and the French 5th Army and the British force advanced into it. By 9 September the German 1st and 2nd Armies were at risk of encirclement and were ordered to retreat to the Aisne, where the Germans dug in on the heights.

The retreat ended the Schlieffen Plan. Moltke is said to have told Kaiser Wilhelm II that Germany had lost the war, though whether he did is not known; on 14 September he was replaced by Erich von Falkenhayn, officially because of ill health.

Both sides then tried to outflank each other's northern wings in the Race to the Sea, which ended at the First Battle of Ypres and led to a stalemate of trench warfare on the Western Front that lasted four years. No exact casualty counts exist, since the battle is hard to separate from others in August and September. The historian Holger Herwig called it the most important land battle of the 20th century, and in French tradition it is the Miracle on the Marne.
first-bulgarian-empire: The Bulgars were Turkic semi-nomadic warrior tribes of the Pontic–Caspian steppe and the Volga region. The Bulgars of Asparuh crossed the Danube into Scythia Minor, a nominal Byzantine province, in the 670s. In 680 the Byzantine Emperor Constantine IV led a large army and fleet against them but suffered a disastrous defeat at Onglos, in or near the Danube Delta. The Bulgars crossed the Balkan Mountains into Thrace, and in 681 the Byzantines signed a treaty acknowledging Bulgaria as an independent state, ceding the lands north of the Balkan Mountains and agreeing to pay an annual tribute. It was the first state the Byzantine Empire recognised in the Balkans.

After Khan Sevar died in 753 the Dulo clan died out, and in fifteen years seven khans reigned and all were murdered. Under Krum (r. 803–814) Bulgaria doubled in size and destroyed the Avar Khaganate. Boris I decided by 863 to accept Christianity, and in 866 he executed 52 leading nobles after an anti-Christian rebellion. The Council of Preslav in 893 made Old Bulgarian the language of state and church.

Under Simeon I (r. 893–927) the empire reached its largest extent. He defeated the Byzantines at Boulgarophygon in 896 and annihilated their army at Anchialus in 917, and the Bulgarians besieged Constantinople in 923 and 924 without success. From 968 the Kievan prince Sviatoslav I invaded, and the Byzantine emperor John I Tzimiskes forced him out in 971. In 1014 Basil II crushed the Bulgarians at the Battle of Kleidion and ordered 15,000 prisoners blinded, sparing every hundredth man one eye to guide the rest home. By 1018 the last strongholds had surrendered.

The Glagolitic alphabet, created by Cyril and Methodius, reached Bulgaria with their disciples in 886, and the Early Cyrillic alphabet was invented in the capital Preslav. Old Church Slavonic literature flourished under Simeon I and spread north, becoming the lingua franca of much of Eastern Europe. The fully independent Bulgarian Patriarchate was recognised in 927. The Madara Rider, a relief carved in a cliff, was listed by UNESCO in 1979. The Second Bulgarian Empire followed in 1185.
first-council-of-nicaea: The council grew out of a dispute among the clergy of Alexandria about the nature of Jesus and his relation to God the Father, which scholars date between 318 and 322. Archbishop Alexander taught that the Son was eternally generated from the Father, while the presbyter Arius held that the Father alone was eternal and that the Son was created and subordinate. A local council of bishops from Egypt and Libya sided with Alexander, and Arius was excommunicated and exiled, then sought support elsewhere in the east. Arius' teaching is known partly from his few surviving writings but chiefly from his opponents.

In 324 Constantine defeated Licinius and became sole ruler of the empire. He learned of the quarrel, probably from Eusebius of Nicomedia, and urged both men to reconcile. When that failed he summoned the bishops to Nicaea and paid the expenses, including their travel, from the imperial treasury.

The council met from May until the end of July 325. Reports of attendance range from 250 to 300, the traditional figure of 318 being given by Athanasius, while lists of signatories hold 200 to 220 names. Almost all came from the eastern half of the empire. Hosius of Corduba may have presided, and two presbyters represented Pope Sylvester I. Constantine opened it with a speech in Latin, though most present spoke Greek. No acts of the council survive, so its work is known from later accounts, such as those of Eusebius of Caesarea and Athanasius.

The council settled the question of the divine nature of the Son and drew up the first part of the Nicene Creed. It ordered uniform observance of the date of Easter, ending reliance on the Jewish community to identify the lunar month of Nisan. It dealt with the Melitian schism in Egypt and issued twenty canons on church discipline.

Nicaea was the first attempt to gather a general council representing the church in every part of the empire, and it set a precedent for later councils to adopt creeds and canons. It did not end the conflict. Arians and Melitians soon regained nearly all the rights they had lost, and Arianism remained a subject of debate for the rest of the fourth century. Constantine's son Constantius II and Valens, who ruled the east after him, both favoured Arianism.

Popular accounts credit the council with things it did not do. There is no record of any discussion of the biblical canon, and the story that books were chosen by whether they fell from an altar was popularised by Voltaire from an account of 887. Constantine did not force the homoousian view on the bishops, and was baptised some eleven or twelve years later.
first-crusade: The expedition began with a request for help. In March 1095 the Byzantine emperor Alexios I Komnenos sent envoys to the Council of Piacenza to ask Pope Urban II for military support against the advancing Seljuk Turks. Urban responded favourably, perhaps hoping to heal the East-West Schism of forty years earlier. Later that year, at the Council of Clermont, he urged Christians to undertake an armed pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Adhemar of Le Puy was the first to take the cross. The response was far greater than the pope or Alexios expected, and most of those who answered were poor people with little fighting skill rather than knights.

Thousands of mostly poor Christians, led by the French priest Peter the Hermit, set out first. This People's Crusade passed through Germany, where it took part in anti-Jewish violence, including the Rhineland massacres, and was destroyed by a Turkish ambush led by Kilij Arslan I at the Battle of Civetot in October 1096. The main armies left in August 1096 under princes including Raymond IV of Toulouse, Godfrey of Bouillon and his brother Baldwin of Boulogne, Bohemond of Taranto and Robert Curthose of Normandy, and gathered at Constantinople by April 1097. Estimates of their numbers run to as many as 100,000 with non-combatants.

In Anatolia the crusaders took Nicaea in June 1097 and defeated Kilij Arslan at the Battle of Dorylaeum on 1 July. The siege of Antioch began on 20 October 1097 and the city was captured in June 1098. The crusaders reached Jerusalem, then held by the Fatimids, in June 1099, with perhaps only 12,000 men left, and took it by assault on 15 July. Crusader eyewitnesses leave little doubt that there was great slaughter in the city, though some historians think later sources exaggerated its scale.

A council in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre made Godfrey of Bouillon leader of Jerusalem after Raymond of Toulouse refused the crown. In August 1099 the crusaders defeated a Fatimid force at the Battle of Ascalon, which ended the expedition, and most of them then went home. Four states were established: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the County of Edessa, the Principality of Antioch and the County of Tripoli. When Godfrey died a year later, Baldwin became the first Latin king of Jerusalem.

Latin Christendom regarded the success as the work of divine providence. This form of religious warfare remained popular for centuries, and the First Crusade became one of the most written-about events of the medieval period.
first-french-empire: The empire grew out of the Consulate. On 9 November 1799 troops led by Napoleon Bonaparte seized control in a coup planned with Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès, and Bonaparte outmaneuvered Sieyès to become First Consul. He was made First Consul for life in 1802, after a plebiscite that gave 3,653,600 votes in favour and 8,272 against. On 18 May 1804 the Senate gave him the title Emperor of the French, and on 2 December 1804 he was crowned in Notre-Dame de Paris by Pope Pius VII. The state nevertheless continued to be formally called the French Republic until October 1808.

In the War of the Third Coalition the French army won a string of victories over Austrian and Russian forces, most notably at Austerlitz in 1805. Napoleon created the Confederation of the Rhine, and on 6 August 1806 the Habsburgs abdicated the title of Holy Roman Emperor. He destroyed the Prussian armies at Jena and Auerstedt, and the Treaties of Tilsit removed about half of Prussia's territory. To build satellite states he installed relatives as rulers, among them his brother Joseph Bonaparte at Naples, later King of Spain.

The Continental System, a blockade against Britain, strained the alliance with Russia, and the seizure of the Spanish throne provoked a guerrilla war across the Iberian Peninsula. Austria was defeated at Wagram in 1809 and ceded the Illyrian Provinces. In 1812 Napoleon invaded Russia and lost nearly his whole army. After defeat at Leipzig in 1813, Paris capitulated on 30 March 1814, and Napoleon abdicated at Fontainebleau on 11 April. He returned from Elba and revived the empire in the Hundred Days of 1815, but was defeated at Waterloo and exiled to Saint Helena, where he died in 1821.

At its height in 1812 the empire had 130 departments and a population of over 44 million, and ruled some 90 million subjects across Europe. The Napoleonic Code increased legal equality, established jury systems and legalised divorce, while seigneurial dues and justice were abolished, as were aristocratic privileges everywhere except Poland. Napoleon preserved many social gains of the Revolution while suppressing political liberty: he rejected electoral democracy and freedom of the press, though his rule included public education and the emancipation of the Jews.
first-indochina-war: Vietnam was absorbed into French Indochina in stages between 1858 and 1887, and Vietnamese nationalism grew until World War II broke French control. After the Japanese surrender in August 1945, Emperor Bảo Đại abdicated on 25 August and handed power to the Viet Minh, and on 2 September Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam. Allied commanders had placed the south under British Admiral Mountbatten, and on 23 September 1945 French forces overthrew the Viet Minh administration in Saigon. A preliminary accord of March 1946 recognised the Democratic Republic as a free state within a French Union, but talks in Paris broke down over independence and the reunification of Cochinchina.

Full war broke out between French and Viet Minh forces in December 1946. In 1947 Ho Chi Minh and General Võ Nguyên Giáp withdrew into the mountainous Việt Bắc, while the French took the main towns by March. In 1949 France united Cochinchina, Annam and Tonkin as the State of Vietnam within the French Union under Bảo Đại. About 325,000 of the 500,000 French troops were Indochinese, and soldiers came from across the French colonial empire, since governments forbade sending metropolitan recruits.

The Chinese Communist victory of 1949 changed the war. In 1950 China and the Soviet Union recognised the Democratic Republic, while the United States recognised the State of Vietnam and began to aid France. Giáp reorganised his forces into five infantry divisions, and the conflict came to resemble a conventional war. The Battle of Dien Bien Phu in 1954, the last major battle, ended in a decisive French defeat.

The Geneva Conference opened in May 1954, and the accords were signed on 21 July. They set a ceasefire, which took effect on 11 August, and divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel, with a free election planned for 1956 to reunify the country. France undertook to respect the independence of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia.

Estimates put military deaths at 400,000 to 842,707 and civilian deaths at 125,000 to 400,000. Both sides committed war crimes. French troops killed over 200 women and children in the Mỹ Trạch massacre of 29 November 1947, and one historian estimates that the Viet Minh assassinated 100,000 to 150,000 civilians. In France leftists called it the dirty war. The Algerian War began on 1 November 1954, and an Algerian leader praised the victory at Dien Bien Phu as an incentive to insurrection.
first-intermediate-period: The First Intermediate Period spanned about 125 years, from c. 2181 to c. 2055 BCE, after the end of the Old Kingdom. It comprises the Seventh Dynasty, mostly considered spurious by Egyptologists, the Eighth, Ninth and Tenth, and part of the Eleventh. Several causes for the Old Kingdom's fall are given, some only hypothetical. One is the very long reign of Pepi II, the last major pharaoh of the Sixth Dynasty, who outlived many heirs and so created problems of succession. Another was the rise of provincial nomarchs, whose posts had become hereditary and who built tombs in their own domains, raised armies and fought their neighbours. A third is low Nile floods in a drier climate, bringing famine, but there is no consensus.

Little is known of the Seventh and Eighth Dynasties at Memphis. Manetho describes 70 kings who ruled for 70 days, almost certainly an exaggeration for disorganised kingship. The Ninth and Tenth Dynasties arose at Heracleopolis, each with nineteen listed rulers, while in the south warlords dominated. Ankhtifi, whose tomb was found in 1928 at Mo'alla, 30 kilometres south of Luxor, ruled the nomes of Hierakonpolis and Edfu but failed to take the Theban nome. His tomb autobiography claims he rescued Egypt from famine: "I gave bread to the hungry and did not allow anyone to die".

The Theban kings descended from Intef, nomarch of Thebes. Intef II began the assault on the north, particularly at Abydos, and Intef III completed its conquest and moved into Middle Egypt. Mentuhotep II then defeated the Heracleopolitan kings and reunified the country, beginning the Middle Kingdom.

The Egyptologists Georg Steindorff and Henri Frankfort coined the term in 1926, and the period is often called a dark age. Ludwig David Morenz has argued it was not one and proposed the name Period of Regions. Very little monumental evidence survives. The Theban kings developed a distinctive Pre-Unification Theban Style of relief and built saff tombs at El-Tarif. The Ipuwer Papyrus, which modern scholarship does not date to the period but which may refer to it, records impoverishment in Egypt.
first-jewish-roman-war: Judaea fell to the Roman Republic in 63 BCE, when Pompey intervened in a succession war between the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobolus. He entered the Temple's Holy of Holies, which only the High Priest was permitted to do, abolished the Jewish monarchy and made Hyrcanus High Priest alone. Judaea later became a province ruled directly by governors, marked by oppression, social divisions and rising religious and ethnic tension. Most scholars see the revolt as an expression of Jewish nationalism, partly inspired by the successful Maccabean revolt against the Seleucids. In May 66 violence broke out in Caesarea after a Greek sacrificed birds at the entrance of a synagogue, and Governor Gessius Florus then looted the Temple treasury and massacred residents of Jerusalem.

Rebels killed the Roman garrison in Jerusalem. Cestius Gallus, the governor of Syria, invaded but was defeated at Bethoron, and a provisional government led by the former High Priest Ananus ben Ananus appointed Josephus commander of Galilee. In 67 Vespasian invaded Galilee and captured Yodfat, Tarichaea and Gamla. Refugees and rebels crowded into Jerusalem, where a three-way factional war developed between Eleazar ben Simon, John of Gischala and Simon bar Giora. Nero died in 68, and when the legions proclaimed Vespasian emperor he left for Rome.

His son Titus returned in the winter of 69 and 70 with more than 48,000 troops and began the siege of Jerusalem in the spring of 70, when the city was swollen with Passover pilgrims. Jerusalem fell in the summer of 70, and the Romans destroyed the Temple and razed the city. Titus and Vespasian held a triumph in Rome in 71. Roman forces under Sextus Lucilius Bassus took Herodium and Machaerus, and the last stronghold, Masada, fell in 73 or 74.

Many Jews died in battles, sieges and famine, were displaced or were sold into slavery. Josephus claimed that 1.1 million died in Jerusalem, a figure widely considered exaggerated. The aristocracy, including the High Priesthood, collapsed, as did the Sanhedrin. Legio X Fretensis garrisoned Jerusalem for nearly two centuries, and the Flavian dynasty commemorated the victory in monuments and coinage and imposed a punitive tax on all Jews.

The destruction of the Second Temple ended sacrifices and the High Priesthood, and the Sadducees and Essenes disappeared from the record. The Pharisees, who had largely opposed the revolt, survived, and the rabbinic sages emerged as leaders and established a centre at Yavneh. The revolt is seen as one stage in the gradual separation of Christianity from Judaism. Two further Jewish revolts against Rome followed in the second century, among them the Bar Kokhba Revolt of 132 to 136. The main source for the war is Josephus, who led the defence of Galilee and was later held captive and then received Roman citizenship.
first-nagorno-karabakh-war: Armenians and Azerbaijanis fought over Karabakh as the Russian Empire dissolved in 1917 and 1918, and in April 1920 the Soviet Eleventh Army invaded the Caucasus. On 4 July 1921 the Caucasus Bureau voted 4 to 3 to assign Nagorno-Karabakh to the Armenian Soviet republic, but a day later it reversed the decision and left the region within the Azerbaijan SSR. Armenian discontent was voiced after Stalin's death: about 2,500 Karabakh Armenians signed a petition in 1963 asking for transfer to Armenia or Russia, and there were large demonstrations in Yerevan in 1965 and 1977.

On 20 February 1988 the parliament of the Nagorno-Karabakh Autonomous Oblast voted to unite the region with Armenia. Inter-ethnic clashes followed and grew more violent as the Soviet Union disintegrated, including the pogroms at Sumgait in 1988 and Baku in 1990 against Armenians and the Gugark pogrom in 1988 against Azerbaijanis.

In late 1991 both sides sought weapons from the Soviet military stores. Azerbaijan had the early advantage, with five divisions and five air bases against Armenia's three divisions and no airfields. Azerbaijani forces blockaded Stepanakert, the capital of Nagorno-Karabakh, through the winter of 1991 and 1992 and shelled it, and Armenian volunteers formed detachments of about forty men.
