Full-scale fighting began in early 1992, and the Khojaly Massacre of that year, confirmed by Human Rights Watch and Memorial, was among the atrocities attributed to the war.

In June 1992 Azerbaijani forces took back dozens of villages in the Shahumian region. In early 1993 Armenian forces overran northern Karabakh and captured seven Azerbaijani-majority districts outside the enclave. Russia shipped large quantities of arms to Armenia in 1993, and Turkey sided with Azerbaijan. The United Nations Security Council passed resolutions 874 and 884 in October and November 1993, recognising Nagorno-Karabakh as a region of Azerbaijan.

By the end Armenians held the enclave and surrounding territory, including the Lachin corridor linking it to Armenia. About 724,000 Azerbaijanis were expelled from Armenia, Nagorno-Karabakh and the surrounding territories, and 300,000 to 500,000 Armenians were displaced. Russia mediated a ceasefire agreed on 5 May 1994, which took effect on 12 May and was signed by the defence ministers of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the Republic of Artsakh.
Mediation by the OSCE Minsk Group from 1995 produced no peace treaty. Armenian forces held about 9 per cent of Azerbaijan's territory outside the enclave until a second war began in September 2020.
first-opium-war: Trade between China and Europe long favoured China, which sustained a trade surplus paid for in silver. The British realised they could reduce their deficit by selling opium produced in India, and sales of Indian opium to China began in 1781 and grew as the East India Company consolidated its control of India. By 1838 the British were selling roughly 1,400 long tons a year. Within the Chinese administration, some officials such as Xu Naiji argued for legalising and taxing opium, while others, later led by Lin Zexu, regarded the trade as a moral evil. The Daoguang Emperor rejected legalisation and in 1839 sent Lin Zexu to Guangzhou to halt the trade completely.

In March 1839 Lin forced British dealers to hand over 1,420 tonnes of opium, which he had destroyed in public on Humen Beach on 3 June. Tension rose after British sailors beat to death a villager, Lin Weixi, in July, and Charles Elliot refused to hand the accused over to Chinese authorities. Fighting began after the Qing blockade of foreign ships. The British government, urged by merchants who demanded compensation, sent an expedition that arrived in late June 1840. After the Second Battle of Chuenpi on 7 January 1841 the British occupied Hong Kong.

Henry Pottinger replaced Elliot as superintendent in August 1841 and moved operations north. British steamships such as the Nemesis could move against winds and tides, and naval guns out-ranged most Qing artillery. In 1842 the fleet advanced up the Yangtze and captured the emperor's tax barges, sharply reducing his revenue. It took Wusong and Baoshan and occupied the outskirts of Shanghai in June. The Treaty of Nanking was signed aboard HMS Cornwallis on 29 August 1842.

The treaty granted an indemnity and extraterritoriality to British subjects, opened five treaty ports and ceded Hong Kong Island in perpetuity. It was the first of the unequal treaties, and the Treaty of the Bogue recognised Britain as an equal of China. The United States and France concluded similar treaties in 1844. The unrest that followed formed the background of the Taiping Rebellion, and a Second Opium War was fought in 1856 to 1860.

The war was contested in Britain. William Ewart Gladstone called it a war unjust in its origin, and he feared the judgments of God on England for its iniquity towards China. Historians still debate whether it was avoidable. Some stress Britain's expanding trade, while others argue that Lord Palmerston's government went to war to uphold national honour. Twentieth-century nationalists in China consider 1839 the start of a century of humiliation.
first-punic-war: The Roman Republic had been expanding in southern Italy for a century and by 272 BCE had conquered the peninsula south of the River Arno. Carthage, with its capital in what is now Tunisia, dominated southern Spain, much of the North African coast, the Balearic Islands, Corsica, Sardinia and the western half of Sicily. Most of what is known of the war comes from Polybius, a Greek sent to Rome as a hostage in 167 BCE, whose Histories were written about a century after the war.

The war began in 264 BCE when the Romans gained a foothold at Messana in Sicily. Syracuse allied with them, and a large Carthaginian army sent to lift the siege of Akragas was heavily defeated in 262 BCE. Land fighting was mostly sieges and raids, so the Romans turned to the sea. In 260 BCE they built a fleet using a shipwrecked Carthaginian quinquereme as a model, and they introduced the corvus, a bridge with a spike that let legionaries board enemy ships instead of ramming them.

In 256 BCE the Romans sailed with 330 warships and won the Battle of Cape Ecnomus, possibly the largest naval battle in history by the number of combatants. Their invasion of North Africa at first went well, but a storm later destroyed most of the fleet sent home, with over 100,000 men lost. They rebuilt repeatedly and took Panormus. By 248 BCE Carthage held only Lilybaeum and Drepana, and Hamilcar Barca held out from Eryx with guerrilla tactics. In 243 BCE the Romans built a new fleet and blockaded the garrisons, and in 241 BCE they destroyed the Carthaginian relief fleet at the Battle of the Aegates Islands.

Carthage paid large reparations and Sicily became a Roman province. Both states were exhausted. Rome became the leading military power in the western Mediterranean, and building about 1,000 galleys laid the base for its maritime dominance for 600 years. Carthage's unpaid foreign troops rebelled, and the revolt was put down with great difficulty and savagery. In 237 BCE the Romans took Carthage's planned expedition to Sardinia as an act of war and made it cede Sardinia and Corsica and pay a further 1,200 talents. This resentment is considered a cause of the Second Punic War of 218 BCE.
first-sino-japanese-war: Korea was a Qing tributary state in the late 19th century, while Japan, transformed by the reforms that followed the Meiji Restoration of 1868, regarded it as a target of expansion. Japan opened Korea to trade by the treaty of 1876, and from 1879 Li Hongzhang directed China's Korea policy. After the Imo Incident of 1882 the Qing stationed troops in Seoul and sent advisers, and Yuan Shikai trained a new Korean military formation.

A reformist faction in Korea, the Enlightenment Party, looked to Japan, and in December 1884 it staged the Kapsin Coup with the help of the Japanese minister. In late April 1894 the Donghak Rebellion, the largest peasant rebellion in Korean history, broke out against oppressive taxation, and the Korean government asked for Qing help.

China sent between 2,465 and 2,800 troops in June, and Japan, which held that it had not been notified as the 1885 Convention of Tientsin required, landed a larger force at Incheon. Japanese troops seized the Korean king in Seoul on 23 July 1894 and set up a pro-Japanese government. On 25 July the Japanese Navy won the Battle of Pungdo and sank the transport Kowshing, which was carrying 1,200 Qing reinforcements. War was declared on 1 August.

After the Battle of Pyongyang on 15 September the Qing troops withdrew to Manchuria. The Beiyang Fleet was decisively defeated at the Battle of the Yalu River two days later. The Japanese Army invaded Manchuria and took Port Arthur on 21 November 1894, after which Japanese forces killed civilians in the Port Arthur Massacre, with unconfirmed estimates in the thousands. Weihaiwei fell on 12 February 1895 after a siege lasting 23 days. The Qing court began negotiations in early March, and Japanese forces occupied the Pescadores Islands later that month.

The Treaty of Shimonoseki was signed on 17 April 1895. China recognised Korea's total independence and ceded the Liaodong Peninsula, Taiwan and the Penghu Islands. It also paid a large indemnity. On 23 April Russia, Germany and France applied diplomatic pressure in the Triple Intervention, and Japan gave up the Liaodong Peninsula in exchange for a larger indemnity. Taiwan's inhabitants resisted the cession with a guerrilla campaign lasting nearly two years.

The war exposed the limits of the Qing effort to modernise its military and shifted regional dominance in East Asia from China to Japan. Historians link the defeat to the political upheavals led by Sun Yat-sen and Kang Youwei that ended in the 1911 Revolution. In Korea, the Japanese-sponsored Kabo Reforms of 1894 to 1896 abolished legal slavery and the privileges of the yangban class. Tension between Russia and Japan over Manchuria grew in the years that followed.
first-world-war: For much of the 19th century the major European powers kept a tenuous balance known as the Concert of Europe. Victory in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871 allowed Otto von Bismarck to consolidate a German Empire, and French policy then aimed to avenge the defeat. Germany and Austria-Hungary formed the Dual Alliance in 1879, which became the Triple Alliance when Italy joined in 1882.

On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to Emperor Franz Joseph I, visited Sarajevo. Six assassins of the Young Bosnia movement lined his route. A grenade injured two aides, but an hour later Gavrilo Princip shot and fatally wounded the Archduke and his wife Sophie.

Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on 28 July, and Russia mobilised in Serbia's defence. In early August Germany declared war on Russia and France, and the United Kingdom entered after Germany invaded Belgium. The German advance was halted in September, and the Western Front settled into a near-continuous line of trenches. Battles at Verdun, the Somme and Passchendaele failed to break the stalemate.

The Ottoman Empire joined the Central Powers in November 1914. The United States joined the Allies in April 1917 after Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare, and Soviet Russia made a separate peace in March 1918. The Allied Hundred Days Offensive from August 1918 collapsed the German front line, and the war ended with the Armistice of 11 November 1918.

Four dynasties fell: the Romanovs, the Hohenzollerns, the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. Poland, Finland, the Baltic states, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia were among the new states. Under the Treaty of Versailles, signed on 28 June 1919, Germany lost territory, was disarmed and had to pay large reparations.

Estimates put the deaths at 15 to 22 million and about 23 million wounded military personnel. Of 60 million European military personnel mobilised, an estimated 8 million were killed. The war also drew women into industry in unprecedented numbers, which aided the struggle for women's voting rights.
firth-of-forth: The Firth of Forth is a bay and inlet of the North Sea that separates Fife to the north from Lothian to the south. Further inland it becomes the estuary of the River Forth and several other rivers. It was formed as a fjord by the Forth Glacier in the last glacial period, which scoured out the existing Forth Valley, and over time natural processes turned most of it into a wide bay with gently sloping banks. Its name combines the Scots word firth, a cognate of fjord, with Forth, from a Proto-Celtic word meaning slow running. It was Bodotria in Roman times, Myrkvifiörd in the Norse sagas and, in an early Welsh name, the sea of Iudeu.

The Romans reportedly made a bridge of around 900 boats, probably at South Queensferry. In the 10th century the river was regarded as the boundary of Scotia and was sometimes called the Scots Water. Culross, on the Fife shore, was established in the 6th century and was the birthplace of Saint Kentigern. The inner firth, between the Kincardine and Forth bridges, has lost about half of its former intertidal area to land reclamation, partly for farming but mainly for industry.

The firth was the site of heavy industry and docks, among them Grangemouth, Leith, Methil, Inverkeithing and the naval dockyard at Rosyth. It is crossed by bridges at two places. The Forth Bridge, a railway bridge on the Edinburgh to Aberdeen line, was begun in 1882 and opened on 4 March 1890. The Kincardine Bridge opened in October 1936 and the Forth Road Bridge on 4 September 1964. From 1964 to 1982 a tunnel dug by coal miners ran under the firth, linking the Kinneil colliery on the south side with the Valleyfield colliery on the north. The Clackmannanshire Bridge was completed in November 2008, and the Queensferry Crossing, begun in 2011, was formally opened on 4 September 2017.

The firth is a Site of Special Scientific Interest. The Firth of Forth Islands Special Protection Area holds more than 90,000 breeding seabirds every year, and there is a bird observatory on the Isle of May. Its islands include Bass Rock, Inchcolm, Inchkeith and the Isle of May. The European oyster, fished to extinction here by the 1900s, has been reintroduced in the 21st century. Edinburgh, Leith and Kirkcaldy are among the many towns on its shores.
five-dynasties-and-ten-kingdoms-period: After the An Lushan Rebellion of 755 to 763, large regional administrations called circuit commissions were laid over the old prefectures, and they became the boundaries of the later southern regimes. By the early 10th century the Tang government had given the jiedushi, the regional military governors, such powers that they were de facto independent, with hereditary succession and armies that rivalled the palace armies. Many states were independent long before 907, and the key event was their recognition as sovereign by foreign powers.

Five dynastic states followed one another in the Central Plain: Later Liang, Later Tang, Later Jin, Later Han and Later Zhou. The term Five Dynasties was coined by Song historians and reflects the view that the successive regimes at Kaifeng held the Mandate of Heaven. Zhu Wen founded the first after forcing the last Tang emperor to abdicate in his favour, and the rest and the Song itself emerged from a military organisation led by Shatuo Turks. The Later Zhou under Chai Rong conquered much of Southern Tang between 956 and 958. In 960 Zhao Kuangyin staged a coup and founded the Northern Song, the official end of the Five Dynasties.

In the south more than a dozen states existed at once, of which ten are traditionally called the Ten Kingdoms. They included Wuyue, Min, Southern Han, Former Shu, Later Shu, Jingnan, Southern Tang and Northern Han. Their founders were mostly men of low social status who rose through military ability. The south was more stable than the north, and its kingdoms promoted trade, land reclamation and infrastructure. Commerce grew so fast that bank drafts called flying money partly met a shortage of metal currency.

The Song dynasty subdued the remaining southern states. It swept away Jingnan in 963, Later Shu in 965, Southern Han in 971 and Southern Tang in 975, and Wuyue gave up its land in 978. The last regime, Northern Han, held out until the Song conquered it in 979. The Liao dynasty remained in the north.

Chronicles written from the northern viewpoint, the Old History and the New History, organised the period around the Five Dynasties and presented the Ten Kingdoms as illegitimate. The period turned away from the international mood of the Tang and was a transition towards the national culture of the Song, and the Song adopted a distinctively southern Chinese cultural outlook. The tradition that it was a time of judicial abuse reflects both real problems and the bias of Confucian historians.
flag-of-denmark: The white-on-red cross emblem dates from the age of the Crusades. The earliest known undisputed colour rendering of the Dannebrog is in the Gelre Armorial, of about 1340 to 1370, which shows such a banner beside the arms of the king of Denmark. Valdemar IV displayed a cross in his arms on a seal of 1356. Why the kings began to display it is unknown. Caspar Paludan-Müller suggested a banner sent by the pope during the Livonian Crusade, and Adolf Ditlev Jørgensen the banner of the Knights Hospitaller.

The origin legend was written down in the 1520s by Christiern Pedersen and the friar Petrus Olai. In Olai's most influential version the Danes under Valdemar II were close to defeat at the Battle of Lindanise, near Tallinn in Estonia, on 15 June 1219. Bishop Anders Sunesen prayed on a hill with his arms raised, and the Danes advanced while they stayed up, a story almost identical to Exodus 17. As defeat threatened, the flag fell from the sky, the king showed it to the troops, and they won. Other versions place the event at Fellin in 1208.

The Dannebrog, meaning red cloth, is a red flag with a white Nordic cross extending to the edges, its vertical arm shifted towards the hoist. A regulation of 1748, still in force, sets the cross at one seventh of the flag's height. No official definition of the red exists. The swallow-tailed Splitflag is used on land, and a deeper red Orlogsflag at sea by the navy.

According to tradition the original flag was lost at the Battle of Hemmingstedt on 17 February 1500 and recaptured by Frederik II in 1559, though contemporary records of the battle do not mention its loss. It was used as a maritime flag from the sixteenth century, and became the flag of the whole army from 1842. In the early nineteenth century, with Romantic nationalism, it came to be seen as representing the nation. A circular of 7 January 1834 outlawed its private use, and a regulation of 7 July 1854 permitted it, after the national enthusiasm of the First Schleswig War. It is often said to be the oldest national flag in continuous use.
flanders: Flanders is mainly flat and incorporates the whole Belgian coast on the North Sea. The word has had several meanings. It first named the County of Flanders, which existed from the 8th century, in Latin Flandria, until the French First Republic absorbed it, and which until the 1600s also extended over parts of what are now France and the Netherlands. French Flanders, in the department of Nord, and Zeelandic Flanders, in the Dutch province of Zeeland, are historically Flemish regions. In the 19th and 20th centuries the term Flemish, which also came to mean the Dutch language, led people to call the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium Flanders.

Julius Caesar described the area as the less developed and more warlike part of Gallia Belgica. The County of Flanders was a feudal fief of West Francia. Its first certain count, Baldwin I of Flanders, is reported in a document of 862, when he eloped with a daughter of his king, Charles the Bald. Cities such as Ghent and Bruges, and later Antwerp in the Duchy of Brabant, made the region one of the richest and most urbanised parts of Europe, weaving the wool of neighbouring lands into cloth, and a sophisticated culture developed there that rivalled that of northern Italy.

The county was weakened when districts fell under direct French royal rule in the late 12th century, and the remaining parts came under Baldwin V of Hainaut in 1191. Charles V was born in Ghent in 1500 and inherited the Seventeen Provinces in 1506. His Pragmatic Sanction of 1549 made the Low Countries an entity separate from the Holy Roman Empire and from France, and on his abdication in 1556 they passed to his son Philip II of Spain. Antwerp became the second-largest city in Europe north of the Alps by 1560.

In 1830 the Belgian Revolution split Belgium from the Netherlands, and the Treaty of London of 1839 confirmed Belgian independence. Dutch became an official language in public secondary schools in 1873, and in 1898 Dutch and French were declared equal in laws and royal orders. The first Flemish university opened in 1930.

Flanders is the Dutch-speaking northern part of Belgium. The Flemish Region and the Flemish Community form one body with a parliament and government, as constitutional institutions of the Kingdom of Belgium. The official capital is Brussels, which lies in its own region. Flanders covers 45 per cent of the territory of Belgium but holds more than half its population.
flavius-aetius: Aetius was born at Durostorum in Moesia Secunda, the son of Gaudentius, a Roman general, and an aristocratic mother from Italy. As a boy he served at the imperial court. Between 405 and 408 he was a hostage at the court of the Visigothic king Alaric I and then at that of the Hun king Uldin. In 423 Honorius died and Joannes took the western throne. Aetius served him and brought Hun troops after Joannes was killed at Ravenna in 425. He then made terms with Galla Placidia, the mother of Valentinian III, sent the Huns home and was made commander of the army in Gaul.

In Gaul he defeated the Visigoths under Theodoric I, who were besieging Arelate, and fought the Salian Franks, the Juthungi and the Bagaudae. In 430 he and the army accused the senior commander Felix of plotting against him, and some sources believe Aetius had Felix killed. After a rivalry with Bonifacius ended at the Battle of Rimini, where Bonifacius was fatally wounded, Aetius took refuge with the Huns and returned to power with their help. From 433 to 450 he was the dominant figure in the Western Empire. He defeated the Burgundians in 436 and sent Hun troops against them the next year.

In 451 Attila invaded Gaul. Aetius persuaded the Visigoths of Theodoric I, the Armoricans, Salian Franks, some Saxons and the Burgundians to join him. On 20 June 451 the joint army fought Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains, where Theodoric died. Attila invaded Italy in 452 and razed Aquileia, but Aetius could only harass him with a small force. Attila turned back after meeting an embassy that included Pope Leo I.

In 453 Aetius betrothed his son Gaudentius to Valentinian's daughter, but the emperor feared he wanted the throne for his son. According to Priscus, on 21 September 454 Valentinian leapt up as Aetius delivered a financial account and, with the chamberlain Heraclius, struck him dead with a sword. In March 455 two Huns who had been friends of Aetius killed Valentinian.

Aetius has often been called the last of the Romans. Edward Gibbon wrote that Attila's retreat confessed the last victory won in the name of the Western Roman Empire. J. B. Bury thought the battle less decisive than the Germanic victory at Nedao three years later. His death was followed by a rapid fragmentation of the West.
flensburg: Flensburg lies in the north of Schleswig-Holstein, very close to the German–Danish border, at the innermost tip of the Flensburg Firth, an inlet of the Baltic Sea. After Glücksburg and Westerland it is Germany's northernmost town, and its eastern shore is part of the Angeln peninsula. After Kiel and Lübeck it is the third-largest urban area in Schleswig-Holstein.

Danish settlers founded Flensburg at the latest by 1200, and German merchants soon joined them. Its town rights were confirmed in 1284, and it became one of the most important towns of the Duchy of Schleswig. Because Schleswig, unlike Holstein, did not belong to the Holy Roman Empire, Flensburg was not a member of the Hanseatic League, though it kept contacts with it. After the League's fall in the 16th century its merchants traded as far as the Mediterranean, Greenland and the Caribbean, in herring, sugar and whale oil. The Thirty Years' War ended this boom, and the town became Protestant and ever more German, while the countryside remained Danish.

Flensburg passed to Prussia after the Second Schleswig War in 1864. At the election to the North German Reichstag in 1867 it still had a Danish majority, which lasted until about 1880, when immigration of workers and the replacement of the bureaucracy by southern Germans shifted it. After the Second World War a strong pro-Danish movement sought to unite Schleswig north of the Eider with Denmark, and for some years the town council was dominated by Danish parties. From 2 May 1945 until early June it was the seat of the Flensburg Government, the final administrative form of Nazi Germany.

Flensburg is the cultural and organisational centre of the Danish minority of Southern Schleswig, which runs its own schools, libraries and Lutheran churches. The bilingual Flensborg Avis is published there. The Old Town was largely spared in the Second World War and remains compact and well preserved. The University of Flensburg was founded in 1946 as a pedagogical college and became a university in 1994.
florence: Florence lies about 275 kilometres north-west of Rome, in a basin formed by the hills of Careggi, Fiesole, Settignano, Arcetri, Poggio Imperiale and Bellosguardo. The Arno river flows through it. The name derives from the Latin Florentia, meaning the Flourishing Town, from florēre, to flourish or blossom, and the modern Italian name Firenze descends from it through the older Fiorenza.

Florence was founded as a Roman garrison in 59 BCE in an area previously inhabited by an Etruscan settlement whose name is unknown. After a long period as a flourishing trading and banking medieval commune, it became the birthplace of the Italian Renaissance and was one of the most important cities in Europe from the 14th to the 16th centuries. In 1200 the city had 50,000 people, and by 1300 its population was 120,000, with another 300,000 in the surrounding Contado.

It was the Republic of Florence from 1115 to 1532, then a duchy and, from 1569 to 1801, part of the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Its turbulent political history includes periods of rule by the powerful Medici family and numerous religious and republican revolutions. From 1865 to 1871 it was the capital of the Kingdom of Italy.

The language spoken in the city in the 14th century came to be accepted as the model for Italian. The works of the Tuscans Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio led to the Florentine dialect being adopted as the basis of a national literary language. The University of Florence was first founded in 1321 and recognised by Pope Clement VI in 1349.

Florence is the capital and most populous city of the Italian region of Tuscany. UNESCO declared its historic centre a World Heritage Site in 1982. The centre lies within medieval walls built in the 14th century. The domed cathedral of Santa Maria del Fiore, known as the Duomo, has a dome built by Filippo Brunelleschi that is still the largest in brick and mortar in the world. The Campanile, partly designed by Giotto, the Baptistery, the Palazzo Vecchio and the Uffizi Gallery are among its landmarks. The city was home to Giotto, Donatello, Masaccio, Botticelli, Leonardo da Vinci and Michelangelo, and it is known as the Cradle of the Renaissance.
florence-cathedral: Santa Maria del Fiore was built on the site of Florence's second cathedral, dedicated to Saint Reparata. According to Giovanni Villani's Nuova Cronica, the old building was crumbling and too small for the growing city, and other Tuscan cities, Pisa and Siena among them, were rebuilding their cathedrals. The city council approved Arnolfo di Cambio's design in 1294, and Cardinal Valeriana, the first papal legate ever sent to Florence, laid the first stone on 9 September 1296. The project was to last 140 years.

After Arnolfo died in 1302 work slowed for almost 50 years. The discovery of the relics of Saint Zenobius in 1330 gave it new impetus, and in 1331 the wool merchants' guild, the Arte della Lana, took over its patronage. In 1334 it appointed Giotto, who began the campanile. He died on 8 January 1337, and Andrea Pisano continued until the Black Death halted work in 1348.

The cathedral is a basilica in the shape of a Latin cross, with a wide central nave of four square bays and an aisle on either side. Its trilobate apses were meant to evoke a flower, in homage to Fiorenza, the city of flowers. It is 153 m long and 38 m wide, and its dome rises 114.5 m. The exterior is faced with polychrome marble panels in green, pink and white.

The dome was planned from the start without external buttresses. In 1367 the model of Neri di Fioravanti was chosen over a rival's, a decision described as one of the first events of the Italian Renaissance, since Gothic flying buttresses were thought ugly and were forbidden in Florence. The original façade was dismantled in 1587 and 1588 on the orders of Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici. The present Gothic Revival façade by Emilio De Fabris was built from 1876 to 1887.

The interior is Late Gothic and bare, which suits the austerity of the mendicant orders. Because public funds paid for the cathedral, its notable works honour Florentine heroes: Dante appears in a fresco of 1465 by Domenico di Michelino, and Paolo Uccello and Andrea del Castagno painted the condottieri Sir John Hawkwood and Niccolò da Tolentino as riders in 1436 and 1456. In 1475 the astronomer Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli pierced a hole in the dome to make a meridian line.

Cracks in the dome were seen even before it was finished. In 1694 two major cracks were measured at up to 29 mm, and a commission proposed iron belts, but after long debate the dome was left as it was. Excavations from 1965 to 1974 uncovered Roman houses and the ruins of Santa Reparata, and Filippo Brunelleschi's simple tomb lies in the crypt.
florida: About two-thirds of Florida occupies a peninsula between the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic Ocean and the Straits of Florida, and it extends northwest into a panhandle. It is the only state that borders both the Gulf and the Atlantic, and it has the longest coastline in the contiguous United States, about 2,170 kilometres. Its climate varies from subtropical in the north to tropical in the south. Everglades National Park is the largest tropical wilderness in the United States, and the Florida Reef is the only living coral barrier reef in the continental United States.

The first inhabitants, the Paleo-Indians, entered Florida at least 14,000 years ago. By the 16th century the major groups included the Apalachee, the Timucua, the Ais, the Mayaimi, the Tequesta and the Calusa. Juan Ponce de León sighted the peninsula on 2 April 1513, and it was the first region of what is now the contiguous United States to be visited and settled by Europeans. The story that he sought the Fountain of Youth is apocryphal and appeared only long after his death. An estimated 700,000 Native Americans lived in Florida in the 1520s, but by 1700 only around 2,000 remained.

Spain founded St. Augustine in 1565, the oldest continuously inhabited European-established settlement in the United States. Britain held Florida briefly from 1763, and Spain recovered it in 1783. Spain later ceded it to the United States. It was the main location of the Seminole Wars (1816–1858), became the 27th state on 3 March 1845, and seceded on 10 January 1861 as one of the seven original Confederate States, returning to the Union on 25 June 1868.

Florida is a state of the United States, with Tallahassee as its capital and 67 counties. Its most populous city is Jacksonville, and the Miami metropolitan area is the largest in the state. Miami Beach's Art Deco District belongs to the state's large collection of Art Deco and Streamline Moderne buildings, and St. Augustine preserves Spanish revival and other early styles.
foligno: Foligno stands in the province of Perugia in east central Umbria, on the Topino river where it leaves the Apennines and enters the wide plain of the Clitunno river system. It lies 40 kilometres south-east of Perugia and 6 kilometres south of Spello, at an elevation of 235 metres. The town stands along the Via Flaminia, where four major roads converge, matching its four gates. Its name derives from an Umbrian form, Fulginia, which became the Roman Fulginium and is linked to the cult of the goddess Fulginia. Of its Roman past no significant trace remains except the regular street plan of the centre and three Roman bridges on the Topino.

The origins of the town are uncertain. Cicero refers to the municipium and prefecture of Fulginia, and Pliny lists it among the cities of Umbria. Totila seized the city in 546, and Belisarius recovered it for the Empire four years later. When the Lombard king Alboin occupied Umbria in 571 and founded the Duchy of Spoleto, Foligno was included in it. Saracen raids in 840 and Hungarian invasions in 915 and 924 caused further damage. Under Pope Innocent III the town passed with much of Umbria under the authority of the Church.

The Trinci family rose to power in the late Middle Ages. On 30 November 1367 Pope Urban V appointed Trincia II as vicar of Foligno for an annual tribute of a sparrowhawk, and Gregory XI later confirmed him. Trincia II was thrown from the windows of the Palazzo Trinci in 1377. Ugolino Trinci acquired the Palazzo Governativo in 1398, and in 1439 it passed from the Trinci to the municipality. Foligno experienced French rule in 1798 to 1799 and again in 1809 to 1814. After 1816 it was a seat of district government under the papacy until Italian unification.

The first printed edition of Dante's Divina Commedia was produced in the Orfini Palace at Foligno on 5 and 6 April 1472 by Johannes Numeister and Evangelista Angelini, with sheets for 300 copies. Foligno also produced the almanac Barbanera in the 18th century, together with Spello. The Palazzo Trinci, decorated by Gentile da Fabriano, and the cathedral of San Feliciano are among its landmarks, and Raphael's Madonna of Foligno once stood on the high altar of the church of Sant'Anna. Foligno is a rail junction on the line from Rome to Ancona. Allied bombing in the Second World War destroyed about 80 per cent of the city, and an earthquake in 1997 caused serious damage.
fontainebleau: Fontainebleau is a commune 55.5 kilometres south-south-east of Paris, in the Seine-et-Marne department, of which it is a sub-prefecture. Its land area is the largest of any commune in the Île-de-France, larger than Paris itself. The Forest of Fontainebleau, a former royal hunting park, surrounds the town and is protected by France's Office National des Forêts. It is popular with hikers, horse riders and climbers.

The name was taken in the sixteenth century from the Fontaine Belle-Eau, a spring in the château garden. Louis VII endowed the hamlet with a royal hunting lodge and chapel in the mid-twelfth century, and Louis IX, who called it his wilderness, built a country house and a hospital. Philip the Fair was born there in 1268 and died there in 1314. Francis I turned the country house into a palace in the largest of his building projects, and from 1528 the court there entertained the new ideas known as the Renaissance. Every monarch from Francis I to Louis XV renovated it.

On 18 October 1685 Louis XIV signed the Edict of Fontainebleau there, revoking the Edict of Nantes and the right of Huguenots to worship publicly. Many Protestants were forced to convert, killed or driven into exile. The Treaty of Fontainebleau of 29 October 1807 allowed French troops to cross Spain to invade Portugal. Pope Pius VII arrived at the château as Napoleon's prisoner on 20 June 1812 and stayed in his apartments until 23 January 1814. On 20 April 1814 Napoleon bade farewell to the Old Guard in the courtyard, now called the Courtyard of Goodbyes, and the Treaty of Fontainebleau of 1814 stripped him of his powers and sent him to Elba.

Until the nineteenth century Fontainebleau was a village and suburb of Avon. In 1946 it hosted the Franco-Vietnamese Conference, which ended in failure, and until 1967 it held Allied land forces headquarters for Central Europe.

About 300,000 people visit the palace each year and more than 13 million the forest. The town is home to the European campus of the INSEAD business school, and the mystic George Gurdjieff and the writer Katherine Mansfield are buried in the cemetery at Avon.
forbidden-city: Construction began in 1406, after the Yongle Emperor, the son of the Hongwu Emperor, moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing. The materials included whole logs of precious Phoebe zhennan wood from the jungles of southwestern China, large blocks of marble from quarries near Beijing, and golden bricks, specially baked paving bricks from Suzhou, laid on the floors of the major halls.

The Chinese name Zijincheng means Purple Forbidden City. Zi, purple, refers to the North Star, which in traditional astrology was the heavenly abode of the Jade Emperor; the Forbidden City was its earthly counterpart. The name first formally appeared in 1576.

The complex is a rectangle measuring 961 m from north to south and 753 m from east to west, enclosed by a wall 7.9 m high and a moat 52 m wide. It has 980 surviving buildings with 8,886 bays of rooms; the common claim of 9,999 rooms is a myth not supported by survey evidence. At the heart of the Outer Court a three-tiered white marble terrace carries three halls, the Hall of Supreme Harmony, the Hall of Central Harmony and the Hall of Preserving Harmony. The first is the largest surviving wooden structure in China. Almost all roofs bear yellow glazed tiles, yellow being the emperor's colour.

From 1420 to 1644 the palace was the seat of the Ming dynasty. In April 1644 rebel forces under Li Zicheng captured it, and he soon fled before the armies of the former Ming general Wu Sangui and the Manchus, setting fire to parts of it. By October a ceremony there proclaimed the young Shunzhi Emperor ruler of all China under the Qing. The Qing renamed some principal buildings to stress harmony rather than supremacy and made the nameplates bilingual in Chinese and Manchu. Anglo-French forces occupied it in 1860 during the Second Opium War, and Empress Dowager Cixi fled in 1900 during the Boxer Rebellion.

Under the Qing the emperor lived and worked almost entirely in the Inner Court, using the Outer Court for ceremony. From 1933 the threat of Japanese invasion forced the evacuation of the museum's most important collections.
forcalquier: Forcalquier lies between the Lure Mountain and Luberon ranges, about 30 km south of Sisteron and 10 km west of the Durance river. Its Latin name, Furnus Calcarius, comes from the lime kilns used in Roman times, and a Roman bridge still stands in the valley to the south of the town. The town is built round the slopes of a steep conical hill.

At the end of the 11th century a family of the counts of Provence created the county of Forcalquier. In the Middle Ages the town was the capital of Haute-Provence along the Durance, a territory that included Manosque, Sisteron, Gap and Embrun. It minted its own currency, and its church was raised to the status of a concathedral.

The counts of Forcalquier grew powerful enough to defy the counts of Provence. The rivalry ended in 1195, when Gersende de Sabran, countess of Forcalquier, married Alfonso II, count of Provence, and their son Ramon Bérenger IV inherited both counties.

The hill is crowned by the octagonal chapel of Notre Dame de Provence, built in 1875 where the medieval citadel stood until its destruction in 1601. The oldest part of the town surrounds the Place Saint-Michel, with a Renaissance fountain of 1511 and doorways from the 12th to 16th centuries. The 12th-century concathedral of Notre Dame de l'Assomption stands across from the Place du Bourguet. Franciscans, called cordeliers for their rope belts, built a convent in the 13th century, occupied by monks until the Revolution. The Port de Cordeliers is all that remains of the town walls. The municipal museum holds prehistoric and Gallo-Roman objects, glass and local pottery.
fort-de-france: Fort-de-France lies on the west coast of Martinique, at the northern entrance to the large Fort-de-France Bay and at the mouth of the Madame River. The city occupies a narrow plain between the hills and the sea but can be reached by road from all parts of the island. Its climate is tropical rainforest, warm and humid all year, with hurricanes a frequent threat from July to November.

Before French settlement the area was known as Iguanacaera, which in the Kariʼnja language means Iguana Island. In 1638 Jacques Dyel du Parquet, first governor of Martinique, had Fort Saint Louis built to protect against attack. The fort was soon destroyed and was rebuilt in 1669, when Louis XIV appointed the Marquis of Baas governor general, and it was built to a design of Vauban. In the 1680s the area was settled and became the French colonial capital in the Caribbean, governed by the Code Noir, the decree Louis XIV issued in 1685 to regulate slavery in the French colonies.

Called Fort-Royal, the administrative capital was overshadowed by Saint-Pierre, the oldest city on the island, known as the Paris of the Caribbean. A British expedition captured the city in 1762, and the Treaty of Paris returned the island to France. A fire in 1890 razed part of the city, and the town hall was completed in 1901. The eruption of Mount Pelée in 1902 destroyed Saint-Pierre and made Fort-de-France economically important. Until 1918 it had an inadequate water supply and was notorious for yellow fever.

Fort-de-France is the capital of Martinique, an overseas department and region of France. Fort Saint Louis is a French naval base. Its sights include Fort Desaix, the park called La Savane, a botanical garden and the cathedral. Its inhabitants are called Foyalais, after Foyal, the Creole form of the old name Fort-Royal. The psychiatrist and political philosopher Frantz Fanon, born in 1925, is among its notable natives.
fougeres: Fougères is a commune and sub-prefecture of the department of Ille-et-Vilaine, in Brittany, on the edge of Brittany, Maine and Normandy. It lies 40 kilometres from Rennes, 58 kilometres from Mont-Saint-Michel and 330 kilometres from Paris. Megalithic monuments in the forest of Fougères suggest that the area was inhabited in the Neolithic era. The town stood at the crossing of two Roman roads, one from Chartres to Carhaix and the other from Avranches to Nantes. It is built on rock, and the castle stands not on a height but on a deposit of hard metamorphic rock, which protected it from attack by mining and from underground.

The creation of Fougères dates to the Middle Ages. Its castle was first mentioned around the end of the 10th century as a simple wooden fortification on a rocky ridge dominating the Nançon valley and its marshes. From the 12th century the population moved away from the banks of the Nançon, and the town grew in two parishes, Saint-Sulpice for the lower town and Saint-Léonard for the upper. Tanners, weavers and drapers developed their crafts in the lower town. A belfry, the first built in Brittany, was erected in 1397 with money from local merchants, who modelled it on Flemish examples seen in their travels. The castle formed part of the Duchy of Brittany's ultimately unsuccessful defence against French aggression, together with Vitré.

In the 16th century the town lost its defensive role. During the French Revolution the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the levée en masse triggered the rebellion known as the Chouannerie. In 1793 the Vendéens and Chouans seized the town, and Republicans took it a few weeks later. For eight years the town and its region passed from hand to hand, with massacres and looting, and the Chouan leader in the Fougères area was the young general Aimé du Boisguy. In the 19th century shoemaking replaced older crafts, and the population rose from 9,344 in 1856 to 20,952 in 1901. Workers struck in the shoe factories in the winter of 1906–07, and Jean Jaurès came to support them.

Fougères has been classified as a town of art and history since 1985. Its castle, a medieval stronghold on a granite ledge, is its most visited site. A large section of the town wall survives, and the Notre-Dame Gate of the 15th century, with a double drawbridge, is the only fortified town gate left. The churches of Saint-Sulpice and Saint-Léonard both date from the 15th century, and the town hall was completed in 1535. Shoemaking, once the town's chief industry, has almost disappeared. The Tour de France has started and finished stages in the town.
four-asian-tigers: Hong Kong was the first of the four to industrialise, developing a textile industry in the 1950s, and by the 1960s its factories in the British colony also made clothing, electronics and plastics for export. After Singapore's independence from Malaysia, its Economic Development Board set up industrial estates and attracted foreign investment with tax incentives. Taiwan and South Korea began to industrialise in the mid-1960s with heavy government involvement. All four were inspired by the Japanese economic miracle and invested in infrastructure and education, and all benefited from economic support from the United States.

By the end of the 1960s the four economies had far more physical and human capital than other countries at similar levels of development. By 1965 all four had achieved universal primary education, and South Korea's secondary enrolment reached 88 percent by 1987. They kept budget deficits within limits, and Hong Kong, Singapore and Taiwan did not borrow from abroad.

Their export policies differed. Hong Kong and Singapore adopted free-trade regimes, since their domestic markets were small, while South Korea and Taiwan used export incentives, and the governments of Singapore, South Korea and Taiwan promoted particular exporting industries. Together they grew by an average of 7.5 percent a year for three decades. The 1997 Asian financial crisis was a setback: South Korea was hit hardest, its currency falling by between 35 and 50 percent, while Singapore and Taiwan were relatively unscathed.

The causes of the growth are disputed. A World Bank report of 1993, The East Asian Miracle, credited neoliberal policies, including export orientation, low taxes and minimal welfare states. Other analyses argue that state intervention and industrial policy mattered much more, and the economist Dani Rodrik holds that the miracle cannot be understood without the role of government policy.

A cultural explanation points to Confucianism, which is said to have valued stability, hard work, discipline and respect for authority, and Lee Kuan Yew of Singapore advocated Asian values. Critics note that mainland China, the birthplace of Confucianism, did not share the success in the same years, and in 1996 Joseph Stiglitz observed that the Confucian heritage had not long before been cited to explain why these countries had not grown. The four have been proposed as models for other developing countries, especially the Tiger Cub economies of Southeast Asia.
fourteen-points: The United States entered the First World War on 6 April 1917, in part because of Germany's resumption of submarine warfare and the Zimmermann telegram. President Woodrow Wilson wanted to separate American participation from the nationalist disputes of the European powers. The need for moral aims grew when the Bolsheviks disclosed secret treaties made between the Allies, and Wilson was also responding to Vladimir Lenin's Decree on Peace of November 1917. Three days before his speech, the British prime minister David Lloyd George had set out British war aims at Caxton Hall, and Wilson briefly considered abandoning his own, but his adviser Edward M. House persuaded him to go ahead.

Wilson delivered the Fourteen Points in a speech on war aims and peace terms to the United States Congress on 8 January 1918. They rested on the research of the Inquiry, a team of about 150 advisers led by House.

The first four points called for open covenants of peace openly arrived at, absolute freedom of navigation on the seas, the removal of economic barriers, and guarantees that national armaments would be reduced to the lowest point consistent with domestic safety. Points ten to thirteen dealt with colonial disputes and the autonomous development of peoples, and point thirteen called for a reborn Polish state with free and secure access to the sea.

The speech was spread as Allied propaganda, translated into many languages, and dropped behind German lines. In October 1918 the German chancellor Prince Max of Baden asked Wilson for an armistice and peace negotiations on the basis of the Fourteen Points. In Germany they became a symbol of the promised basis of peace, and through the interwar period critics argued that the Treaty of Versailles contradicted them. The Allied leaders Georges Clemenceau, Lloyd George and Vittorio Emanuele Orlando were sceptical of Wilsonian idealism, and Theodore Roosevelt called the document high-sounding and meaningless.

At the Paris peace conference the points guided disputes over Alsace-Lorraine, the Rhineland and Danzig, which the treaty made a Free City with special Polish rights. They also drew the attention of anti-colonial leaders, who saw an opportunity to seek independence. The Korean March First Movement of 1919 and the Egyptian Revolution of 1919 followed, and the Allies did not support either.
fourth-crusade: Pope Innocent III, who succeeded to the papacy in January 1198, made the preaching of a new crusade the main goal of his pontificate. The Ayyubid Sultanate under Saladin had taken Jerusalem in 1187, and the Third Crusade had ended in 1192 without recovering it. The intended target of the new expedition was Egypt, the centre of Ayyubid power. In 1201 the Republic of Venice contracted with the crusader leaders to build a fleet to carry the army. The leaders greatly overestimated how many men would sail from Venice, since many chose other ports, and about 12,000 arrived instead of the expected 33,500. They could not pay the agreed price of 85,000 silver marks.

In lieu of payment, the Doge Enrico Dandolo proposed that the crusaders help Venice attack the rebellious city of Zara. The sack of Zara in November 1202 was the first attack by a Catholic crusader army on a Catholic city, and the Pope briefly excommunicated the army.

In January 1203 the leaders agreed with the Byzantine prince Alexios Angelos to divert to Constantinople and restore his father Isaac II Angelos as emperor, with the promise of payment and support for the crusade. The army reached Constantinople on 23 June 1203, and Alexios IV was crowned co-emperor in August. He could not raise the promised sums, and a popular uprising deposed him in January 1204. The crusaders decided on outright conquest after his murder on 8 February.

The crusaders sacked Constantinople for three days in April 1204. Many civilians were killed, churches and monasteries were looted, and ancient and medieval works of art were stolen or ruined. Eyewitnesses including Niketas Choniates and Geoffrey of Villehardouin accuse the crusaders of rapacity. Several leaders, including Simon de Montfort, refused to take part in the attacks on Zara and Constantinople, and many crusaders had sailed directly to the Holy Land.

A treaty apportioned the Byzantine Empire between Venice and the crusader leaders. Baldwin of Flanders became emperor of the Latin Empire based in Constantinople, and Boniface of Montferrat founded the Kingdom of Thessalonica. Byzantine refugees founded successor states at Nicaea, Trebizond and Epirus, and the Nicaean Empire retook Constantinople in July 1261. Greeks call the period of Western rule in their lands the Frankokratia.

Historians regard the crusade as having solidified the East-West Schism and dealt a lasting blow to Byzantine power, leaving the restored empire territorially diminished and exposed to the expanding Ottomans. Sir Steven Runciman wrote in 1954 that there was never a greater crime against humanity than the Fourth Crusade. Whether the capture of Constantinople was the aim from the start is debated, and the traditional view was challenged by Donald E. Queller and Thomas F. Madden in their book of 1997.
france: Celtic tribes known as Gauls settled the area in the Iron Age. Ionian Greeks from Phocaea founded Massalia around 600 BCE, and the Romans conquered the south of Gaul around 125 BCE. Julius Caesar conquered the rest and overcame a revolt by the Gallic chieftain Vercingetorix in 52 BCE, after which Gaul was divided into provinces and a Gallo-Roman culture developed. In the 5th century the Visigoths, the Burgundians and the Franks settled in the region. The Franks formed the kingdom of Francia, the heartland of the Carolingian Empire, and the Treaty of Verdun of 843 partitioned that empire, with West Francia evolving into the Kingdom of France.

In the High Middle Ages France was a powerful but decentralised feudal kingdom. After Philip II defeated the Angevin Empire and won the Battle of Bouvines, it became more centralised. From the mid-14th to the mid-15th centuries a dynastic conflict with England, the Hundred Years' War, followed. The 16th century brought the French Renaissance, the French Wars of Religion between Catholics and Huguenots, and the emergence of a French colonial empire. Under Louis XIV the nation built Europe's strongest army.

The French Revolution of 1789 overthrew the ancien régime and produced the Declaration of the Rights of Man. Napoleon Bonaparte established the First French Empire and subjugated much of continental Europe. Later came the Bourbon Restoration, the Second Republic and the Second French Empire under Napoleon III, which collapsed during the Franco-Prussian War in 1870 and gave way to the Third Republic. France emerged victorious from World War I at great human and economic cost, and surrendered and was occupied by Germany in 1940. After liberation in 1944 the Fourth Republic was established and later dissolved over the course of the Algerian War. Charles de Gaulle formed the Fifth Republic in 1958, and Algeria and most French colonies became independent in the 1960s.

Metropolitan France covers 551,500 square kilometres and is bordered by the Pyrenees, the Alps, the Jura Mountains and the Rhine along much of its edge. The estimated population is 69,081,996, and Paris is the capital. France is a unitary semi-presidential republic under the Constitution of 1958, with a president elected for five years and a bicameral Parliament. It is one of the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council and has 54 UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
france-preseren: France Prešeren was born on 3 December 1800 in the Upper Carniolan village of Vrba, then in the Habsburg monarchy, the third of eight children of a well-off farmer and a better-educated mother. At eight he attended schools run by the Catholic clergy, and in 1812 he entered the State Gymnasium in Ljubljana, where he learned Latin, Greek and German, then the language of education and administration among Slovenes. The poet Valentin Vodnik encouraged him to write in Slovene, and he befriended the future philologist Matija Čop. In 1821 he began studying law at the University of Vienna, where he read Homer, Goethe, Dante and Petrarch.

After taking his law degree in 1828 Prešeren worked in Ljubljana as an assistant to lawyers, and he filed as many as six applications before he was allowed to open his own firm in Kranj in 1846. In 1833 he met Julija Primic, the daughter of a rich merchant, who became the unfulfilled love of his life; she married another man in 1835. Around 1836 he began a lasting relationship with Ana Jelovšek, with whom he had three children.

His first important poem, A Farewell to Youth, was written in 1828 and published in 1830 in the almanac Krajnska čbelica, which also printed The Water Man, the first Slovene ballad. Čop persuaded him to adopt Romanic poetic forms, and he became a master of the sonnet. A Wreath of Sonnets, fifteen sonnets published on 22 February 1834, joins his unhappy love to the theme of an unhappy, subjugated homeland. After Čop drowned in 1835 he wrote the epic-lyric poem The Baptism on the Savica, set in the forced Christianisation of the Carantanians, predecessors of the Slovenes. In 1844 he wrote the patriotic poem Zdravljica, A Toast, and in 1847 a volume of his collected poems appeared.

Prešeren lived in conflict with the civil and religious establishment and developed severe alcoholism and liver disease. He died in Kranj on 8 February 1849. Recognition came slowly, and a new edition of his poems in 1866, with an essay by Josip Stritar setting him in a European context, secured his standing as the leading Slovene poet. His monument in Ljubljana's central square, now Prešeren Square, dates from 1905, and Prešeren Day, the anniversary of his death, became a Slovene cultural holiday in 1945. Zdravljica was declared the national anthem of Slovenia in 1989.
francesco-guicciardini: Francesco Guicciardini was born in Florence on 6 March 1483, the third of eleven children of Piero di Iacopo Guicciardini. The family belonged to the Florentine oligarchy and supported the Medici. His godfather was the philosopher Marsilio Ficino, and he received a humanist education before studying law at the Universities of Ferrara and Padua until 1505. At twenty-three he was appointed by the Signoria to teach legal studies at the Florentine Studio. In 1508 he married Maria Salviati, daughter of Alamanno Salviati, and in the same year wrote a family memoir and began his Ricordi, a collection of personal maxims.

In 1512 the Signoria sent him as ambassador to Ferdinand the Catholic of Aragon. He came to regard Ferdinand as a model of political deceit. Pope Leo X made him governor of Reggio in 1516 and of Modena in 1517, and in 1523 Clement VII appointed him viceregent of the Romagna.

He urged Clement to join the League of Cognac in 1526 against Charles V, and was made lieutenant-general of the papal army, though he could not move its commander to act. The Sack of Rome followed in 1527. Florence's new republic declared him a rebel in March 1530. After the city fell to imperial troops, he was charged with punishing those who had resisted the Medici, and Benedetto Varchi called him more cruel than the others.

He governed Bologna from 1531 and later advised Alessandro de' Medici, defending him before Charles V at Naples in 1535. Cosimo de' Medici dismissed him soon after taking power, and he retired to his villa at Arcetri, where he died in 1540 without male heirs.

None of his works was published in his lifetime. The first sixteen of the twenty books of his History of Italy appeared in 1561, and the first English translation in 1579. The Ricordi, about 220 maxims, and his other writings came to light only after his descendants opened the family archives in 1857. He wrote the History in his last years, drawing on government records and his own experience, and he traced events to the self-interest of the emperors, princes and popes in command.

He corresponded with Niccolò Machiavelli until the latter's death in 1527, but objected that Machiavelli put things too absolutely, and he did not agree that Rome could serve as a perfect norm. Like many Florentine aristocrats he favoured a mixed republican government on the Venetian model, though he worked closely with the Medici.
francis-i-holy-roman-emperor: Francis was born on 8 December 1708 in Lunéville, in Lorraine, the fourth and oldest surviving son of Leopold, Duke of Lorraine, and Élisabeth Charlotte d'Orléans. Through his grandmother Eleonore, a daughter of Emperor Ferdinand III, he was connected with the Habsburgs. Emperor Charles VI favoured the family and had meant his daughter Maria Theresa to marry Francis's older brother Léopold Clément. When Léopold Clément died, Charles adopted the younger brother as his future son-in-law, and Francis was brought up in Vienna alongside Maria Theresa, with whom a real affection arose.

At 15 he was established in the Silesian Duchy of Teschen, and he succeeded his father as Duke of Lorraine in 1729. In 1731 he was initiated into freemasonry at a specially convened lodge in The Hague, and in 1732 he became lord lieutenant of Hungary, at Maria Theresa's wish to have him closer.

The War of the Polish Succession began in 1733, and France seized Lorraine, since its chief minister, Cardinal Fleury, feared Austrian power so close to France. Under the peace terms Stanisław Leszczyński, the losing claimant to the Polish throne, received Lorraine, and Francis became heir to the Grand Duchy of Tuscany, which he received in 1737. He married Maria Theresa in February 1736, though he had hesitated three times before agreeing, and his mother and his brother Prince Charles Alexander opposed the loss of Lorraine.

After Charles VI died in 1740, Francis and Maria Theresa ruled the Habsburg domains, and she gave him responsibility for finance, which he handled well. In the Treaty of Füssen she secured his election as emperor on 13 September 1745, and he was crowned at Frankfurt am Main on 4 October. He succeeded Charles VII and was the last non-Habsburg monarch of the Empire; she made him co-regent of her hereditary lands.

Francis died suddenly in his carriage on 18 August 1765, while returning from the opera at Innsbruck, and is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna. He and Maria Theresa had sixteen children, among them Marie Antoinette, the last pre-revolutionary queen consort of France. His eldest son Joseph II succeeded him as emperor, and his younger son Peter Leopold, later Emperor Leopold II, as Grand Duke of Tuscany.
francis-xavier: Francis Xavier was born on 7 April 1506 in the Castle of Xavier in the Kingdom of Navarre, the youngest son of an influential noble family. His father, Don Juan de Jasso y Atondo, was president of the Royal Council of Navarre and later finance minister to King John III of Navarre.

On 15 August 1534 he and six other students met in a crypt on Montmartre, Paris: Ignatius of Loyola, Alfonso Salmeron, Diego Laínez, Nicolás Bobadilla, Peter Faber and Simão Rodrigues. They took private vows of poverty, chastity and obedience to the Pope and vowed to go to the Holy Land. Xavier was ordained on 24 June 1537, and Pope Paul III approved the Society of Jesus in 1540.

King John III of Portugal asked for Jesuit missionaries for his possessions in India, where he believed Christian values were eroding among the Portuguese. Xavier left Lisbon on 7 April 1541 with a papal brief naming him apostolic nuncio to the East, and reached Goa on 6 May 1542. His first task was to restore Christianity among the Portuguese settlers, many of whom, according to recent critical accounts, had been sent out from the jails and lower ranks of Portuguese society.

In 1545 he went to Malacca, and from about January 1546 he preached in the Maluku Islands, including Ambon, Ternate and Morotai. In Malacca in December 1547 he met Anjirō, the first Japanese Christian, who later served as interpreter. Xavier left Goa on 15 April 1549 for Japan with Anjirō, Cosme de Torres and Juan Fernández, carrying gifts for the King of Japan. He set out for China again in April 1552, but was refused recognition of his title in Malacca, and he died on Shangchuan Island on 3 December 1552.

He was first buried on a beach at Shangchuan Island, and in 1553 his body was taken to Malacca and then to Goa, where his relics are kept in the Bom Jesus Basilica. He was beatified by Pope Paul V on 25 October 1619 and canonised by Pope Gregory XV on 12 March 1622, and Pope Pius XI named him co-patron of all foreign missions in 1927. He is also co-patron of Navarre.

Called the Apostle of the Indies, he is said to have converted more people than anyone since Paul the Apostle. His efforts most affected religious practice in India and the East Indies, with less success in Japan and Borneo. In Japan and China Christians later went underground.
franciscans: Francis of Assisi was the son of a rich cloth merchant who gave up his wealth. In 1209 a sermon on Matthew 10:9 made such an impression on him that he decided to devote himself wholly to apostolic poverty, and he began to preach repentance, barefoot and in a rough garment. Bernard of Quintavalle joined him, and within a year he had 11 companions, who lived in the deserted leper colony of Rivo Torto near Assisi and travelled through the mountains of Umbria. The name Ordo Fratrum Minorum, the Order of Lesser Brothers, expresses his rejection of wealth, and he gave his followers the simple tunic of peasants as their habit.

The original Rule approved by Pope Innocent III did not allow the ownership of property, and the friars begged for food while preaching. Clare of Assisi, under Francis's guidance, founded the Poor Clares, and a Third Order was created for men and women who stayed in secular life.

The friars reached the Holy Land in 1217, and in 1219 Francis went to Egypt with the Fifth Crusade and met the Sultan Malik al-Kamil. The extreme poverty required of members was relaxed in the final revision of the Rule in 1223, and how strictly to observe it became a major source of conflict within the order, with numerous secessions. After 1232 Brother Elias gathered money for a great basilica at Assisi, which alienated the zealots, and in the 14th century the quarrels produced a number of separate congregations. In about 1236 Pope Gregory IX appointed the Franciscans, with the Dominicans, as inquisitors, and in 1252 Pope Innocent IV approved their use of torture to extract confessions.

In New Spain the first three Flemish friars arrived in 1523, and in May 1524 the Twelve Apostles of Mexico came, led by Martín de Valencia. They built the Convento Grande de San Francisco, which was the Franciscan headquarters of New Spain for the next three hundred years. Pedro de Gante began the evangelisation and studied Nahuatl through the children of the Indian elite of Tetzcoco.

The First Order comprises three groups, each with its own minister general: the Friars Minor, called the Observants, the Conventuals, formed in 1209, and the Capuchins, founded in 1520. In 1897 Pope Leo XIII combined several smaller orders into the present Order of Friars Minor. Franciscans view creation as good, and Francis expressed affection for animals and natural objects in his Canticle of the Creatures. Among the early members were the scholastics Alexander of Hales, Bonaventure and John Duns Scotus, and the scholar Roger Bacon.
francisco-de-quevedo: Francisco Gómez de Quevedo y Santibáñez Villegas was born in Madrid on 14 September 1580 into a family of hidalgos from Cantabria. His father was secretary to Maria of Spain, and his mother was lady-in-waiting to the queen. Orphaned by six, he attended the Jesuit Imperial School and the university at Alcalá de Henares from 1596 to 1600. He had a club foot and poor sight, and because he wore pince-nez the word quevedos came to mean pince-nez in Spanish. By 1606 he was a well-known man of letters, befriended by Miguel de Cervantes and Lope de Vega.

In 1613 Quevedo went to Italy as secretary to Pedro Téllez-Girón, 3rd Duke of Osuna, and worked at court to win him the viceroyalty of Naples in 1616. He was made a knight of Santiago in 1618. When Osuna fell in 1620 Quevedo was exiled to Torre de Juan Abad, a fiefdom his mother had bought him, whose inhabitants refused to acknowledge him. He wrote some of his best poetry there and studied Seneca, becoming a leading figure of Spanish Neostoicism.

Philip IV's accession in 1621 ended his exile, and under the Count-Duke of Olivares he returned to court, becoming secretary to the king in 1632. A forced marriage in 1634 lasted about three months. He quarrelled with many writers, above all Luis de Góngora, mocking his obscure vocabulary in the sonnet Aguja de navegar cultos and his prominent nose in A una nariz. In 1639 Quevedo was arrested and his books confiscated, and he was taken to the convent of San Marcos in León. He left in 1643, frail and ill, and withdrew to Torre de Juan Abad.

Quevedo wrote in the style called conceptismo, marked by rapid rhythm, simple vocabulary, witty metaphor and wordplay. His vast poetry ranges from satire to love poems and philosophical pieces and was not published in book form in his lifetime. His one novel, the picaresque Vida del Buscón, appeared in 1626, and Los Sueños, five satirical dream-visions, in 1627. He wrote about fifteen theological and ascetic books and political works such as La política de Dios. His writings also include antisemitic attacks on Jews and on Portuguese new Christians. He died at Villanueva de los Infantes on 8 September 1645.
francisco-de-zurbaran: Francisco de Zurbarán was born in 1598 in Fuente de Cantos, Extremadura, and was baptised on 7 November. His father Luis was a haberdasher. In 1614 he was sent to Seville to apprentice for three years with Pedro Díaz de Villanueva, of whom little is known. He married María Paet in 1617 and, after her death in 1624, the wealthy widow Beatriz de Morales in 1625. A contract of 17 January 1626 with the Dominican monastery of San Pablo el Real in Seville for 21 paintings, fourteen of them on the life of Saint Dominic, established him as a painter.

In 1628 the Mercedarians of Seville commissioned 22 paintings for their cloister, and in 1629 the elders of Seville invited him to settle there. In 1631 he painted the altarpiece of The Apotheosis of Saint Thomas Aquinas, his largest composition. Around 1630 he became painter to Philip IV, and in the 1630s he painted the Labours of Hercules for the Hall of Realms in Madrid, his only group of mythological subjects.

After 1640 his austere style was compared unfavourably with Murillo's sentimental religiosity, and his reputation declined. From the late 1630s his workshop exported many paintings to South America. He married a third time in 1644, and in 1658 moved to Madrid in search of work and renewed contact with Velázquez. He died on 27 August 1664. Popular myth has him dying in poverty, but his estate was valued at about 20,000 reales.

Zurbarán was nicknamed the Spanish Caravaggio for his forceful use of chiaroscuro, though it is unknown whether he saw Caravaggio's paintings. Juan Sánchez Cotán and the polychrome sculpture of Seville are thought to have shaped his severe compositions. He painted from nature and used a lay-figure to study drapery, with a special gift for white robes, hence the many Carthusians in his work. His subjects were mostly ascetic religious vigils, often a single figure against a dark, featureless background, and his settings resemble shallow theatre stages. His late works, such as Saint Francis, show Murillo's and Titian's influence in looser brushwork.
francisco-del-rosario-sanchez: Sánchez was born in Santo Domingo on 9 March 1817. His mother, Olaya del Rosario Belén, was a free woman of colour; his father, Narciso Sánchez Ramona, a descendant of slaves, worked in the cattle and meat trade. The parents married only in 1819, which is why he bore his mother's surname before his father's. He was taught first by his mother and then by the Peruvian priest Gaspar Hernández. Juan Pablo Duarte, a classmate, recruited him to La Trinitaria, founded in 1838.

When Duarte and others left the country on 2 August 1843 to escape Haitian persecution, Sánchez, who was ill, stayed behind in hiding and took over the leadership of the movement. On the night of 27 February 1844 his men took the Ozama Fortress, and at the Puerta del Conde, after Matías Ramón Mella fired his blunderbuss, he raised the flag. He presided over the Central Government Board, and assured freed people who had mutinied under Santiago Basora that slavery would not return.

Pedro Santana marched on Santo Domingo and on 12 July 1844 drove the Trinitarios from the board. On 22 August Duarte, Sánchez and Mella were declared traitors and deported for life. He lived as a teacher in Curaçao until an amnesty granted by President Manuel Jimenes in 1848. Back home, he sided with Buenaventura Báez against Santana, was exiled again to Curaçao, returned in August 1856 and became governor of the province of Santo Domingo, and in 1859 was banished a third time, to Saint Thomas.

In 1861 Sánchez formed the Dominican Revolutionary Board and obtained from the Haitian president Fabre Geffrard passage through Haitian territory and weapons for a force of 500 men. He entered through Hondo Valle on 1 June 1861. When Haiti withdrew its support under threat from a Spanish squadron at Port-au-Prince, the expedition turned back. On 20 June Sánchez was ambushed near Hondo Valle by Santiago de Óleo, a former ally, wounded in the leg and groin, and captured.

A war council at San Juan under General Domingo Lazala tried the prisoners; Sánchez, conducting his own defence, asked that he alone be condemned. He was shot at San Juan de la Maguana on 4 July 1861 with some twenty companions, some of whom were finished off with machetes and clubs. Spain withdrew from the country in 1865. Dominicans honour him with Duarte and Mella as a founder of the republic, and the Order of Merit of Duarte, Sánchez and Mella bears his name.
francisco-franco: Francisco Franco Bahamonde was born on 4 December 1892 in Ferrol, Galicia, into a family that had given the Spanish Navy officers for six generations. He would have followed his father into the navy, but after the Spanish-American War the Naval Academy admitted no new entrants from 1906 to 1913. He entered the Infantry Academy at Toledo in 1907 and graduated in July 1910 as a second lieutenant. Serving in Morocco, where officers could win promotion on the battlefield, he became a brigadier general in 1926 at the age of 33.

A conservative and monarchist, Franco regretted the end of the monarchy in 1931 but did not challenge the Second Republic. He led the suppression of the 1934 uprising in Asturias, and after the Popular Front won the 1936 election he was sent to the Canary Islands. He joined the military coup of July 1936 and took command of the 30,000 soldiers of the Army of Africa, securing the Moroccan protectorate in part by the summary execution of some 200 senior officers loyal to the Republic. With aircraft from Italy and Germany he began an air bridge to Seville.

Franco was proclaimed Generalísimo and head of state of the Nationalists in October 1936. On 19 April 1937 he merged the Falange and the Carlist parties into a single party. Barcelona fell in January 1939 and Madrid on 28 March, and he proclaimed victory on 1 April 1939. Repression followed. Paul Preston estimates that Franco's forces killed about 420,000 people in the war and afterwards, while Antony Beevor cites at least 35,000 official executions after 1939, and figures vary widely. Spain stayed non-belligerent in the Second World War though it supported the Axis, and the economy grew rapidly from the late 1950s.

In 1969 Franco named Prince Juan Carlos de Borbón as his heir. He died on 20 November 1975, aged 82, and was entombed in the Valley of the Fallen; in 2018 the government approved legal changes that led to plans to exhume his remains. His legacy remains disputed. Scholars debate whether his regime should be called fascist, a military dictatorship or something between, and Paul Preston and Stanley Payne hold differing views.
francisco-i-madero: Francisco Ignacio Madero González was born on 30 October 1873 at the hacienda of El Rosario in Parras de la Fuente, Coahuila, into one of Mexico's wealthiest families. His grandfather Evaristo Madero Elizondo built a large fortune, in part by shipping cotton to Mexican ports during the American Civil War. Between 1886 and 1892 Francisco was educated in France and the United States, at the Lycée Hoche in Versailles, the École des Hautes Études Commerciales in Paris and the University of California, Berkeley. In Paris he took up Spiritism and came to believe he was a medium. Returning in 1893, he managed a family hacienda at San Pedro, where he installed irrigation and built schools, hospitals and a soap factory.

After Bernardo Reyes violently crushed a demonstration on 2 April 1903, Madero, who believed his dead brother's spirit was advising him, decided to enter politics. He founded the Benito Juárez Democratic Club, lost a municipal election in 1904 and started opposition newspapers. His 1908 book The Presidential Succession in 1910 urged voters to stop Díaz's reelection, and he funded the Anti-Reelectionist Party. Díaz had said in 1908 that the 1910 election would be free. The regime arrested Madero on 6 June 1910, and about 5,000 other members of the movement were jailed. A fraudulent election on 21 June gave Díaz a huge majority.

Madero fled to San Antonio, Texas, and issued the Plan of San Luis Potosí, which declared the election void and called for revolt on 20 November 1910. It also promised the return of land to villages and Indian communities. After a defeat at Casas Grandes he gave up military command, and Pancho Villa and Pascual Orozco took Ciudad Juárez against his orders. Díaz resigned on 25 May 1911 under the Treaty of Ciudad Juárez. Madero kept the Federal Army and demobilised the revolutionaries. Elected in a landslide, he was sworn in as president on 6 November 1911.

His slowness on land reform led Emiliano Zapata to proclaim the Plan of Ayala on 25 November 1911, and Orozco rebelled in 1912. Conservatives opposed him, and the press he had freed criticised him. In February 1913 Félix Díaz, Bernardo Reyes and Victoriano Huerta led a coup, supported by the United States, during the Ten Tragic Days of 9 to 19 February. Huerta switched sides, and Madero was arrested and forced to resign. He and Vice President José María Pino Suárez were murdered, and his brother Gustavo A. Madero was kidnapped, tortured and killed.

His death united revolutionaries against Huerta. Venustiano Carranza, governor of Coahuila, led the Constitutionalist Army. He was known as the Apostle of Democracy, and the Monument to the Revolution, completed in 1938, holds his remains.
francisco-pizarro: Francisco Pizarro was born in Trujillo, in the Crown of Castile, probably in the 1470s, the illegitimate son of the infantry colonel Gonzalo Pizarro and Francisca González, a woman of poor means. Little attention was paid to his education, and he grew up and remained illiterate. In 1513 he accompanied Vasco Núñez de Balboa across the Isthmus of Panama to the Pacific. Under the governor Pedro Arias Dávila he was assigned a repartimiento, arrested Balboa on the governor's orders, and served as mayor of Panama City from 1519 to 1523.

In 1524 Pizarro formed a partnership with the priest Hernando de Luque and the soldier Diego de Almagro to explore and conquer the south. His first expedition left Panama in November 1524 and failed, and the second, from March 1526, produced Bartolomé Ruiz's capture of a balsa raft carrying textiles, gold, silver and emeralds. When the new governor refused a third expedition, Pizarro went to Spain, and Queen Isabel signed the Capitulación de Toledo on 6 July 1529, naming him governor of New Castile, a grant that later angered Almagro, who held lesser positions.

The third expedition left with three ships, 180 men and 27 horses. In May 1532 Pizarro founded San Miguel de Piura, the first Spanish settlement in Peru, and on 24 September he advanced inland with 200 men. At Cajamarca in November 1532 he captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa. Atahualpa filled a room with gold as a ransom, but Pizarro charged him with crimes and had him garrotted in July 1533. He entered Cuzco that year and founded Lima in January 1535, and in 1537 he was made 1st Marquess of the Conquest.

On 26 June 1541 about twenty supporters of Diego de Almagro II stormed Pizarro's palace in Lima and killed him, and he reportedly drew a cross in his blood before dying. His remains were buried under the cathedral.

He destroyed the Inca state and ruled the area for almost a decade. The Inca religion was replaced by Christianity, and much of the local population was reduced to effective serfdom under the encomienda system.
