He is reviled for ordering Atahualpa's death despite the ransom, which he kept after paying the king his due, and some Peruvians, particularly those of indigenous descent, regard him negatively.
franco-prussian-war: The war grew out of the unification of the German states under Otto von Bismarck. France had been the dominant power of continental Europe after the Franco-Austrian War of 1859, and the decisive Prussian victory over Austria in 1866 appeared to call that position into question. In 1870 Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was offered the vacant Spanish throne and withdrew his acceptance, but the French ambassador then asked King Wilhelm I at Ems to renounce any future claim. Wilhelm refused, and Bismarck made the report of the exchange public in altered wording. Crowds in Paris demanded war.

France mobilised on 15 July 1870, and its parliament voted for war the next day. The German coalition mobilised more effectively, and its forces were superior in numbers, training and leadership and made better use of railways and artillery.

France invaded German territory on 2 August, and German armies entered north-eastern France on 4 August. French defeats followed at Wissembourg, Spicheren and Wörth, and the largest battle of the war, at Gravelotte on 18 August, drove Marshal Bazaine's Army of the Rhine back into Metz. At the Battle of Sedan on 1 September the Prussians surrounded the Army of Châlons, and on 2 September Napoleon III surrendered with 104,000 of his soldiers.

On 4 September a popular uprising overthrew the Second Empire, and Jules Favre, Léon Gambetta and General Louis-Jules Trochu proclaimed a Government of National Defence and the Third Republic. The Germans began the siege of Paris on 19 September. Bazaine's army at Metz surrendered on 26 October. Paris, starving, fell on 28 January 1871, and an armistice was agreed.

In the last days of the war the German states proclaimed the German Empire under Wilhelm I. By the Treaty of Frankfurt of 10 May 1871, France paid an indemnity of five billion francs and ceded most of Alsace and parts of Lorraine, which became the Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine.

In France the war ended imperial rule and began the first lasting republican government. Resentment at its handling led to the Paris Commune, held from 18 March until the army retook Paris in the Semaine Sanglante of 21 to 28 May. The defeat also produced revanchism in France, a demand for revenge and the return of Alsace and Lorraine. Germany supplanted France as the dominant land power, and other armies adopted the Prussian general staff, universal conscription and detailed mobilisation systems.
francois-duvalier: François Duvalier was born in Port-au-Prince on 14 April 1907, the son of Duval Duvalier, a justice of the peace, teacher and journalist whose family came from Martinique, and Ulyssia Abraham, a baker. He completed a degree in medicine at the University of Haiti in 1934 and spent a year at the University of Michigan studying public health. From 1943 he took part in a campaign to control typhus, yaws, malaria and other tropical diseases, and his patients called him Papa Doc. The racism and violence of the United States occupation of Haiti, which began in 1915, inspired a black nationalism in him, and in 1938 he co-founded the journal Les Griots.

Duvalier became Director General of the National Public Health Service in 1946 and Minister of Health and Labor in 1949 under President Dumarsais Estimé. He left the government after Paul Magloire's coup of 1950 and went into hiding in the countryside in 1954. In the 1957 campaign he stood against the mulatto landowner Louis Déjoie, appealing to the black majority's resentment of the small mulatto elite. He was elected president on 22 September 1957 with 679,884 votes to Déjoie's 266,992, although there are accounts of fraud and intimidation.

After an attempted coup in July 1958 he dismissed the general staff and turned the Presidential Guard into an elite corps. In 1959 he created the militia known as the Tonton Macoute, which by 1961 was twice as big as the army. A sole-candidate election in 1961 extended his term, and a referendum on 14 June 1964 made him president for life, with ballots reportedly premarked yes. His government is estimated to have killed between 30,000 and 60,000 people, and many educated professionals fled to New York, Miami, Montreal, Paris and African states.

He cultivated a personality cult that drew on Vodou, modelling his image on the lwa Baron Samedi, and he expelled foreign bishops, which brought his excommunication. A concordat of 15 August 1966 lifted it and let him nominate Haitian bishops.

Duvalier died of heart disease and diabetes on 21 April 1971, aged 64, and his 19-year-old son Jean-Claude, called Baby Doc, succeeded him. He had suffered a heart attack in 1959, and he had been a diabetic since early adulthood. The regime fell on 8 February 1986, when a crowd attacked his mausoleum. Many books treat the Duvalier era, the best known being Graham Greene's novel The Comedians.
francois-fenelon: François de Salignac de la Mothe-Fénelon was born on 6 August 1651 at the Château de Fénelon in Sainte-Mondane, Périgord, into an old noble family reduced to modest means, in which fifteen generations had held the bishopric of nearby Sarlat. Private tutors taught him the Greek and Latin classics, and his uncle arranged his studies in Paris, where he preached a public sermon at 15. He was ordained about 1675.

In 1679 the Archbishop of Paris made him director of the Nouvelles-Catholiques, a community for young Huguenot girls about to join the Catholic Church, and in 1687 he published his Treatise on the Education of Girls. After Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, he preached to Protestants in Saintonge at Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet's suggestion.

In 1689 he became tutor to the seven-year-old Duke of Burgundy, second in line to the throne. For his pupil he wrote Fables, Dialogues of the Dead and, in 1693 and 1694, The Adventures of Telemachus, a novel about the son of Ulysses that also attacks the divine-right absolute monarchy of Louis XIV's France. It contains the line that good kings are rare and most monarchs bad.

Published in 1699, it was a best seller across Europe and supplied the plot of Mozart's opera Idomeneo. It is read as the programme of the circle of the Duc de Beauvilliers and the Duc de Chevreuse, who hoped for a less centralised monarchy after the king's death. Fénelon also argued that all wars are civil wars, since each person owes more to humanity than to a single country.

Fénelon defended the Quietism of his cousin Madame Guyon. He refused to sign Bossuet's Instructions on the states of prayer and set out his own view in the Maxims of the Saints. Louis XIV removed him as tutor and confined him to the archdiocese of Cambrai, and on 12 March 1699 the Inquisition condemned the book, Pope Innocent XII listing 23 propositions. Fénelon at once submitted. Telemachus angered the king the same year, so the confinement stayed. He sheltered refugees from the War of the Spanish Succession in his palace, wrote against the Jansenist party and died on 7 January 1715.
francois-guizot: François Guizot was born on 4 October 1787 at Nîmes into a bourgeois Protestant family. His father was executed on the scaffold there on 8 April 1794, during the Reign of Terror, when François was six. His mother took him to Geneva, where he was educated, and in 1805 he arrived in Paris as a tutor. He began writing for the journal Publiciste and in 1812 married Pauline de Meulan, a fellow contributor. Under the Restoration he was one of the leaders of the Doctrinaires, a small party attached to the charter and the crown that favoured the juste milieu, a middle path between absolutism and popular government. In 1822 his lectures were banned.

After the July Revolution of 1830 he supported the constitutional monarchy of Louis Philippe I. In 1832 he became minister of public instruction and carried the law of 28 June 1833, which established primary education in France. He also revived the Académie des Sciences Morales et Politiques and founded the Société de l'histoire de France, which published medieval chronicles at the state's expense. He went to London as ambassador in the spring of 1840. From 29 October 1840 he led the government for nearly eight years, as foreign minister and, after Marshal Soult retired, as prime minister from September 1847.

With Lord Aberdeen he built an understanding between France and Britain, and Napoleon's ashes were brought from St Helena. Opponents called his foreign policy subservient to England, and he answered that they would never reach the height of his disdain. He was unpopular with the more advanced liberals for restricting the vote to propertied men. When he banned the reform banquets in January 1848, the opposition grew, and on 23 February 1848 the king told him he doubted he could keep him as prime minister. Guizot resigned and escaped to London, where he arrived on 3 March.

He never returned to public life and spent most of each year at Val Richer in Normandy, supporting himself by writing. His works include histories of England under Cromwell, the Mémoires pour servir à l'histoire de mon temps, and a history of France told to his grandchildren. He was elected to the Académie Française in 1836. He died in 1874, after reciting verses of Pierre Corneille and texts from the Bible, according to report.

In the 1820s his Histoire générale de la civilisation en Europe was admired by John Stuart Mill, Goethe and Alexis de Tocqueville. His critics call him a conservative or reactionary for resisting universal suffrage, but he defended representative government against both absolutism and the excesses of democracy, and he called for the abolition of capital punishment.
francois-mitterrand: François Mitterrand was born on 26 October 1916 in Jarnac, Charente, into a devoutly Catholic and conservative family; his father was a stationmaster. He studied at the École Libre des Sciences Politiques in Paris. Called up in 1938, he was wounded by shrapnel on 14 June 1940 and captured by the Germans on 21 June. He escaped from a prisoner-of-war camp on 28 November 1941 with forged papers, and then worked as a mid-level official of the Vichy government looking after prisoners of war. In 1943 he built up a resistance network of former prisoners. His wartime conduct caused much controversy in France in the 1980s and 1990s.

Under the Fourth Republic Mitterrand held ministerial office several times, among them Minister of the Interior in the cabinet of Pierre Mendès-France in 1954–1955, when he had to direct the response to the Algerian War of Independence. In 1958 he was one of the few who opposed Charles de Gaulle's plan for a Fifth Republic, and his book Le Coup d'État permanent (1964) criticised de Gaulle's personal power. In 1971 he became first secretary of the Socialist Party, arguing that an alliance with the Communists was necessary to win power. He was the left's standard bearer in 1965 and 1974.

On 10 May 1981 Mitterrand became the first socialist President of the Fifth Republic. His first term began with nationalisation of key firms and a 39-hour work week, alongside the abolition of the death penalty, but facing economic tensions he soon turned to austerity and market liberalisation. In July 1985 French intelligence agents sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland, killing a photographer.

He was re-elected in 1988, and twice governed in cohabitation with conservative cabinets led by Jacques Chirac and Édouard Balladur. With the German chancellor Helmut Kohl he advanced European integration through the Maastricht Treaty. He left office in 1995 and died in Paris on 8 January 1996 of prostate cancer, which had been concealed for most of his presidency.
franconia: Franconia is not a political entity with a fixed area, and it is debated whether some districts belong to it. It is defined by its history, its culture and especially the East Franconian dialect, and in part by the territory of the former Duchy of Franconia and the Franconian Circle. Most of it lies north and south of the River Main and its tributary the Regnitz, in the three Bavarian districts of Lower, Middle and Upper Franconia. Upland ranges such as the Franconian Jura, the Fichtel Mountains, the Rhön and the Spessart surround it. Its highest mountain is the Schneeberg in the Fichtel Mountains, at 1,051 metres.

Fossil finds show people were living in the region about 600,000 years ago. In the Iron Age, from about 800 BCE, the Celts were the first people discernible there, and they built hill forts and settlements such as the one Ptolemy called oppidum Menosgada on the Staffelberg. As Rome expanded in the first century BCE and Germanic tribes advanced from the north, Celtic culture declined. The southern parts came under Roman control, but most of the region stayed in free Germania.

The Franks gained the region through victories over the Alamanni and Thuringians in the 6th century. Its name does not mean it was the homeland of the Franks, since it was only partly settled by Franks from the Rhineland. After the Frankish Empire was divided, East Francia was formed from the territories of the dioceses of Mainz, Worms, Würzburg and Speyer, and Bamberg was added later. Slavs began to settle the north-east from the 7th century. Irish and Anglo-Saxon monks first spread Christianity strongly there, and Saint Kilian was martyred at Würzburg in the late 7th century. Saint Boniface probably carried the mission to the ordinary people.

On 2 July 1500, under Emperor Maximilian I, the Empire was divided into Imperial Circles, and the Franconian Circle was formed in 1512. The region was severely affected by Kleinstaaterei, a patchwork of tiny states, and the bishops of Würzburg used the nominal title of Duke of Franconia. In 1559 the circle was given jurisdiction over coinage. After the Holy Roman Empire ended, Napoleon's restructuring of the south German states gave most of Franconia to Bavaria.

Franconia is divided among Bavaria, Thuringia, Baden-Württemberg and Hesse, and its largest part belongs to Bavaria. Its largest city is Nuremberg, followed by Fürth, Würzburg and Erlangen, and the region has roughly five million inhabitants. Franconians count as one of the four tribes of Bavaria. Large areas of Middle and Upper Franconia are Protestant, while Lower Franconia and western Upper Franconia are mostly Catholic, reflecting the territories of the Franconian Circle.
frankenstein: Mary Shelley's mother, Mary Wollstonecraft, died of infection eleven days after her birth, and she grew up among the writers and political figures who gathered at the home of her father, William Godwin. She met Percy Bysshe Shelley at sixteen, and in the summer of 1816 she, Percy and Claire Clairmont visited Lord Byron at the Villa Diodati by Lake Geneva. It was the rainy summer known as the Year Without a Summer, after the eruption of Mount Tambora in 1815, and the party stayed indoors reading German ghost stories. Byron proposed that each of them write a ghost story.

Shelley could think of nothing for days. After a night of talk about the principle of life and galvanism, she imagined a pale student of unhallowed arts kneeling beside the thing he had put together. She finished writing in April or May 1817.

Victor Frankenstein, born in Naples to an upper-class Genevese family, is obsessed with alchemy in youth and then turns to chemistry and electricity. At the University of Ingolstadt he finds a way to create life and assembles a large humanoid creature from body parts. Repelled when it awakens, he flees. In Shelley's text Victor discovers an unknown principle of life and does not say how it works; the electric jolt and the stitched-together image come from James Whale's 1931 film.

The creature teaches himself to speak and read, learns his origin from papers in his clothes, and is driven away by a family he has watched. Embittered, he travels to Geneva, kills Victor's younger brother William and frames the servant Justine, who is executed. He then asks Victor to make him a female companion. He compares himself to Adam and to the fallen angel of Milton, and the subtitle The Modern Prometheus alludes to the Titan who gave fire to humans.

Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus appeared anonymously on 1 January 1818 in three volumes, in an edition of 500 copies, with a preface by Percy Shelley and a dedication to Godwin. The second English edition, of 11 August 1823, named Mary Shelley as author after the success of Richard Brinsley Peake's stage play Presumption, which she attended on 29 August 1823.

The revised one-volume edition of 31 October 1831 added a new introduction and a more moral tone, and it is the one most widely read. The novel has influenced literature and popular culture and produced a genre of horror stories, films and plays, and the name Frankenstein is often wrongly given to the creature.
frankenthal: Frankenthal was first mentioned in 772. An Augustinian monastery was built there in 1119, and its ruins, known after the founder as the Erkenbertruine, still stand in the town centre. In the second half of the 16th century people from Flanders, persecuted for their religious beliefs, settled in the town. They were industrious and artistic, brought economic prosperity and included important carpet weavers, jewellers and artists, whose Frankenthaler Malerschule, or Frankenthal school of painting, acquired some fame. In 1577 Count Palatine Johann Casimir raised the settlement to the status of a city.

In 1600 Frankenthal was converted into a fortress. In 1621 English soldiers under Sir Horace Vere garrisoned it and the Spanish besieged it during the Thirty Years' War, after which troops of the opposing sides occupied it in turn. Trade and industry were ruined, and the town was not rebuilt until 1682. French troops burnt it to the ground in 1689 in the War of the Grand Alliance, and it did not fully recover for more than fifty years.

In 1750 Elector Charles Theodore made Frankenthal a centre of industry. A port was built between 1772 and 1781, factories were opened and mulberry trees were planted for silk production. The porcelain factory opened in 1755 and remained in production until 1800. The town came under French occupation in 1797 and passed to Bavaria in 1816, and modern industrialisation began around 1859. The synagogue built in 1884 was burnt to the ground on Kristallnacht in 1938, and a bombing raid in 1943 almost destroyed the town centre. Since 1946 Frankenthal has been part of the state of Rhineland-Palatinate, and it had 49,051 inhabitants in 2022 and some medium-sized industries.
frankfurt: Frankfurt lies on both sides of the river Main, south-east of the Taunus mountain range, in the western part of Germany. Its downtown is north of the Main in the Altstadt, the historical centre. The southern part of the city holds the Frankfurt City Forest, Germany's largest forest within a city. A ring-shaped Green Belt, formally created in 1991, covers a third of the administrative area.

The name derives from Franconofurd, from the Germanic tribe of the Franks and furt, a ford where the river was shallow enough to cross on foot. The first written records of 794 give Frankonovurd in Old High German and Vadum Francorum in Latin.

The first traces of Roman settlement along the river Nidda date to the reign of Emperor Vespasian, from 69 to 79 CE, and Nida was a Roman civitas capital. Alemanni and Franks later lived in the area, and in 794 Charlemagne presided over an imperial assembly and church synod at which Franconofurd was first mentioned. It was one of the two capitals of his grandson Louis the German, together with Regensburg, and Louis founded the collegiate church, rededicated in 1239 to Bartholomew the Apostle and now Frankfurt Cathedral.

Frankfurt has been an imperial city since 1372. As the Free City of Frankfurt it was a city state for nearly five centuries and one of the most important cities of the Holy Roman Empire, as a site of imperial coronations. It lost its sovereignty when the empire collapsed in 1806, regained it in 1815 and lost it again in 1866, when the Kingdom of Prussia annexed it after the Austro-Prussian War. It has been part of the state of Hesse since 1945.

Frankfurt am Main is the most populous city in the German state of Hesse, with 778,589 inhabitants. It is a financial centre, home to the European Central Bank, the Deutsche Bundesbank and the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, and Frankfurt Airport is the busiest in Germany.

The Römer, a complex of nine houses that the city council acquired in 1405 from a wealthy merchant family, is the city hall. Its Kaisersaal, the Emperor's Hall, is where newly crowned emperors held their banquets. The Römer was partly destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt, and the Goethe House, where Johann Wolfgang von Goethe was born in 1749, was destroyed and rebuilt in 1947.
franklin-d-roosevelt: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on 30 January 1882 in Hyde Park, New York, to James Roosevelt I and his second wife, Sara Ann Delano, who were sixth cousins from wealthy families. Apart from a stint in public school in Germany at nine, he was educated by tutors until 14, when he entered Groton School, whose headmaster Endicott Peabody urged students into public service. He graduated from Harvard University and married Eleanor Roosevelt, a niece of Theodore Roosevelt, on 17 March 1905.

In the Democratic landslide of 1910 Roosevelt won a surprising victory for a strongly Republican seat in the New York State Senate. In August 1921, at Campobello Island, he fell ill with what was diagnosed as polio, which left him permanently paralyzed from the waist down. He taught himself to walk short distances with iron braces and in 1926 established a rehabilitation centre at Warm Springs, Georgia.

He was elected governor of New York in 1928 by less than one percent. After winning the Democratic nomination on the fourth ballot in 1932, he pledged a new deal for the American people and defeated President Herbert Hoover.

Roosevelt had declined in health since at least 1940. On 12 April 1945, at the Little White House in Warm Springs, he said he had a terrific headache, slumped forward while sitting for a portrait, and was pronounced dead of a massive intracerebral hemorrhage, aged 63. The expansion of government programmes under Roosevelt redefined the role of government in the United States and permanently increased the power of the president at the expense of Congress. Surviving programmes include the Securities and Exchange Commission, the National Labor Relations Act and Social Security.
frans-hals: Hals was born in 1582 or 1583 in Antwerp, the son of the cloth merchant Franchois Fransz Hals van Mechelen. His parents fled to Haarlem in the new Dutch Republic during the Fall of Antwerp in 1584 and 1585, and he lived there for the rest of his life. He studied under the Flemish émigré Karel van Mander, whose Mannerist influence is barely noticeable in his work. In 1610 he joined the Haarlem Guild of Saint Luke and began to earn money restoring pictures for the town council, which had confiscated Catholic religious art. With the market for religious themes gone, he turned to portraiture.

His earliest known work is the portrait of Jacobus Zaffius of 1611, and his breakthrough came in 1616 with the life-sized group portrait The Banquet of the Officers of the St George Militia Company. His best-known sitter was René Descartes, painted in 1649. He married Anneke Harmensdochter around 1610, and after her death in 1615 he married Lysbeth Reyniers in 1617, and they had eight children.

Hals painted wealthy citizens, civic guards and the regents of local hospitals, and also itinerant players, fishwives and tavern figures. In his group portraits each sitter is shown differently, with unidealised faces and a variety of poses. Between 1620 and 1640 he painted many married couples as pairs of panels, and only once on a single canvas. He worked with visible brushstrokes, which earlier painters had treated as a flaw, though most of his works were built up in layers rather than thrown onto the canvas in one go.

His palette darkened over his life, probably because of the sober dress of his Protestant sitters. Unlike Rembrandt, he refused to travel to his clients, and when he began a militia portrait in Amsterdam it was finished by Pieter Codde because he insisted that the sitters come to Haarlem. Five of his sons became painters, as did his brother Dirck Hals.

Hals lived so long that he went out of fashion and fell into financial difficulty. In 1652 he sold his belongings to settle a debt with a baker, and in 1664 the city gave him an annuity of 200 florins. He died in Haarlem on 26 August 1666 and was buried in the Grote Kerk. His reputation waned, and for two centuries some of his paintings sold for a few pounds or shillings. From the 1860s the critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger restored his standing. His technique influenced Édouard Manet, Claude Monet, Gustave Courbet and others, and Vincent van Gogh wrote to his brother of the joy of seeing a Frans Hals. Several of his main works hang in the Frans Hals Museum in Haarlem.
frantz-fanon: Frantz Fanon was born on 20 July 1925 in Fort-de-France, Martinique, then part of the French colonial empire, into a middle-class family. His father was a customs officer and his mother a shopkeeper. After the fall of France in June 1940, Martinique came under the control of naval elements loyal to the Vichy regime, whose rule Fanon later described as that of authentic racists. In January 1943 he left for the British colony of Dominica to join Allied sympathisers, and after a local uprising overthrew the regime in June 1943 he returned and enlisted in the 5th Antillean Marching Battalion of the Free French Forces. He later studied at the University of Lyon, including literature, drama and philosophy, and qualified as a psychiatrist in 1951.

Fanon did his residency at Saint-Alban-sur-Limagnole under François Tosquelles, who emphasised the role of culture in psychopathology. While finishing his residency in Lyon he published Black Skin, White Masks in 1952, an analysis of the psychological effects of colonial subjugation on black people. The book began as a doctoral dissertation that Lyon rejected. From 1953 he worked in Algeria as head of a service at the Blida-Joinville Psychiatric Hospital. He developed sociotherapy and trained nurses and interns.

After the Algerian revolution began in November 1954, Fanon joined the Front de Libération Nationale (FLN). He treated both French soldiers who had carried out torture and Algerian victims of it. In November 1956 he submitted a letter of resignation to the Resident Minister, and he was expelled from Algeria in January 1957. He then moved to Tunis, wrote for the FLN newspaper Al Moudjahid and served as ambassador to Ghana for the Provisional Algerian Government.

A Dying Colonialism, published in 1959, recounts how Algerians changed old cultural patterns during the revolution. In The Wretched of the Earth, published shortly before his death, Fanon defends the right of a colonised people to use violence to gain independence. He also describes the forces leading either to national independence or to neocolonialism, and the French government censored the book. He was influenced by Jean-Paul Sartre, Jacques Lacan, Marxism and the Négritude of Aimé Césaire. Fanon died on 6 December 1961, having gone to the United States for leukaemia treatment in October. His work influenced Steve Biko in South Africa, Amílcar Cabral in Guinea-Bissau and the Black Power movement in the United States.
franz-grillparzer: Franz Grillparzer was born in Vienna on 15 January 1791. His father, a lawyer ruined by Napoleon's invasion, wanted him to follow the same profession, and Franz entered the University of Vienna in 1807 as a student of jurisprudence, and his father died two years later. After his degree in 1811 he tutored privately, and in 1813 he became a clerk at the Imperial Hofkammer. In 1832 he became director of its archives and held the post until he retired in 1856. He regarded his official career merely as a means of independence, and he never married. From early youth he had a strong literary impulse, and he studied Spanish drama, especially Pedro Calderón de la Barca.

The Ancestress, published in 1816, was a gruesome fate-tragedy, and its first performances in 1817 brought him wide recognition. Sappho followed in 1818, and in 1821 he completed the trilogy The Golden Fleece. Some critics consider its last part, Medea, his highest achievement. He wrote King Ottokar's Fortune and Rise in 1823, but difficulties with the censor delayed its performance until 19 February 1825.

His only comedy, Woe to Him Who Lies, failed at its premiere on 6 March 1838, and he turned his back on the theatre. After that he published only the fragment Esther, but three finished tragedies were found among his papers, among them The Jewess of Toledo and Libussa. He also wrote the novella The Poor Musician in 1848.

After 1840 he almost passed from the memory of his contemporaries. Heinrich Laube became artistic director of Vienna's court theatre in 1849 and staged his forgotten works, and Grillparzer became the most popular author of the day, ranked with Goethe and Schiller. He was made a member of the Academy of Sciences and in 1861 was elected to the Austrian Herrenhaus. His eightieth birthday was marked by all classes from the court downwards.

He died in Vienna on 21 January 1872. He was buried first in the Währinger Cemetery, now Schubertpark, and now lies at Hietzing Cemetery. He is regarded as the national poet of Austria, and the Grillparzer Prize and Grillparzer Ring are named after him. He wrote the oration for Ludwig van Beethoven's funeral and the epitaph for Franz Schubert.
franz-joseph-i: Franz Joseph was born on 18 August 1830 at Schönbrunn Palace in Vienna, the eldest son of Archduke Franz Karl and Sophie, Princess of Bavaria. His uncle Ferdinand, emperor from 1835, was disabled by seizures and his father was unambitious, so his politically ambitious mother raised him as a future emperor, stressing devotion, responsibility and diligence. During the Revolutions of 1848 he joined Field Marshal Radetzky's campaign in Italy and received his baptism of fire at Santa Lucia on 5 May. In December 1848 Ferdinand abdicated at Olomouc as part of Felix zu Schwarzenberg's plan to end the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, and Franz Joseph took the throne at eighteen.

Largely considered a reactionary, he spent his early reign resisting constitutionalism. After Schwarzenberg's death in 1852 the emperor effectively became his own prime minister, and he was forced to issue the February Patent of 1861 to borrow money abroad. Austria lost influence in Italy after the Second Italian War of Independence in 1859 and the war of 1866. The Austro-Prussian War of 1866 ended in the Peace of Prague, which settled the German Question in favour of Prussia, though he ceded no territory to it. His main foreign-policy goal had been unification of Germany under the Habsburgs. In 1854 he married his cousin Elisabeth of Bavaria, whom he had chosen in place of the bride his mother favoured.

In the Compromise of 1867 he granted Hungary greater autonomy and created the dual monarchy of Austria-Hungary, which he then ruled peacefully for 45 years. In 1873 he joined the League of Three Emperors with Wilhelm I of Germany and Alexander II of Russia. His troops occupied Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Congress of Berlin in 1878, and in 1908 he annexed it, causing the Bosnian Crisis. In 1903 he used the last veto by a Catholic ruler on a papal election, against Cardinal Rampolla.

He suffered personal tragedies: the execution of his brother Maximilian of Mexico in 1867, the suicide of his son Rudolf in 1889, and the assassinations of his wife Elisabeth in 1898 and of his nephew and heir, Archduke Franz Ferdinand, in Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Austria-Hungary's declaration of war on Serbia then began the First World War. Told of the killing, he said that a superior power had restored the order he had been unable to maintain.

Franz Joseph died at Schönbrunn on the evening of 21 November 1916, at the age of 86, of pneumonia caught after a walk with King Ludwig III of Bavaria. After almost 68 years on the throne he was succeeded by his grandnephew Charles I, and he is buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna. Franz Josef Land in the Arctic was named for him in 1873.
franz-marc: Franz Marc was born in Munich on 8 February 1880. His father, Wilhelm Marc, was a landscape painter, and his mother was a devout Calvinist. At 17 he wanted to study theology, as his older brother Paul had, but two years later he enrolled in an arts programme. After a year of military service he began studies at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich in 1900. He spent time in Paris in 1903 and 1907, copying paintings in museums, and found a strong affinity with the work of Vincent van Gogh. He married twice, first Marie Schnür and then Maria Franck, and both were artists.

In 1906 Marc travelled with his brother, a Byzantine expert, to Thessaloniki and Mount Athos. In 1910 he became a friend of the artist August Macke. A critic, Morgan Meis, writes that Marc became an artist in the winter of 1910 to 1911, when his animals began to emerge on the canvas with color as the main thing. In 1911 he founded the journal Der Blaue Reiter with Macke, Wassily Kandinsky and others who had split from the Neue Künstlervereinigung. The first Blue Rider exhibition was held at the Thannhauser Galleries in Munich between December 1911 and January 1912, and travelled to Berlin, Cologne, Hagen and Frankfurt.

In 1912 Marc met Robert Delaunay, whose use of color and the Cubist method influenced him. He painted The Tiger and Red Deer in 1912, and The Tower of Blue Horses, The Foxes and Fate of the Animals in 1913. His work is characterised by bright primary color and a near-cubist treatment of animals. Marc gave colors a meaning, using blue for masculinity and spirituality, yellow for feminine joy and red for violence. He made some sixty prints in woodcut and lithography. He wrote to his wife that Fate of the Animals was like a premonition of the war.

Marc was drafted into the Imperial German Army as a cavalryman in 1914. By 1916 he was a lieutenant, had been awarded the Iron Cross, and had turned to camouflage, painting canvas covers to hide artillery from aerial observation. The government had listed notable artists to be withdrawn from combat for their own safety, but he was killed instantly by a shell splinter at the Battle of Verdun before orders reached him. In 1936 and 1937 the Nazis condemned him as a degenerate artist and ordered about 130 of his works removed from German museums. The Blue Horses was auctioned in Lucerne in 1939. Most of his work survived the war, and the Franz Marc Museum at Kochel am See opened in 1986.
franz-schubert: Franz Schubert was born in Himmelpfortgrund, now part of Alsergrund in Vienna, on 31 January 1797, the twelfth child of the parish schoolmaster Franz Theodor Florian Schubert and Maria Elisabeth Katharina Vietz. His father gave him lessons from the age of five, and his brother Ignaz taught him the piano, though Schubert surpassed him within a few months. In 1808, aged eleven, he entered the Stadtkonvikt school, where he came to know the orchestral music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. He left in November 1813 for teacher training and in 1814 taught the youngest pupils at his father's school, while continuing private lessons in composition with Antonio Salieri until 1817.

Schubert was immensely prolific. In 1815 he composed over 20,000 bars of music, including about 140 Lieder. In 1816 Franz von Schober invited him to lodge at his mother's house, and Schubert gave up teaching to devote himself to composition. In 1817 he met the baritone Johann Michael Vogl, who sang many of his songs. In March 1821 Vogl sang Erlkönig at a concert that was extremely well received. Publishers remained distant, and Anton Diabelli agreed to print the first seven opus numbers only on commission.

In 1822 he began the Symphony in B minor, known as the Unfinished Symphony, with two movements and sketches of a third; why he left it unfinished is still discussed. In 1823 he wrote his first large-scale song cycle, Die schöne Müllerin, and the later cycle Winterreise, of 1827, is widely considered one of the pinnacles of Lieder. In his career he wrote roughly 630 songs, seven complete symphonies, seven masses and a large body of piano and chamber music. In March 1828 he gave a concert of his works to critical acclaim, the only one of his career.

Schubert's health deteriorated in the late 1820s, and symptoms of syphilis had first appeared in 1823. At the beginning of November 1828 he fell ill with headaches, fever, swollen joints and vomiting, and he died on 19 November 1828. The cause was officially attributed to typhoid fever, but some historians believe it was syphilis. During his lifetime his appreciation was limited to a small circle of admirers in Vienna, and about 100 opus numbers were published, mainly songs, chamber music and small piano pieces. Many larger works stayed hidden in cabinets and file boxes until George Grove and Arthur Sullivan travelled to Vienna in October 1867 and found manuscripts of six of the symphonies. Mendelssohn, Schumann, Liszt and Brahms discovered and championed his works.
franz-von-papen: Franz von Papen was born on 29 October 1879 in Werl, Westphalia, into a wealthy noble Catholic family. His father was a Prussian cavalry officer. Papen entered a cadet school at the age of 11 and trained for the German General Staff, which he joined as a captain in March 1913. He became a military attaché in the United States in December 1913 and also observed the Mexican Revolution, where he was involved in selling arms to the government of General Victoriano Huerta.

He later commanded a battalion on the Western Front, fighting on the Somme and at Vimy Ridge, and ended the war on the General Staff in the Middle East as a lieutenant colonel. After 1920 he entered politics as a monarchist on the national conservative wing of the Centre Party.

President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Papen chancellor on 1 June 1932, on the advice of General Kurt von Schleicher. His cabinet was nicknamed the cabinet of barons, and he had little support in the Reichstag. He governed by presidential decree, launched the Preußenschlag against the government of Prussia led by the Social Democratic Party, and dissolved the Reichstag twice. Hindenburg removed him in favour of Schleicher.

Papen met Adolf Hitler secretly in Cologne on 4 January 1933 and on 22 January agreed to support him as chancellor with himself as vice-chancellor. Hindenburg appointed Hitler on 30 January. Papen believed Hitler could be contained, but Hitler and his allies quickly marginalised him. On 17 June 1934 he gave a speech at the University of Marburg calling for an end to SA terror. During the Night of the Long Knives his office was ransacked and associates including Herbert von Bose, Erich Klausener and Edgar Julius Jung were shot. Papen resigned, then served as ambassador in Vienna from 1934 to 1938 and in Ankara from 1939 to 1944. He joined the Nazi Party in 1938.

Papen was captured on 14 April 1945 and was one of the defendants at the main Nuremberg trial. The tribunal found no solid evidence that he had been involved in the annexation of Austria. It acquitted him, saying that his actions were political immoralities that were not punishable under the charge of conspiracy to commit crimes against peace. A West German denazification court later sentenced him to eight years of hard labour, but he was released on appeal in 1949. His memoirs of 1952 downplayed his involvement and portrayed him as a tragic patriot. He died on 2 May 1969. He is largely remembered for his role in Hitler's rise to power.
frascati: Frascati is a city in the Metropolitan City of Rome Capital, in Lazio, on the Alban Hills 20 kilometres south-east of Rome and close to the ancient city of Tusculum. The most important archaeological find nearby is a patrician Roman villa of the late Republic, probably belonging to Lucullus. In the first century CE its owner was Gaius Sallustius Crispus Passienus, who married Agrippina the Younger, mother of Nero.

According to the Liber Pontificalis Frascati was a little village in the ninth century. Its name probably comes from a local tradition of collecting firewood, called frasche in Italian. After the destruction of Tusculum in 1191 the population increased and the bishopric moved to Frascati. Raids impoverished it, and baronial families such as the Colonna held it until Pope Pius II fortified it with walls in 1460. In 1538 Pope Paul III conferred the title of civitas on it, with the name Tusculum Novum, and building of the cathedral began in 1598.

On 1 May 1527 a Landsknecht company that had sacked Rome approached the town but turned aside at a shrine of the Virgin Mary, and a church commemorates the event. On 15 September 1616 the first public and free school in Europe was established on the initiative of Saint Joseph Calasanz. Frascati was annexed to the French Empire in 1809, and in 1837 it was the only town to open its doors to 5,000 people fleeing plague in Rome. In 1943 it held the German general headquarters for the Mediterranean zone and was heavily bombed, and about half its buildings were destroyed. It was liberated on 4 June 1944.

From the sixteenth century popes, cardinals and Roman nobles built villas on the slopes as status symbols, designed for social life rather than farming, among them Villa Aldobrandini, Villa Falconieri and Villa Mondragone. The cathedral, rebuilt after the bombing, holds the tombstone of Charles Edward Stuart. The town produces a white wine of its name and hosts scientific laboratories, among them the Laboratori Nazionali di Frascati, where the first Italian particle accelerator was developed in the late 1950s.
fraser-river: The Fraser rises at Fraser Pass in the Canadian Rocky Mountains, near the border with Alberta, and flows for 1,375 kilometres into the Strait of Georgia just south of Vancouver. It drains 220,000 square kilometres and discharges about 20 million tons of sediment into the ocean each year. It turns sharply south at Giscome Portage and meets the Nechako River at Prince George. South of Williams Lake it cuts the Fraser Canyon. At Hell's Gate the walls force the whole river through a gap only 35 metres wide. Yale is the head of navigation, and below it the river crosses the Fraser Valley and splits around Lulu Island and Sea Island before reaching the sea.

The river is named after Simon Fraser, who led a North West Company expedition in 1808 from the site of present-day Prince George almost to its mouth. On 14 June 1792 the Spanish explorers Dionisio Alcalá Galiano and Cayetano Valdés anchored in the North Arm, the first Europeans officially to enter it. Alexander Mackenzie explored the upper reaches in 1793, and Fraser traced the river in 1808 and confirmed it was not connected to the Columbia.

The Hudson's Bay Company built the original Fort Langley in 1827, the first settlement of mixed European and Indigenous ancestry in southern British Columbia. In 1828 George Simpson went down the canyon and wrote that the passage would be certain death in nine attempts out of ten, so Fort Vancouver stayed the company's main Pacific depot. After the Oregon Treaty of 1846 the Fraser was the essential route between the Interior and the Lower Coast, and in 1858 the Fraser Canyon Gold Rush brought prospectors. The worst floods came in 1894 and 1948. In 1998 it was designated a Canadian Heritage River.

The Fraser is the largest producer of salmon in Canada, and holds white sturgeon, steelhead trout and all five Pacific salmon species. Its banks are rich farmland, its water serves pulp mills, and a few dams on its tributaries make electric power, but the main flow has never been dammed. The estuary is a site of hemispheric importance in the Western Hemisphere Shorebird Reserve Network.
frauenfeld: Frauenfeld is the capital of the canton of Thurgau in Switzerland and lies along both banks of the Murg river. The earliest traces of human settlement are La Tène graves east of Langdorf, and a Roman road from Oberwinterthur to Pfyn ran through what is now the Allmend. Two Roman villas have been found, at Thalbach and Oberkirch, and by the 9th century a church stood at Oberkirch. By the end of the 1220s a fortified tower with a mill and chapel had been built, and a village grew around it on land owned by Reichenau Abbey. The tower grew into Frauenfeld Castle.

Frauenfeld is first mentioned in 1246 as Vrowinvelt, and in 1286 as a city. By then it had been integrated into the Habsburg territories, and it belonged to the Habsburg district of Kyburg. How the city came into being is not clear. In 1374 the Habsburgs gave the right of judgment for all Thurgau to the Duke of Frauenfeld, and the castle became the centre of the Habsburg district of Frauenfeld. The Landsberger family held it until 1534. In 1460 the Swiss Confederation captured Thurgau, including Frauenfeld.

Under the Confederation Frauenfeld became the centre from which the Confederates managed Thurgau. After 1499 it was the home of a Confederation court, and after 1504 the Thurgau governor lived there, after 1532 in the castle. The Reformation affected the city, and Catholic and Protestant councils shared its government. Protestants had no church of their own until 1645. The assembly of the Confederacy, the Tagsatzung, met at Frauenfeld in the 18th century, and the fall of the old Confederacy in 1798 ended those gatherings. Fires in 1771 and 1788 destroyed nearly all the houses, so the present old city dates from the end of the 18th century.

The constitution of 1798, under the Helvetic Republic, made Frauenfeld the capital of the new canton of Thurgau, although Weinfelden, geographically central, was the main alternative. Since 1832 the cantonal parliament has met twice a year alternately in Frauenfeld and Weinfelden. On 25 May 1799 French and Austrian forces fought a battle in the city, and the Austrians were victorious. The city walls were demolished between 1808 and 1834. The old city is included in the Inventory of Swiss Heritage Sites, and the castle, which holds the Historical Museum, and the town hall are among ten buildings of national significance. The Thurgauer Zeitung, founded in 1798 as a weekly journal, is still published.
frederic-chopin: Frédéric François Chopin was born in Żelazowa Wola, 46 kilometres west of Warsaw, in the Duchy of Warsaw. The baptismal record gives his birthday as 22 February 1810, but the composer and his family used 1 March, now generally accepted. His father, Nicolas Chopin, was a Frenchman from Lorraine who had emigrated to Poland in 1787 and insisted on Polish at home; his mother was Justyna Krzyżanowska. In October 1810 the family moved to Warsaw, where his father taught French at the Warsaw Lyceum. His first professional tutor, from 1816 to 1821, was the pianist Wojciech Żywny. A child prodigy, Chopin gave public concerts by the age of seven.

Chopin wrote his early works in Warsaw, among them six works for piano and orchestra, including two piano concertos. He left Poland at 20, less than a month before the November 1830 Uprising, and at 21 settled in Paris. He gave only about thirty public performances, preferring the salon, and lived by selling compositions and giving piano lessons, for which he was in high demand. He befriended Franz Liszt and was admired by Robert Schumann. After a failed engagement to Maria Wodzińska in 1836 to 1837 he kept up an often troubled relationship with the writer George Sand. Their brief and unhappy visit to Mallorca in 1838 to 1839 proved one of his most productive periods of composition.

More than 230 of Chopin's works survive, all involving the piano. His influences included Bach and Mozart, Polish folk music and the Paris salons. He took the nocturne, invented by John Field, to a deeper level of sophistication, was the first to write ballades and scherzi as individual concert pieces, and established the free-standing prelude with his Op. 28, published in 1839. His mazurkas were written for the concert hall rather than the dance hall, and his waltzes for the salon.

In his last years Jane Stirling supported him financially. He died in Paris on 17 October 1849 at the age of 39. Debussy dedicated his 1915 piano Études to Chopin's memory, and the Fryderyk Chopin Institute, created by the Polish parliament, hosts the International Chopin Piano Competition.
frederick-banting: Frederick Banting was born on 14 November 1891 on his family's farm near Alliston, Ontario, the youngest of five children. He was a shy boy who struggled at school, and he failed French and English composition in his matriculation examinations before passing in July 1910. He enrolled at the University of Toronto, failed his first year, then entered the medical programme in 1912 and specialised in surgery. He joined the Royal Canadian Army Medical Corps in 1915 and served in England and France. At the Battle of Cambrai in 1918 he was struck by shrapnel, and he was awarded the Military Cross for exceptional bravery in attending the wounded under fire. After the war he set up a practice in London, Ontario, which proved unsuccessful.

Preparing a talk on the pancreas for 1 November 1920, Banting read reports suggesting that diabetes resulted from a lack of a hormone made in the islets of Langerhans. An article by Moses Barron on closing the pancreatic duct suggested to him a way to extract the hormone before digestive enzymes destroyed it. John Macleod, professor of physiology at the University of Toronto, provided facilities and a student, Charles Best, and the biochemist James Collip later helped. In November 1921 Banting obtained insulin from the pancreas of fetal calves. The first injection was given to 14-year-old Leonard Thompson at Toronto General Hospital on 11 January 1922.

Banting and Macleod shared the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Banting split his half with Best, and Macleod split the other with Collip. At 32 he was the youngest laureate in the field. Parliament granted him a life annuity of $7,500, and he was knighted in 1934. He researched silicosis, cancer and drowning, and from 1938 he worked with the Royal Canadian Air Force on the problems of high-altitude pilots, helping Wilbur Franks with the G-suit. He was also a keen amateur painter and friend of the Group of Seven artists A. Y. Jackson and Lawren Harris.

In February 1941 Banting was a passenger on a Lockheed aircraft bound for England to test the Franks flying suit. After leaving Gander, Newfoundland, both engines failed and the plane crashed at Musgrave Harbour. Banting survived the impact and gave first aid, but died of his injuries the next day, 21 February. He is buried in Mount Pleasant Cemetery in Toronto. His former home in London, Ontario, was declared a National Historic Site of Canada in 1997 and contains a museum of the history of insulin. The Banting Research Foundation was created in 1925, and the American Diabetes Association has awarded Banting Medals since 1941. In 1991 his birthday was made World Diabetes Day.
frederick-barbarossa: Frederick was born in mid-December 1122, probably at Hagenau, the son of Duke Frederick II of Swabia of the Hohenstaufen family and Judith of Bavaria of the rival House of Welf. Descent from the two leading families of the empire made him an acceptable candidate to the princes who elected the king. He could neither read nor write and did not speak Latin until later in life. In 1147 he joined the Second Crusade, and after his father's death that April he succeeded him as Duke of Swabia.

When his uncle Conrad III died in February 1152, Frederick and the prince-bishop of Bamberg both said that the dying king had handed him the royal insignia. The princes chose Frederick at Frankfurt on 4 March 1152, and he was crowned at Aachen on 9 March. He sought to restore the empire to the position it held under Charlemagne and Otto the Great. He made six expeditions into Italy. The first, in 1154–55, brought the destruction of Tortona and the suppression of the republican commune of Rome led by Arnold of Brescia, who was hanged.

The Diet of Roncaglia in 1158 began a long struggle with Pope Alexander III. The Lombard League opposed him, and the cities beat him at the Battle of Legnano on 29 May 1176, where he was wounded and for a time believed dead. In the Peace of Venice in 1177 he was formally reconciled with Alexander. His use of Roman law gave him trained lawyers to administer his lands, and from 1165 he pursued policies to encourage trade; the number of mints in Germany rose ninefold in the reigns of Frederick and his son Henry.

In 1188 at the Diet of Mainz Frederick took the crusader's vow. On the advice of local Armenians he followed a shortcut along the Saleph River, and he drowned there on 10 June 1190. Accounts differ: one says he swam across against advice, another that he was thrown from his horse and drowned weighed down by armour. Most of his army abandoned the crusade before reaching Acre.

Legend says he sleeps with his knights in a cave in the Kyffhäuser mountains and will wake to restore Germany. The nickname Barbarossa, Red Beard, was first used by the Florentines in 1298. In the 19th and early 20th centuries the Risorgimento, the German Empire and the Nazi movement each used him as a symbol.
frederick-douglass: Frederick Augustus Washington Bailey was born into slavery in Talbot County, on the Eastern Shore of Maryland. His mother, Harriet Bailey, was enslaved, and his father, who may have been her master, was apparently white; Douglass later wrote that he searched in vain for his father's name. He did not know his age. Records of his former owner, Aaron Anthony, led the historian Dickson J. Preston to place his birth in February 1818, and Douglass chose to celebrate 14 February.

At six he was moved to the Wye House plantation. After Anthony's death he was sent to Baltimore, to Hugh and Sophia Auld, and in 1835 he was hired out as a ship caulker, where white workers who feared competition from enslaved labour abused him. In 1837 he met Anna Murray, a free Black woman, who encouraged him and gave him money. He escaped to the North in September 1838 and settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts, taking the surname Douglass on the suggestion of Nathan Johnson, who had read Walter Scott's The Lady of the Lake.

Douglass became a leader of the abolitionist movement in Massachusetts and New York. His Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave (1845) was an immediate bestseller, reprinted nine times in three years. Fearing that publicity would draw the attention of his former owner, friends sent him to tour Ireland and Britain from August 1845. On his return in 1847, with £500 from English supporters, he began the North Star in Rochester, New York, which he later merged into Frederick Douglass' Paper.

In 1848 he was the only Black person at the Seneca Falls Convention, where he spoke for women's suffrage. During the Civil War he argued that African Americans should fight, published Men of Color to Arms! in March 1863, and two of his sons joined the 54th Massachusetts Infantry Regiment. After the war he campaigned for the rights of freed people, became president of the Freedman's Savings Bank in 1874 shortly before its failure, and in 1872 was nominated, without his knowledge, as vice president on the Equal Rights Party ticket.

Douglass wrote two further autobiographies, My Bondage and My Freedom (1855) and Life and Times of Frederick Douglass (1881, revised 1892). On 20 February 1895 he attended a meeting of the National Council of Women in Washington, D.C., received a standing ovation and died of a heart attack shortly after returning home. His funeral was held at the Metropolitan African Methodist Episcopal Church.
frederick-i-of-prussia: Frederick was born in Königsberg on 11 July 1657, the third son of Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, and Louise Henriette of Orange-Nassau. His cousin on his mother's side was King William III of England. On the death of his father on 29 April 1688 he became Elector Frederick III of Brandenburg and Duke of Prussia, two lands ruled in personal union as Brandenburg-Prussia. Soon after succeeding he founded a new city next to Dorotheenstadt and named it Friedrichstadt after himself. Unlike his father, who had sought an alliance with Louis XIV, he opposed France, took Brandenburg into the League of Augsburg and in 1689 captured Bonn, yet he styled his court on that of Louis XIV.

Frederick wanted the more prestigious title of king, but under Germanic law no kingdom could exist within the Holy Roman Empire except Bohemia. Frederick argued that Prussia had never been part of the Empire and that he ruled it with full sovereignty. Emperor Leopold I agreed in the Crown Treaty of 16 November 1700, ostensibly in exchange for an alliance against Louis XIV in the War of the Spanish Succession and 8,000 Prussian troops. Frederick crowned himself on 18 January 1701 in Königsberg. The Sejm of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth called this illegal. Because Hohenzollern sovereignty over the Duchy of Prussia depended on the male line continuing, Frederick took the style King in Prussia rather than King of Prussia.

England recognised him first, and he provided it with troops, though he often withheld them until he got the ceremonial concessions he wanted. His royal title applied to Prussia only, and in Brandenburg he remained an elector under the emperor. He founded the Prussian Academy of Arts in 1696 and the Academy of Sciences in 1700. His grandson Frederick the Great, who first styled himself King of Prussia in 1772, called him the mercenary king, because he profited from hiring out Prussian troops.

Frederick married three times: Elizabeth Henrietta of Hesse-Kassel in 1679, Sophia Charlotte of Hanover, with whom he had the future Frederick William I, and in 1708 Sophia Louise of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. He died in Berlin on 25 February 1713 and is entombed in Berlin Cathedral. Frederick the Great wrote of him that he was great in small matters, and small in great matters.
frederick-iii-holy-roman-emperor: Frederick was born on 21 September 1415 at Innsbruck, the eldest son of Duke Ernest of Inner Austria and Cymburgis of Masovia. His father died in 1424, making the nine-year-old duke of Inner Austria, which comprised Styria, Carinthia and Carniola, with his uncle Frederick IV of Austria as regent. Relatives kept him from ruling until 1435, and his younger brother Albert VI began a long rivalry by asserting a claim to co-rule. In 1436 he made a pilgrimage to the Holy Land. From 1439 he was regent for Sigismund in Tyrol and for his nephew Ladislaus the Posthumous in the duchy of Austria. On 2 February 1440 the prince-electors met at Frankfurt and unanimously elected him King of the Romans.

In 1452 he travelled to Italy to receive his bride, Eleanor of Portugal, and to be crowned emperor. He was crowned with the German crown as King of Italy on 16 March, married that afternoon, and crowned emperor on 19 March. He was the last Holy Roman Emperor crowned in Rome. His reign of 41 years was the longest in the empire's history. His style was hesitant, and Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, said he wanted to conquer the world while remaining seated. Historians now see his delaying as a way of coping with far-flung possessions.

He prevailed over his Habsburg rivals largely by outliving them. He gained Lower Austria from Ladislaus in 1457 and Upper Austria from Albert VI, who besieged him in Vienna in 1462. He failed against Matthias Corvinus of Hungary, who defeated him in 1485 and held Vienna until his death. Frederick fled to Graz and later Linz. Ottoman raids struck Carniola, Styria and Carinthia, prompting the Carinthian Peasant Revolt of 1478. In 1486 Maximilian was elected king in his father's lifetime, and he joined the empire's reform first under pressure in Frederick's last years. His personal motto was the string A.E.I.O.U., which he never explained.

Frederick's son Maximilian married Mary of Burgundy, heir to the Burgundian lands, which gave rise to the Habsburg saying that others should wage wars while Austria should marry. In 1493 his left leg was amputated at Linz on 8 June, a well-documented medieval operation, and he died on 19 August 1493, aged 77. His tomb in St Stephen's Cathedral, made by Nikolaus Gerhaert, is among the most important sculptures of the late Middle Ages.

The Austrian historian Adam Wandruszka calls him the true founder of the Habsburg imperial position, and German historians tend to be more critical than Austrian ones. He collected 110 books that formed the core of the later Bibliotheca Regia, forerunner of the Austrian National Library.
frederick-iii-of-denmark: Frederick was born on 18 March 1609 at Haderslev in Slesvig, the second-eldest son of Christian IV and Anne Catherine of Brandenburg. Until the death of his older brother Christian in June 1647 he had no prospect of the throne. He was educated at Sorø Academy and studied in the Netherlands and France, with interests in theology, natural sciences and Scandinavian history, and he is described as reserved, a prince who seldom laughed and wrote little.

His collection of books became the foundation of the Royal Library in Copenhagen. As a young man he administered the Prince-Archbishopric of Bremen and the Prince-Bishopric of Verden on his father's behalf, and on 1 October 1643 he married Sophie Amalie of Brunswick-Lüneburg.

Christian IV died on 28 February 1648, and Frederick was elected only after signing a charter, the Haandfæstning, that curtailed royal power in favour of the Rigsraadet, the royal council. He nevertheless held more effective power than the charter allowed, and in 1651 he removed two of the council's most influential members, his brothers-in-law Corfitz Ulfeldt and Hannibal Sehested.

He declared war on Sweden in 1657, but in January and February 1658 Charles X Gustav marched across the frozen Belts, and Frederick had to accept the treaties of Taastrup and Roskilde. When the Swedish army landed at Korsør on 17 July 1658, Frederick is said to have refused to flee Copenhagen, saying "I will die in my nest", and led the defence with the mayor Hans Nansen. A Dutch fleet defeated Charles X in the Battle of the Sound on 29 October. The Treaty of Copenhagen of May 1660 confirmed the loss of Scania, Halland and Blekinge, while Bornholm and parts of Schleswig returned to Denmark.

Frederick used his popularity to turn the elective monarchy into an absolute one by the Revolution of 1660. At the Estates in September 1660 he played the different Estates against one another and won support for a hereditary monarchy and the annulment of the Haandfæstning. In 1665 the Kongeloven, or Lex Regia, set down absolute rule in writing and led to the abolition of the Council of the Realm.

Frederick changed the administration from a chancellery to colleges and replaced fiefs with amt counties. He died at Copenhagen Castle in 1670 and is buried in Roskilde Cathedral. Absolute monarchy lasted until 1814 in Norway and 1848 in Denmark.
frederick-vi-of-denmark: Frederick was born at Christiansborg Palace in Copenhagen on 28 January 1768, the eldest of two children of Christian VII and Caroline Mathilde. His father suffered increasing mental illness, and from 1770 to 1772 the king's physician Johann Friedrich Struensee was de facto regent and the queen's lover. Struensee had the boy raised on the principles of Rousseau's Émile. In a palace coup on 17 January 1772 he was deposed and later executed, and the queen was exiled, so that the four-year-old Frederick never saw his mother again. Real power then lay with the queen dowager Juliana Maria and Ove Høegh-Guldberg.

The sixteen-year-old crown prince was confirmed on 4 April 1784, and on 14 April he seized full power as regent, dismissing ministers loyal to the queen dowager. He ruled under his father's name until 1808. With the minister Andreas Peter Bernstorff he introduced reforms in the spirit of enlightened absolutism: the abolition of serfdom in Denmark in 1788, of hanging in 1789, and in 1803 of Dano-Norwegian involvement in the transatlantic slave trade.

He became king on 13 March 1808. After the British bombardment of Copenhagen in 1807 he allied Denmark-Norway with France, and the Gunboat War with Britain lasted until the Treaty of Kiel in 1814, which cost him the Norwegian crown. He refused a request from the Allies to change sides after the French defeat in Russia in 1812. Many historians have called him stubborn and misguidedly loyal to Napoleon, but others argue he stayed in the alliance to protect Norway, which depended on grain imports and was a target of Swedish ambitions. After 1814 he gave up his liberal ideas, and censorship and a poor economy marked the years. In 1834 he created the consultative Assemblies of the Estate.

Frederick patronised astronomy and in 1832 offered gold medals to anyone who discovered a comet with a telescope. He had no surviving legitimate sons, and died at Amalienborg Palace on 3 December 1839, succeeded by his half-cousin Christian. He was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. Of eight children by his wife Marie Sophie only two daughters, Caroline and Wilhelmine, lived to adulthood. The Royal Frederick University in Oslo was named in his honour.
frederick-vii-of-denmark: Frederick was born on 6 October 1808 at Levetzau's Palace, part of the Amalienborg Palace complex in Copenhagen, the second but eldest surviving child of Prince Christian Frederick, the future Christian VIII, and Duchess Charlotte Frederica of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. After his parents divorced he had a rather neglected childhood, and his youth was marked by private scandals.

His first two marriages ended in scandal and divorce: in 1828 to his second cousin Princess Vilhelmine Marie, a daughter of Frederick VI, divorced in 1837, and in 1841 to Duchess Caroline Charlotte Mariane of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, divorced in 1846. On 7 August 1850 he married morganatically Louise Christina Rasmussen, a milliner and former ballet dancer, whom he created Lensgrevinde Danner. The marriage aroused indignation among the nobility and the bourgeoisie, but she seems to have steadied him.

Frederick succeeded in January 1848 and was at once met by demands for a constitution. The Schleswig-Holsteiners wanted an independent state, while the Danes wished to keep South Jutland Danish. The king soon yielded to the Danes, and in March he accepted the end of absolutism, which led to the June Constitution of 1849. During the First War of Schleswig in 1848 to 1851 he appeared as the national leader, though he took no active part in the fighting.

He behaved on the whole as a constitutional monarch but kept interfering in politics: in 1854 he helped bring down the conservative Ørsted cabinet, and in 1859-60 he accepted a liberal government appointed on his wife's initiative. The National Liberal Party was in office from 1854, and free trade was introduced in 1857. Disputes over Schleswig-Holstein pushed the National Liberals to a more resistant course against the Germans, and shortly before his sudden death the king was ready to sign the November Constitution for Denmark and Schleswig.

Frederick had no legitimate children. In 1852 his second cousin Prince Christian of Glücksburg was chosen heir presumptive, and when Frederick died in 1863 at Glücksburg of erysipelas, Christian became Christian IX. Frederick was buried in Roskilde Cathedral. His death ended the male line of the Oldenburg kings, and the rival claims to the duchies of Schleswig and Holstein led to the Second War of Schleswig. He became one of the best-loved Danish kings, and as a keen antiquarian he helped arouse wide interest in Danish antiquities.
frederick-william-i-of-prussia: Frederick William was born in Berlin on 14 August 1688, the son of King Frederick I of Prussia and Princess Sophia Charlotte of Hanover. A Huguenot governess, Marthe de Roucoulle, raised him in his first years. When the plague of the Great Northern War devastated Prussia, he and a party at court brought down the leading minister Johann Kasimir Kolbe von Wartenberg after an investigation exposed large-scale embezzlement. The episode made him resent crime, corruption and waste, and it was the first time he took an active part in politics. He married his first cousin Sophia Dorothea of Hanover on 28 November 1706, and they had fourteen children.

His father had paid heavily for the royal title and enlarged palaces at great expense, which ruined the state's finances. On taking the throne in 1713 Frederick William dismissed his father's Cabinet of Three Counts and reorganized the finances. He raised excise taxes, subjected the nobility to a land tax and dictated Regulations for State Officials, which set out every public servant's duties; a minister who missed a committee meeting lost six months' pay. He encouraged commerce and farming, reclaimed marshes and stored grain in good years to sell in bad ones.

He expanded the Prussian Army from 38,000 men in 1713 to 80,000 in 1740, so that about one man in twenty-five served. With Leopold I, Prince of Anhalt-Dessau, he reformed training, tactics and conscription, introducing the canton system, and the iron ramrod raised the infantry's rate of fire. Peasants bore military obligations, while the middle class paid an annual tax in place of service. In 1717 he sold the Brandenburg Gold Coast to the Dutch West India Company, preferring to spend on the army. In 1732 he invited Salzburg Protestants to settle in East Prussia, which plague had depopulated in 1709. He joined the Great Northern War briefly, in alliance with Peter the Great, and gained part of Swedish Pomerania with new Baltic ports.

Frederick William had a short temper and sometimes struck servants and even his own children with a cane, and a hereditary disease gave him gout and stomach pains. His relations with his eldest surviving son, the future Frederick II, were hostile. After the prince tried to flee to England with his tutor Hans Hermann von Katte, the king had Katte beheaded in front of him. He died in 1740, aged 51, and was interred at the Garrison Church in Potsdam. His reforms left his son the most formidable army in Europe.
frederick-william-ii-of-prussia: Frederick William was born in Berlin on 25 September 1744, the eldest son of Prince Augustus William of Prussia and Duchess Luise of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. In 1747 his uncle, King Frederick II, took him from his family and had him educated in the spirit of the Enlightenment under the tutor Nicolas de Béguelin, though not for affairs of state. The shy boy could not meet his uncle's demand for audacity, and was punished for rebelliousness.

His father was dismissed from the army in 1757, and after his death Frederick William was confirmed in December 1758 as Prince of Prussia, the heir presumptive. Relations with his uncle cooled. Frederick II arranged his marriages, to Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel in 1765, ended after four years, and to Frederica Louisa of Hesse-Darmstadt in 1769, and kept him ignorant of day-to-day politics.

Frederick William acceded on 17 August 1786. He lightened the burdens of the people, reformed the oppressive French system of tax-collecting, cut customs dues, built roads and canals and ended the state monopolies on coffee, tobacco and sugar. The codification known as the Allgemeines Preußisches Landrecht, begun under Frederick II, was completed in 1794. He turned the kingdom's culture from French towards German: the French Theatre in Berlin became the National Theater on the Gendarmenmarkt, where he declared "We are Germans, and we intend to remain so."

Prussia was isolated in foreign policy when Frederick II died. In reaction to the French Revolution the king ended the German dualism between Prussia and Austria, and at home he tightened censorship and religious control. A devout Protestant, he joined the Rosicrucians in 1781. He was a keen cellist with a court orchestra of 70 musicians, and he patronised the building of the Brandenburg Gate and the Marmorpalais in Potsdam.

In October 1797 Frederick William withdrew to the Marmorpalais, and on 9 November he handed government to his son, Frederick William III. He died there on 16 November 1797, aged 53, and was buried on 11 December in a vault of the old Berlin Cathedral. A eulogy called him the happy enlarger of his country, and his contemporaries called him the Kind One.
frederick-william-iv-of-prussia: Frederick William was born on 15 October 1795, the son of King Frederick William III of Prussia and Queen Louise, and was his mother's favourite son. His tutors included the historian and statesman Friedrich Ancillon. When Louise died in 1810 he saw her death as a punishment from God, and he later tried to live in a way that would absolve him of his guilt. The execution of Louis XVI in 1793 had helped create the conditions for his later orientation toward tradition and historical continuity. After Prussia lost the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt on 14 October 1806 he and his brother William were taken to Königsberg and then fled with their parents to Memel.

He became king in 1840 and was also sovereign prince of Neuchâtel until 1848. Called the romanticist on the throne, he was deeply religious and believed he ruled by divine right. His ideal was a state governed by the Christian estates rather than a constitutional monarchy. He reconciled with the Catholic population by authorising the Cologne Cathedral Building Association in 1840, and in 1842 he founded the civil class of the Order Pour le Mérite on the advice of Alexander von Humboldt. He also promoted architecture, including the Neues Museum in Berlin.

The overthrow of the French July Monarchy in February 1848 set off revolution across Europe. About 300 demonstrators were killed in the Berlin barricade fighting of March, and the king blamed foreigners in his manifesto To my dear Berliners. In December 1848 he dissolved the Prussian National Assembly and imposed a constitution. The Frankfurt Parliament elected him Emperor of the Germans on 28 March 1849. He refused, writing that he did not want it because Austria would then be separated from Germany. He sent troops to put down the Dresden uprising in May 1849, and his Erfurt Union lost the support of Hanover and Saxony by the winter of 1849.

His strokes began on 14 July 1857 and affected his speech. On 7 October 1858 he signed a regency charter for his brother William, and the new regent dismissed the reactionary minister president Otto Theodor von Manteuffel, starting what is called the New Era. Frederick William suffered further strokes in 1859 and 1860 and died on 2 January 1861. He was buried in the Friedenskirche in Potsdam, and his heart was buried separately beside his parents in the Charlottenburg mausoleum. The Berlin-Potsdam palace landscape and Museum Island, which he extended, and the Cologne Cathedral, which he helped to complete, are now UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
fredericton: Fredericton lies in the west-central part of New Brunswick on the Saint John River, which flows through the city from west to east and is its dominant natural feature. The Nashwaak River, a major tributary, joins it here. The downtown stands on flat, low-lying ground on both banks, and the region's water and arable soil make it good farmland. The climate is warm-summer humid continental, with short, warm summers and long, cold winters.

There is evidence of a camp here 12,000 years ago, and the Wolastoqiyik farmed upriver. In the late 1600s French colonists built Fort Nashwaak on the north bank as the capital of Acadia, and it withstood a British attack in 1696. In 1713 Acadians escaping the British takeover of Nova Scotia settled the site and called it Pointe Ste-Anne. It was destroyed in 1758, when its population of about 83 was exiled in the expulsion of the Acadians.

Modern Fredericton begins with the arrival of United Empire Loyalists from New England in 1783. New Brunswick was separated from Nova Scotia the next year, and Pointe-Ste-Anne was renamed Fredericstown after Frederick, second son of George III. It became the capital because its position was thought easier to defend than that of the larger Saint John. Its streets, Charlotte, Brunswick, George, King and Queen, were laid out in a grid and named in keeping with Loyalist sympathies. The Legislative Building went up in 1790, and King's College, now the University of New Brunswick, became the first English-language university in Canada.

It was a British garrison town from 1784 to 1869, and its military compound is preserved as a National Historic Site of Canada. In the 1960s the province's Equal Opportunity program centralised government services there, which increased jobs and population.

Fredericton is an educational and cultural centre of the province. The University of New Brunswick and St. Thomas University are based there, with the Beaverbrook Art Gallery and the Playhouse, the main venue of Theatre New Brunswick. The 2021 census counted 63,116 people in the city, and English is the mother tongue of about 80 per cent.
freetown: The area around the Sierra Leone estuary has been inhabited for millennia, and the earliest known group was the Bullom people. In the sixteenth century the Mane people invaded and established chiefdoms, integrating with the Bullom. In 1787 some 400 formerly enslaved black people sent from London under the Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor founded the Province of Freedom and the settlement of Granville Town on land bought from the Koya Temne subchief King Tom and the regent Naimbana. Some historians question how well the Koya leaders understood the agreement, since they had a different conception of property.

After this colony collapsed, the directors of the Sierra Leone Company were eager to recruit new settlers, and Lieutenant John Clarkson, an abolitionist, was sent to Nova Scotia to register emigrants. Freetown was founded on 11 March 1792 by 1,196 African Americans under Clarkson at the foot of the Cotton Tree, as a settlement for free and freed African American, Afro-Caribbean and Liberated African slaves, whose descendants are the Creole people.

The Temne attacked the colony in 1801 and were repulsed. The British made Freetown a Crown Colony in 1808, and from 1808 to 1874 it was the capital of British West Africa. It was also the base of the Royal Navy's Eastern Squadron, which enforced the ban on the slave trade and brought most of the slaves it freed from trading ships to Freetown. Fourah Bay College, the oldest university in West Africa, was founded there in 1827.

Freetown is the capital and largest city of Sierra Leone, a major port on the Atlantic with a harbour in the estuary of the Sierra Leone River. The Krio language of the Creole people is by far the most widely spoken language in the city.
