Landmarks of its founding include the Cotton Tree, King's Yard Gate, whose inscription declares any slave who passes through it free, and the ruins of the slave fortress on Bunce Island, a boat ride away. St George's Cathedral opened in 1828.
freiberg: Freiberg lies on the northern slope of the Ore Mountains, on the Freiberger Mulde, a tributary of the Mulde. Its centre is about 412 m above sea level, about 31 km west-southwest of Dresden. The nucleus of the town was the forest village of Christiansdorf in the valley of the Münzbach stream. The unwalled town grew on the two slopes of the valley and on the ridge to the west, so that the streets running to the east of the main axis are very steep. The east is the Lower Town, with its lower market, and the west the Upper Town, with the upper market.

The town was founded around 1168, after a silver discovery led to the first Berggeschrey, or mining rush, and for centuries it was a centre of the mining industry in the Ore Mountains. It belonged to the Margraviate of Meissen from 1186, to the Electorate of Saxony from 1423 and to the Kingdom of Saxony from 1806. A fire destroyed the town in 1484, and its Renaissance quarter was built afterwards. The Bergakademie, the mining academy, was established in 1765 by Prince Franz Xaver, regent of Saxony, on plans by Friedrich Wilhelm von Oppel and Friedrich Anton von Heynitz.

Silver mining was discontinued in 1913 because the price of silver had fallen. After it resumed before the Second World War, mining of lead, zinc and tin continued until 1969, and the town was dominated by mining and smelting for around 800 years. In 1944 a subcamp of the Flossenbürg concentration camp was built outside the town, housing over 500 women, including survivors of Auschwitz, until its evacuation in April 1945.

Freiberg has around 41,000 inhabitants. Its historic centre is under monument protection, and together with mining monuments such as the Reiche Zeche ore mine it has been part of the World Heritage Site of the Erzgebirge/Krušnohoří Mining Region since 2019. Freiberg Cathedral holds two organs by Gottfried Silbermann, a tulip pulpit and the Golden Gate, and its choir became a burial place of the Albertine Wettins. The university, the oldest of mining and metallurgy in the world, has since 1969 turned the town towards semiconductor and solar technology. The Christmas market keeps the mining traditions of the Ore Mountains.
freising: Freising lies on the Isar river in Upper Bavaria, north of Munich, and is the capital of the district of Freising. It is built around two hills. One is the Cathedral Hill, with the former bishop's residence and Freising Cathedral, and the other is Weihenstephan Hill, where the former Weihenstephan Abbey stands, which houses what is described as the oldest working brewery in the world. Freising is described as the oldest town between Regensburg and Bolzano. Archaeological finds show settlement in the late Stone Age and Bronze Age, but no proof has been found of continuous settlement before the 8th century CE. The earliest recorded tornado in Europe struck Freising in 788.

Around 700 the Frankish Agilolfing dukes built a simple palace on the highest hill as part of the Duchy of Bavaria. Saint Corbinian was sent to Bavaria by the Church to spread Christianity and built a Benedictine monastery and school on the hill, where a sanctuary already stood. According to his life by Bishop Arbeo, a bear killed his packhorse on the way to Rome and was made to carry his luggage over the Alps. The bear still appears in the city's coat of arms. Saint Boniface established Freising as a diocese after Corbinian's death, and between 764 and 783 Bishop Arbeo founded a library and scriptorium. In 996 Emperor Otto III granted Freising city rights.

Monks from Freising built a toll bridge on the Salt Road in the 10th century, at the village that became Munich, and in 1158 Duke Henry the Lion destroyed it and built another downriver. The present Romanesque cathedral was begun in 1159 and finished in 1205. During the Thirty Years' War King Gustavus Adolphus demanded 30,000 guilders in 1632 to spare the city, yet his army sacked it. The bishopric, more than a thousand years old, was abolished when church lands were secularised in the early 19th century, and the diocese's seat moved to Munich in 1821.

Freising remains the seat of diocesan administration, and the Diocesan Museum is there. Manuscripts made in its monastery between 900 and 1200 include the Freising manuscripts in Slovenian, regarded as the first continuous text in a Slavic language written in Roman script, and the chronicle of the two cities by Otto of Freising. The Cathedral Library, founded by Bishop Arbeo, is one of the largest church libraries in Germany. The Weihenstephan campus holds institutes of the Technical University of Munich and a university of applied sciences. The town has about 50,000 inhabitants.
frejus: Fréjus lies in the Var department on the coast of south-eastern France, next to Saint-Raphaël, with which it forms one urban agglomeration, and below the Massif de l'Esterel. It stood at an important crossroads formed by the Via Julia Augusta, between Italy and the Rhône, and the Via Domitia. Tacitus called its port claustra maris, the gateway to the sea. Its origins probably lie with the Celto-Ligurian people who settled round the natural harbour of Aegytna, and the Phocaeans of Marseille later set up an outpost on the site.

Julius Caesar refounded the city as Forum Julii to counter Massalia, the later Marseille, which had sided with Pompeius in the civil war. The date is unclear, but 49 BCE is most likely. Octavius brought the galleys taken from Mark Antony at Actium in 31 BCE to Forum Julii, and between 29 and 27 BCE it became a colony for veterans of the 8th legion. Augustus made it the capital of the new province of Narbonensis in 22 BCE, and its port became the only naval base of the Roman fleet of Gaul until the reign of Claudius.

Under Tiberius the major monuments were built: the amphitheatre, the aqueduct, the lighthouse, the baths and the theatre. The walls, 3.7 km long, protected 35 hectares and about six thousand inhabitants. Gnaeus Julius Agricola, later the conqueror of Britain, was born there in 40 CE. A bishop was elected in 374, and Saint Léonce, bishop from 433, built the first cathedral with its baptistery. Muslim raiders attacked repeatedly between the 7th and 9th centuries, and silt clogged the port and left a swampy plain between the town and the sea.

Fréjus has the richest concentration of Roman architecture in France after Arles. Its amphitheatre and theatre survive, and the aqueduct from Mons, 42 km long, is largely well preserved. The baptistery of the cathedral dates from the 5th century, and remains of the ancient harbour, with the lighthouse and the quay of Augustus, can be seen. The Malpasset Dam above the town ruptured on 2 December 1959, killing over 400 people. Napoleon landed at Fréjus on 9 October 1799, returning from Egypt. The town is a resort that hosts three to four times its regular population in summer.
french-colonial-empire: French colonisation of the Americas began in the sixteenth century with the voyages of Giovanni da Verrazzano and Jacques Cartier. Spain's defence of its American monopoly and the French Wars of Religion prevented steady settlement, and early attempts in Brazil and Florida failed. After 1598 Henry IV encouraged trade with Asia and Africa. French presence in Senegal began in 1626, with Saint-Louis founded in 1659 and Gorée in 1677, and Fort Dauphin in Madagascar in 1642. Plantation economies based on forced African labour were especially lethal for the enslaved.

A series of wars with Britain, from the War of the Austrian Succession to the Napoleonic Wars, destroyed most of the first empire and nearly expelled France from the Americas. Spain returned Louisiana to France in 1800, and France sold it to the United States in 1803. At the end of the Napoleonic Wars Britain restored Guadeloupe, Martinique, French Guiana, Réunion and the small Indian possessions, but kept Saint Lucia, Tobago, the Seychelles and Mauritius.

The second empire began with the invasion of Algeria in 1830, fully conquered by 1903. The historian Ben Kiernan estimates that 825,000 Algerians died in the conquest by 1875. France forced a protectorate on Tahiti in 1842, ruled Morocco as a protectorate from 1912 to 1956, and held mandates over Syria and Lebanon. On the eve of the First World War the empire was the second largest in the world, after the British. In the Second World War Free France and Vichy France struggled for the colonies, and by 1943 all but Indochina under Japanese control had joined the Free French.

After 1945 the French Union replaced the empire in name while Paris kept control. Demonstrations in Algeria in May 1945 were repressed with an estimated 6,000 to 45,000 killed, and the Malagasy Uprising of 1947 with estimates from 11,000 to 89,000 dead. France lost Indochina and Algeria in costly wars, and most other colonies became independent after 1960.

The ideological basis of French colonialism was the civilising mission, which aimed to spread French language, institutions and values; some French politicians contested it. Colonial subjects lived under unequal legal systems and rarely received full citizenship. France sent few settlers to most colonies, Algeria being the main exception. Remaining possessions were integrated into France as overseas departments and territories, and links with former colonies persist through La Francophonie and the CFA franc.
french-directory: The Directory grew out of the Constitution of the Year III, which the National Convention debated from 4 July to 17 August 1795 and adopted on 22 August. It was a long document of 377 articles, against 124 in the constitution of 1793. Of five million eligible voters, 1,057,390 approved it in a referendum and 49,978 opposed it. The Convention required that five hundred of its own members remain in the new legislature.

In October 1795 royalists and constitutional monarchists, hostile to that rule, tried to seize power in Paris and were put down. The elections that followed returned 379 members of the old Convention, and the Convention required that every Director be a former member who had voted for the execution of Louis XVI.

The Directory began with an empty treasury and almost worthless assignats. It stopped printing them in 1796, replaced them with the mandats territoriaux, which also collapsed, and then returned to silver and gold coin, which brought falling prices and wages. Bread shortages in Paris in 1796 fed the Conspiracy of the Equals of François-Noël Babeuf, which the government crushed.

The main task was the war against Britain and Austria. The Directory annexed Belgium and the left bank of the Rhine, and set up twenty-nine short-lived sister republics in Italy, Switzerland and the Netherlands, which sent France money and art treasures. By the Treaty of Campoformio of 17 October 1797 France received the Ionian Islands, Belgium and the left bank of the Rhine as far south as Andernach.

The royalists triumphed in the elections of 1797 and were then put down by a coup, and in 1798 the Directors disqualified Jacobin candidates. In 1799 Britain, Austria and Russia formed a Second Coalition. Bonaparte returned from Egypt and, with Abbé Sieyès and others, overthrew the Directory on 9 November 1799.

Five Directors held executive power. The presidency was an entirely ceremonial post, held first by Jean-François Rewbell, chosen by lot on 2 November 1795, and passed on every three months. Louis Gohier was the last president.

Under the Directory the middle and upper classes replaced the nobility at the top of Paris society, and enormous fortunes were made by army suppliers and property speculators. Young Parisians known as Incroyables and Merveilleuses dressed in extravagant costumes and attended the Bals des victimes. The Goncourt brothers reported 640 balls in Paris in 1797 alone. Crime and highway robbery increased, and the death penalty was applied to robberies on the main roads.
french-first-republic: Under the Legislative Assembly, France was already at war with Prussia and Austria. In July 1792 the Duke of Brunswick, commanding the Austro-Prussian army, issued the Brunswick Manifesto, threatening the destruction of Paris if the royal family were harmed. On 10 August 1792 citizens stormed the Tuileries Palace, killing six hundred of the king's Swiss guards. In the first week of September mobs broke into the city's prisons and killed over half of the prisoners in the September Massacres.

The Convention met for the first time on 21 September 1792 and unanimously abolished the monarchy. The Republic was never formally proclaimed, but acts were dated from the year I of the Republic, and on 25 September it was declared one and indivisible. From 1792 to 1802 France was at war with the rest of Europe, and it also fought internal conflicts such as the wars in Vendée.

Louis XVI was tried for treason from December 1792, convicted on 16 January 1793 and executed on 21 January. Food riots and hunger continued, and on 6 April 1793 the Convention created the Committee of Public Safety, which adopted a policy of terror under which perceived enemies were guillotined at an increasing rate. The Constitution of 1793 was ratified in early August, but the rights it guaranteed were suspended under the committee.

After Robespierre was executed on 28 July 1794, the Jacobin club was closed. The Constitution of the Year III restored freedom of worship, and on 3 November 1795 the Directory was established, with a Council of Elders of 250 members, a Council of Five Hundred and an executive of five directors. Hyperinflation of the paper assignats and military disasters in 1798 and 1799 brought it down after four years.

The Consulate began with the coup of 18 Brumaire, on 9 November 1799, planned by members of the Directory itself, with Napoleon Bonaparte as a co-conspirator and then First Consul. It had four bodies: a Council of State that prepared draft laws, a Tribunate that debated them, a Legislative Body of three hundred that voted on them without debate or amendment, and a Conservative Senate of sixty irremovable members appointed by Bonaparte. On 18 May 1804 the Senate proclaimed Napoleon Emperor of the French, which ended the Republic.
french-foreign-legion: Louis Philippe, King of the French, created the Foreign Legion on 10 March 1831 to bring foreign nationals into the French Army from the foreign regiments of the old kingdom. Its recruits included soldiers from the recently disbanded Swiss and German regiments of the Bourbon monarchy. The royal ordinance allowed the foreigners to serve only outside France. The French expeditionary force that had occupied Algiers in 1830 needed reinforcements, so the Legion was sent by sea from Toulon to Algeria. It was first divided into six national battalions: Swiss, Poles, Germans, Italians, Spanish and Dutch-Belgian.

The Legion was initially stationed only in Algeria, where it took part in the conquest, described as a genocide, and in the drying of marshes near Algiers. It served in the First Carlist War in Spain from 1835, the Crimean War in 1854 and the Italian campaign of 1859. It was part of the French intervention in Mexico from 1863 to 1867 and the Tonkin campaign and Sino-French War of the 1880s. French law kept it out of metropolitan France except in an invasion, so it was not in the army that capitulated at Sedan in 1870.

It helped extend the French colonial empire in Africa. After 1871 volunteers from Alsace and Lorraine joined it, and it fought in many critical battles on the Western Front in the First World War. Its numbers swelled in the First Indochina War, and it suffered heavy losses at Dien Bien Phu, which fell on 7 May 1954.

In the Algerian War its parachute regiments fought the National Liberation Front. By the mid-1960s the Legion had lost its home in French Algeria, and Charles de Gaulle, who considered disbanding it, cut it from 40,000 to 8,000 men and moved it to metropolitan France. Over its history it has lost nearly 40,000 men.

The Legion is the only unit of the French Army open to people of any nationality, and most of its commissioned officers are French, with about 10 per cent promoted from the ranks. Legionnaires may apply for French citizenship after three years' service, or at once if wounded in the line of duty, a provision known as Français par le sang versé. Its flags bear the motto Honneur et Fidélité rather than Honneur et Patrie. It marches at 88 steps a minute, against 116 for other French units, and always comes last in a parade. Its marching song is Le Boudin.
french-invasion-of-russia: Napoleon began the campaign to force the Russian Empire to comply with the continental blockade of the United Kingdom. France had been at war with the major European powers since 1792, and Napoleon had won the War of the Third Coalition, the War of the Fourth Coalition and the War of the Fifth Coalition. Russia had learned from earlier defeats at Austerlitz and Friedland. Between 1810 and 1812 it built and rebuilt fortresses, created military intelligence offices and formally established the corps system. In April 1812 Alexander I issued an ultimatum demanding that French troops leave Prussia and the Grand Duchy of Warsaw. Napoleon chose war, and called it the Second Polish War to win support from Polish nationalists.

The multinational Grande Armée crossed the Neman River on 24 June 1812. Estimates of its size vary, with figures of 400,000 to 500,000 men commonly given, and only about half the soldiers were French. The Russian armies under Barclay de Tolly and Pyotr Bagration, together about 180,000 to 220,000 men, retreated eastward and used scorched earth tactics. Heat, disease, desertion and supply failures cost the French heavily before they took Smolensk in August. Mikhail Kutuzov then became commander-in-chief.

At the Battle of Borodino on 7 September, more than 250,000 troops fought and at least 70,000 were killed or wounded. The French took the main positions but failed to destroy the Russian army. Kutuzov decided at the council at Fili to abandon Moscow, and Napoleon entered it on 14 September to find it deserted and set ablaze by its military governor Fyodor Rostopchin. He waited five weeks for a peace offer that never came and left on 19 October. After losing the Battle of Maloyaroslavets he had to retrace his earlier route. Snow, frost, hunger, typhus and attacks by peasants and Cossacks followed. Napoleon left the army at Smorgonie on 5 December and returned to Paris.

Estimates of the losses differ. Richard K. Riehn gives 685,000 men entering Russia and fewer than 70,000 known survivors, while Adam Zamoyski estimates that as many as 400,000 of the 550,000 to 600,000 who crossed the Neman died, counting prisoners who died in captivity. About 100,000 prisoners were taken, and more than 50,000 died. The campaign is also said to have claimed around a million soldiers and civilians. The saying that General Winter defeated Napoleon is disputed, since Minard's map shows the French losses were highest in summer and autumn, owing to inadequate logistics and disease. The campaign remains present in Russian culture through Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace and Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture.
french-revolution: Between 1715 and 1789 the French population grew from 21 to 28 million, and the middle class tripled in size. The benefits of rising prosperity were largely restricted to the rentier and mercantile classes, while living standards fell for wage labourers and peasant farmers who rented their land. An economic recession from 1785 and bad harvests in 1787 and 1788 led to high unemployment and food prices.

The state's finances were in crisis. The nobility and the Church benefited from exemptions, so the tax burden fell mainly on the lower classes, and the parlements could block new tax laws. By 1788 half of state revenue went on servicing the debt. Reforms proposed by the finance minister Calonne in 1786 were rejected, and the notables and parlements argued that new taxes could be approved only by an Estates-General, last held in 1614.

The Estates General met in May 1789, and in June the representatives of the Third Estate re-constituted themselves as a National Assembly. On 14 July a crowd, joined by soldiers, attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress with large stores of arms. Its governor surrendered after fighting that cost the lives of 83 attackers. The Bastille held only seven prisoners but was a potent symbol of the Ancien Régime. The Assembly then abolished feudalism, placed the Catholic Church under state control and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

Military defeats after the outbreak of war in April 1792 led to the insurrection of 10 August 1792. The monarchy was replaced by the First Republic in September, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793. Political power then passed to the Committee of Public Safety, dominated by Jacobins led by Maximilien Robespierre. About 16,000 people were sentenced by the Revolutionary Tribunal and executed in the Reign of Terror, which ended in July 1794.

The Directory replaced the Committee in November 1795 but faced internal unrest, a weak economy and an expensive war. It ended with the coup of 18 Brumaire on 9 November 1799 and the Consulate, with Napoleon Bonaparte as First Consul. The Revolution also began the French Revolutionary Wars, which lasted until Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo in 1815, involved every major European power and redrew the map of Europe.

Historians disagree about the role of ideology: Jonathan Israel holds that the radical Enlightenment was the primary driving force, while Cobban argues that the revolutionaries mostly sought practical solutions to immediate problems.
french-revolutionary-wars: As early as 1791 the other monarchies of Europe looked with outrage on the French Revolution and considered whether to intervene in support of King Louis XVI or to profit from the chaos. On 27 August 1791 Emperor Leopold II and King Frederick William II of Prussia issued the Declaration of Pillnitz, threatening vague but severe consequences if anything befell the king and his family. Leopold meant it as a non-committal gesture, but it was seen in France as a serious threat. France declared war on Austria and Prussia in the spring of 1792, and their coordinated invasion was turned back at the Battle of Valmy in September.

The wars fall into the War of the First Coalition, from 1792 to 1797, and the War of the Second Coalition, from 1798 to 1802. In 1793 France declared war on Great Britain and the Dutch Republic, and drafted hundreds of thousands of men by mass conscription. After reverses, the French regained the initiative at Fleurus in June 1794 and occupied Belgium, the Rhineland and the south of the Netherlands. In 1795 the Batavian Republic was founded, and Prussia signed the Peace of Basel on 6 April, ceding the west bank of the Rhine to France. In Italy in 1796 and 1797 Napoleon Bonaparte drove the Habsburg forces out of the peninsula, and Austria agreed to the Treaty of Campo Formio on 17 October 1797.

In 1798 Napoleon invaded Egypt and won at the Battle of the Pyramids, but Nelson sank his fleet at the Battle of the Nile. The allies gradually pushed the French out of Italy until the French victory at Zurich in September 1799 made Russia drop out of the war. Napoleon failed at the siege of Acre in 1799 and returned to France. Austria signed the Treaty of Lunéville on 9 February 1801. Britain and France signed the Treaty of Amiens in 1802, which is generally taken as the transition to the Napoleonic Wars.

France had conquered territories in Italy, the Low Countries and the Rhineland. The wars spread revolutionary principles over much of Europe, and French armies, mobilized by mass conscription, replaced eighteenth-century armies with their rigid protocols and aristocratic officer classes. Scholars identify the era as the beginning of modern war. The peace with Britain lasted less than a year, though it was the longest period of peace between the two countries between 1793 and 1815.
french-wars-of-religion: Tensions between Catholics and Protestants had been building since the 1530s. After the Affair of the Placards in October 1534, when Protestant radicals put up posters rejecting the Catholic doctrine of the real presence, Protestantism was clearly defined as heresy. The accidental death of Henry II in July 1559 left a political vacuum and a struggle for power between his widow Catherine de' Medici and powerful nobles: a Catholic faction led by the Guise and Montmorency families and Protestants headed by the House of Condé and Jeanne d'Albret, queen of Navarre. Spain and Savoy supported the Catholics, and England and the Dutch Republic the Protestants.

Catherine, ruling as regent for her son Charles IX, at first backed the moderates known as Politiques. Her Edict of Saint-Germain of January 1562 was opposed by the Guise, and fighting broke out in March after the massacre of Vassy. Condé seized Orléans on 2 April 1562, and the Huguenots took towns along the Loire. In 1572 Catherine backed the St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in Paris, in which Catholic mobs killed between 5,000 and 30,000 Protestants throughout France. The wars were commonly counted in eight numbered phases, ended by edicts and peaces such as Amboise and Longjumeau.

The Catholic League, formed by Henri, Duke of Guise, opposed concessions. When the Duke of Anjou died in 1584 the Calvinist Henry of Navarre became heir to Henry III, and the League allied with Philip II of Spain. On 23 December 1588 Henry III had the Duke of Guise killed at Blois, and in July 1589 a Dominican friar, Jacques Clément, stabbed the king to death. Navarre, now Henry IV, abjured Protestantism on 25 July 1593 and was crowned at Chartres on 27 February 1594.

Between two and four million people died from violence, famine or disease directly caused by the conflict, and the power of the monarchy was severely damaged. The Peace of Vervins with Spain was signed in May 1598. The Edict of Nantes granted the Huguenots substantial rights, but it was less a sign of genuine toleration than a grudging truce with guarantees for both sides.

Henry IV was assassinated in 1610, and the political freedoms of the Huguenots, which detractors called a state within the state, caused trouble in the 17th century. Their revolts ended with the Siege of La Rochelle and the Peace of La Rochelle in 1629. Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685.
friedberg-hesse: Friedberg is the capital of the Wetteraukreis district, about 30 kilometres north of Frankfurt am Main in the Wetterau region. It stands on the river Usa just before it flows into the Wetter, on a basalt plateau, and extends west into the Taunus up to the 518-metre Steinkopf. It has been populated at least since Roman times: relics of a Mesolithic settlement have been found in the suburb of Bruchenbrücken, and Castle Hill was the site of a Roman military camp on the limes, presumably the castellum in monte tauno of Roman records of the 1st century, though this is still discussed. The remains of Roman baths survive. The Roman settlement was abandoned in the retreat from the Rhine frontier by 260 CE.

The Hohenstaufen dynasty of the Holy Roman Empire refounded the old city at a point convenient for important trade routes. It at first rivalled Frankfurt with an important annual trading fair and rapid growth, but its fortunes soon dwindled. Friedberg consisted of two entities, the city and the castle, which were politically independent and in permanent, often malicious competition, and which once ended with angry citizens ransacking and destroying the castle. The city became a Free Imperial City of the Holy Roman Empire by a charter of 1211.

From the 14th to the 15th century the castle was a noble republic in which twelve noble families shared a single castle. Between 1337 and 1498 its constitution developed, with knightly families holding the right to elect a burgrave, two Baumeister and twelve Regimentsburgmannen, who represented the community, kept up the buildings and governed its affairs. The arrangement was unusual in being sustained by many families under a formal constitution. Under Napoleon Friedberg was incorporated in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, or Hesse-Darmstadt.

Friedberg's old town once housed a prosperous Jewish community. Many Jews fled to Palestine and the United States before the Holocaust, and all who remained were deported to Treblinka in 1942. The medieval Jewish ceremonial bath, the Judenbad, a memorial to the old synagogue burned down, and a plaque at a school remain. From about 1956 to 2007 the town was the home of a United States Army installation, Ray Barracks.

Friedberg has seven districts: Bruchenbrücken, Friedberg, Dorheim, Ockstadt, Bauernheim, Fauerbach and Ossenheim. Its most prominent feature is the castle's Adolfsturm, whose crown was restored in the 1980s. The main station lies on the Main-Weser Railway and is the northern terminus of Frankfurt's S-Bahn line S6.
friedrich-durrenmatt: Friedrich Reinhold Dürrenmatt was born on 5 January 1921 in Konolfingen, in the canton of Bern, the son of a Protestant pastor. His grandfather Ulrich Dürrenmatt was a conservative politician. The family moved to Bern in 1935. In 1941 he began studying philosophy and literature at the University of Zürich but moved to Bern after one semester and also studied natural science. As a student he was briefly a member of the Fröntler, a far-right movement, an activity he later attributed to a wish to rebel against his father. In 1943 he decided to become an author and left academic life.

Like Bertolt Brecht, Dürrenmatt explored epic theatre, and he has been called its most original theorist after Brecht. His first play, It Is Written, premiered in April 1947 amid fights and protests in the audience. It sets a sensation-craving cynic against a religious fanatic in a city under siege. From 1948 to 1949 he wrote sketches for the anti-Nazi Cabaret Cornichon in Zürich. His first major success was Romulus the Great, set in 476 CE during the last days of the Roman Empire.

The Visit (1956) is his most widely performed and translated play, a grotesque mixture of comedy and tragedy about a wealthy woman who offers her hometown a fortune if its people avenge the wrongs done to her. The Physicists (1962) is a satire on the responsibility of science for dangerous changes to the world. He also wrote radio plays and detective novels, among them The Judge and His Hangman (1950) and Suspicion (1951). In 1970 he announced his intention to abandon literature and adapt established works for the theatre instead.

Dürrenmatt married the actress Lotti Geißler in 1946, and they had three children. After her death in 1983 he married Charlotte Kerr in 1984. In 1990 he gave a speech for Václav Havel, Switzerland, a Prison, after learning that he and 800,000 other left-leaning Swiss had been spied on for five decades by the Swiss secret service. He died of heart failure on 14 December 1990 in Neuchâtel. Over 1,000 of his paintings and drawings have been exhibited since 2000 in the Centre Dürrenmatt Neuchâtel, designed by Mario Botta around his former home.
friedrich-ebert: Friedrich Ebert was born in Heidelberg on 4 February 1871, the seventh of nine children of a tailor. His family could not afford university, so he trained as a saddle-maker from 1885 to 1888 and then travelled as a journeyman. He joined the Social Democratic Party in Mannheim in 1889. He read Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels but cared more for practical and organisational questions that would improve workers' lives.

After settling in Bremen in 1891 he worked on a socialist newspaper, ran a pub that became a centre of socialist and union activity, and was elected to the Bremen assembly in 1900. In 1905 he became Secretary-General of the party and moved to Berlin, and in 1913, after August Bebel's death, he was elected party leader.

In August 1914 Ebert led the party's Reichstag members to vote almost unanimously for war loans, regarding the war as a defensive measure against the autocratic regime of the Tsar. He backed the Burgfrieden, the truce among parties for the duration of the war, a stance that contributed to a split in 1917 when opponents of the war formed the Independent Social Democratic Party. Two of his four sons were killed in the war. In October 1918 he persuaded his party to join the government of Prince Maximilian of Baden, arguing that it was a duty. He did not favour a republic, and told the prince that he hated social revolution like sin.

After the revolution reached Berlin on 9 November 1918, Ebert and the party leadership sided with the civil service, army, police and judiciary against those who wanted a more radical revolution. He and General Wilhelm Groener planned the return of army units to Berlin in December. On 11 February 1919 the National Assembly, meeting at Weimar, elected him provisional president, and he was sworn in under the new constitution on 21 August 1919. He denounced the Treaty of Versailles as unbearable but accepted it after Hindenburg concluded the army could not resume the war.

Ebert suffered from gallstones. A Magdeburg court in December 1924 fined a journalist who had called him a traitor, yet said that, in strict legal terms, he had committed treason by his role in the January 1918 strike. He gave evidence and delayed medical help. In February 1925 he underwent an emergency appendectomy and died of septic shock on 28 February, aged 54. Paul von Hindenburg succeeded him on 12 May. Historians remain divided. Some defend his actions as the price of preventing a socialist state on the model promoted by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, while leftist critics call him a traitor who paved the way for the far right.
friedrich-engels: Friedrich Engels was born on 28 November 1820 in Barmen, in Prussia, now part of Wuppertal. He was the eldest of nine children of Friedrich Engels Sr., a prosperous cotton mill owner, in a devout Pietist Protestant family. He grew up in the Wupper valley, an early industrial centre known as the German Manchester, and saw polluted rivers, dangerous working conditions and the contrast between the merchant elite's houses and the poverty of the workers.

In September 1841 he began a year of military service in Berlin, where he attended the University of Berlin as a non-matriculated student and joined the Young Hegelian circle known as Die Freien. In 1842 his father sent him to Manchester to work in a cotton mill in which the family had an investment, and his experience of the industrial working class led to The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845).

In August 1844 Engels met Karl Marx for the second time in Paris, and over ten days they found their complete agreement in all theoretical fields. Their first joint work was The Holy Family (1845). After moving to Brussels they wrote The German Ideology, which argued that social structures, politics and ideas are determined by the economic base; it was never published in their lifetimes. The Communist League commissioned them to write the Manifesto of 1848, and Engels fought in the Revolutions of 1848 before exile in England.

In November 1850 he returned to Manchester and the firm of Ermen & Engels to support Marx financially. He led a double life as a respectable cotton merchant and a clandestine communist, became a partner in 1864, and over twenty years sent the Marx family between 3,000 and 4,000 pounds, which effectively funded Das Kapital. He retired in 1870 and moved to London, where he joined the General Council of the International Working Men's Association.

Anti-Dühring (1878) explained their shared scientific socialism in response to Eugen Dühring's influence in Germany, and a section of it appeared separately as Socialism: Utopian and Scientific (1880). After Marx's death in 1883 Engels devoted his life to editing his writings, completing the second and third volumes of Das Kapital. His application of dialectics to science, in works such as Dialectics of Nature, was later controversially developed into the state ideology of the Soviet Union. He died of cancer in London on 5 August 1895, and his ashes were scattered off Beachy Head.
friedrich-schiller: Johann Christoph Friedrich Schiller was born on 10 November 1759 in Marbach, in the Duchy of Württemberg, the only son of the military doctor Johann Kaspar Schiller and Elisabetha Dorothea Schiller. He grew up in a devoutly Lutheran family and spent much of his youth studying the Bible. His parents wanted him to become a priest, and the village priest taught him Latin and Greek. In 1773 he entered the Karlsschule Stuttgart, an elite military academy founded by Karl Eugen, Duke of Württemberg, and graduated as a doctor of medicine in 1780.

At the school he read Rousseau and Goethe and wrote The Robbers, a play about two aristocratic brothers, one of whom leads rebellious students into the Bohemian forest as Robin Hood-like bandits. Its critique of social corruption astounded its first audience and made him an overnight sensation.

In 1780 Schiller became a regimental doctor in Stuttgart, a post he disliked. He left his regiment without permission to see the first performance of The Robbers in Mannheim, was arrested, sentenced to 14 days of imprisonment and forbidden by the duke to publish further works. In 1782 he fled Stuttgart and went by way of Frankfurt, Mannheim, Leipzig and Dresden to Weimar. On 26 May 1789 he gave his inaugural lecture as professor of History and Philosophy at the University of Jena and wrote historical works there. On 22 February 1790 he married Charlotte von Lengefeld.

From 1788 until his death he kept a productive but complicated friendship with Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who convinced him to return to playwriting. Together they founded the Weimar Theater and wrote the Xenien, satirical short poems aimed at their opponents. The Duke of Saxe-Weimar ennobled him in 1802.

Schiller's philosophical work was concerned above all with human freedom, a theme that runs through his histories and plays: the Wallenstein trilogy concerns the Thirty Years' War, and Don Carlos the revolt of the Netherlands against Spain. His On the Aesthetic Education of Man, first published in 1794, was prompted by his disillusion with the French Revolution and its descent into violence, and argues that a people's moral character can be raised by first touching their souls with beauty. He died of tuberculosis in Weimar in 1805, aged 45. A skull long believed to be his was shown by DNA tests in 2008 not to be.
friedrich-schlegel: Friedrich Schlegel was born on 10 March 1772 at Hanover, where his father, Johann Adolf Schlegel, was pastor at the Lutheran Market Church. The family was fervently Protestant, but as a young man he rejected religion in favour of atheism and individualism. He studied law for two years at Göttingen and Leipzig and met Friedrich Schiller, then in 1793 devoted himself entirely to literary work. In 1796 he moved to Jena, where his brother August Wilhelm lived, and collaborated with Novalis, Ludwig Tieck, Fichte and Caroline Schelling. In 1797 he quarrelled with Schiller, who disliked his polemical work.

Schlegel published Die Griechen und Römer in 1797 and a history of Greek and Roman poetry in 1798, then turned to Dante, Goethe and Shakespeare. With his brother he founded the journal Athenaeum, in which fragments, aphorisms and essays set out the principles of the Romantic school. They are generally recognised as deep and significant expressions of the subjective idealism of the early Romanticists. In 1799 he published the first part of the novel Lucinde, seen as an account of his affair with Dorothea Veit, which caused a scandal in German literary circles. It contributed to the failure of his academic career in Jena.

In Paris from 1802 he studied Sanskrit and Persian. In 1808 he published Über die Sprache und Weisheit der Indier, arguing that a people originating from India founded the first European civilizations. He compared Sanskrit with Latin, Greek, Persian and German and noted many similarities in vocabulary and grammar. The common features he asserted are now generally accepted with significant revisions, while the Out-of-India model has been discredited. He was the first to notice what became known as Grimm's law, and he was a pioneer of comparative linguistics.

Schlegel married Dorothea Veit in Paris in April 1804, and in 1808 the couple joined the Catholic Church in Cologne Cathedral. From then on he increasingly opposed political and religious liberalism. In 1809 he moved to Vienna and was appointed imperial court secretary at the military headquarters, editing the army newspaper and issuing proclamations against Napoleon. After the Congress of Vienna he was councillor of legation at the Austrian embassy in Frankfurt, and in 1820 he started a conservative Catholic magazine, Concordia. He died on 12 January 1829 at Dresden while preparing a series of lectures.
frisia: Frisia is a cross-border cultural region in northwestern Europe along the Wadden Sea, taking in the north of the Netherlands and parts of northwestern Germany. It is commonly divided into West Frisia, roughly the Dutch province of Friesland, East Frisia in Lower Saxony, and North Frisia, between the Eider River and the Danish border, which belonged to the Danish Duchy of Schleswig until 1864. The name comes from the Latin Frisii, possibly from a Proto-Germanic word meaning curly or crisp, presumably referring to the hair of the tribesmen.

The people later known as Frisii began settling in the 6th century BCE, and in Roman times lived, according to Pliny the Elder, on terps, man-made hills. The Frisians of the early Middle Ages were, according to archaeology, descendants of Anglo-Saxon immigrants from the German Bight. The Frisian Realm of 650 to 734 had its centre in Utrecht and its law written down as the Lex Frisionum. It ended at the Battle of the Boarn in 734, when the Franks conquered the western part up to the Lauwers; they took the area east of it in 785. From the 7th to the 10th centuries Frisian merchants took a large part in the luxury trade, with districts in cities such as Hedeby, York and Cologne.

In the 12th century Frisian noblemen and the city of Groningen founded the Upstalsboom League under the slogan of Frisian freedom, to counter feudalising tendencies; it collapsed after 1337. In 1464 a nobleman of the Cirksena family became count of East Frisia, with the help of the Hanseatic League, and Friesland was conquered in 1498 by Duke Albert of Saxony-Meissen. West Friesland had fallen to the count of Holland in 1289. Friesland joined the nascent Dutch Republic in 1577 and Groningen was conquered by the Dutch in 1594.

About half a million Frisians in the province of Friesland speak West Frisian, several thousand people in Nordfriesland and Heligoland speak North Frisian dialects, and a small number in four villages speak Saterland Frisian. Friesland has been called Fryslân since 1996. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries Frisian freedom became the slogan of a regionalist movement demanding equal rights for the Frisian language and culture within the Netherlands.
friuli: Friuli covers about 8,240 square kilometres between the Livenza river in the west, the Carnic Alps in the north, the Julian Alps and the Timavo river in the east and the Adriatic Sea in the south. The Tagliamento crosses its hills and flows into a large flood plain, and the lagoons of Marano and Grado lie to the south. The historical capital and most important city is Udine, which was also the capital of the medieval Patria del Friuli.

In prehistory the area belonged to the Castellieri culture and the Raeti, and in the 4th century BCE the Carni settled there. From the 2nd century BCE the Romans colonised it. Aquileia became the fourth largest city of Italy under the empire, a river port that dominated trade between the Adriatic and northern Europe. In 452 Attila razed it to the ground. The Patriarchate of Aquileia ranked among the highest ecclesiastical authorities in Italy from the mid-6th century.

In 568 the Lombards took the region, and King Alboin established the Duchy of Friuli, the first Lombard duchy, which he gave to his relative Gisulf I, with its capital at Forum Iulii. The historian Paul the Deacon was born in Friuli. After the Frankish conquest the region became the March of Friuli in 846. On 3 April 1077 Emperor Henry IV granted the county of Friuli to Sigaerd, Patriarch of Aquileia, and the patriarchal state became one of the best organised polities of medieval Italy. It had a parliament from the 12th century, which met for the last time in 1805, when Napoleon Bonaparte abolished it.

Venice conquered the patriarchate in 1420 but left Friuli its own parliament. On 27 February 1511 starving citizens of Udine began a revolt known as Joibe Grasse, which spread through the whole territory and was put down by 1 March, when Venice sent about a hundred cavalry. From 1516 the Habsburg Empire controlled eastern Friuli. In 1866 central and western Friuli were annexed by Italy with the Veneto, while the east stayed under Austria until the First World War.

Friuli forms the major part of the autonomous region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, with the provinces of Udine, Pordenone and Gorizia. Its people, the Friulians, speak the Friulian language, which around 350,000 people claim as their native language. Slovene, German and Venetian dialects are also spoken in parts of the region.
fuhrer: Führer has been used as a military title in Germany since at least the 18th century. A company's temporary or less qualified commander, for example, was a Kompanieführer, while a fully qualified commanding officer was a Kompaniechef. The first political use of the word was for Georg Ritter von Schönerer (1842–1921), the pan-German Austrian nationalist, whose followers called him the Führer. According to the historian Richard J. Evans, this probably introduced the term to the German far right, though the Nazis may also have been influenced by Benito Mussolini's informal title of Duce, which likewise means leader.

Adolf Hitler took the title to denote his function as head of the Nazi Party. He received it in 1921, when he resigned in anger at party founder Anton Drexler's plan to merge with another party and returned only on condition that he be made chairman with dictatorial powers. After he became Chancellor on 30 January 1933, a law of 1934 merged the offices of president and chancellor on the death of President Paul von Hindenburg. Hitler then became Führer und Reichskanzler, although Reichskanzler was quietly dropped from everyday use. Soldiers swore allegiance to him as Führer of the German Reich and Nation, and on 23 June 1941 he declared himself Germanic Führer, to assert leadership over peoples the Nazis counted as Nordic-Germanic.

The slogan Ein Volk, ein Reich, ein Führer, meaning One People, One Empire, One Leader, was among the most repeated of the Nazis and appeared on countless posters. It stressed the leader's absolute control over almost every part of German society, with the churches formally the main exception. The term spread from the party to the state, the armed forces, the nation and finally all Germanic peoples. Hitler kept up a pretence of legality, issuing thousands of decrees based on the Reichstag Fire Decree, and his vague orders set subordinates against one another. Lower ranks also used the word: Gauleiter led Nazi regions, and the SS and SA used Führer in their rank titles.

In German the word remains common in compounds such as Reiseführer, travel guide, and Führerschein, driving licence. Because of its link with Hitler, the isolated word usually has negative connotations when it means a political leader.
fujian: Fujian is bordered by Zhejiang to the north, Jiangxi to the west, Guangdong to the south and the Taiwan Strait to the east. The province is mostly mountainous, traditionally described as eight parts mountain, one part water and one part farmland, and its highest point is Mount Huanggang, at 2,157 metres. The name Fujian, 'happy establishment', combines the names of Fuzhou and Jianzhou, which is now Nanping. Because of the mountains and successive waves of migration, it is one of China's most culturally and linguistically diverse provinces.

Excavations at Keqiutou on Pingtan Island show that Fujian had entered the Neolithic by the middle of the sixth millennium BCE. The kingdom of Minyue was located there; its name joins Min, perhaps an ethnic name and also that of the main river, with Yue, after the State of Yue in Zhejiang, whose royal family fled to Fujian after Chu annexed that kingdom in 306 BCE. King Wuzhu built a fortified city at Fuzhou, and his kingdom reached into eastern Guangdong, eastern Jiangxi and southern Zhejiang.

A first wave of settlers from the north arrived in the early fourth century, mainly from eight families of central China, among them Chen, Lin, Huang and Zheng, which remain the commonest surnames in the province. In the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period a second wave came with the brothers Wang Chao, Wang Shengui and Wang Shenzhi, who set up a Kingdom of Min with its capital at Fuzhou. The name Fujian was first used for an administrative region in 985.

From 1357 to 1366 Muslims of Quanzhou took part in the Ispah Rebellion before the Yuan crushed it, and the city then lost its foreign trade. Under the Ming, Fujian became a province, and Changle served as the base for Zheng He's expeditions. A sea trade ban hampered it, and the Qing imposed another ban of about twenty years against Koxinga's Ming loyalists on Taiwan.

Fujian has a population of about 41.5 million, with Fuzhou as its capital. Quanzhou is its largest prefecture-level city by population, and Xiamen was one of China's first special economic zones. Southern Min, or Hokkien, is spoken by much of the ethnic Chinese population of Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and the Philippines, because of emigration. The province has four UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Fujian Tulou, earth buildings of the Hakka, listed in 2008.
fukui-prefecture: Fukui Prefecture lies in the Chūbu region of Honshū and borders Ishikawa Prefecture to the north, Gifu Prefecture to the east, Shiga Prefecture to the south and Kyoto Prefecture to the southwest. It covers about 4,190 square kilometres and faces the Sea of Japan, within the historic Hokuriku region. The western part, formerly Wakasa, is a narrow plain between the mountains and the sea. The larger eastern part, formerly Echizen, has wider plains and holds the capital and most of the population. The area lies within Japan's snow country, and parts of it are protected as Hakusan National Park and the Echizen-Kaga Kaigan and Wakasa Wan Quasi-National Parks.

The Kitadani Dinosaur Quarry on the Sugiyama River, in the city of Katsuyama, has yielded dinosaurs such as Fukuiraptor, Fukuisaurus, Koshisaurus, Fukuivenator, Fukuititan and Tambatitanis, and fossils from the prefecture are shown at the Fukui Prefectural Dinosaur Museum.

Fukui originally consisted of the old provinces of Wakasa and Echizen before the prefecture was formed in 1871. During the Edo period the daimyō of the region bore the surname Matsudaira and descended from Tokugawa Ieyasu. The Matsudaira clan was headquartered at Fukui Castle, which stood on the site of the modern prefectural offices. Fukui was heavily bombed in World War II, and the castle, surrounded by a moat, was demolished; the prefectural government buildings were built on its site.

Fukui is the capital and largest city, and other major cities include Sakai, Echizen and Sabae. Sabae produces 90 per cent of Japan's domestically made glasses, and Fukui has long been a centre of papermaking, with makers of traditional Echizen paper. The prefecture is also known for sake, rice and soba noodles, and its people speak a distinctive accent, Fukui-ben.

Among its historic sites are Eihei-ji, a Buddhist training temple founded by Dōgen in 1244 on about 33 hectares; the Ichijōdani Asakura Family Historic Ruins; the National Treasures of Myōtsū-ji, its three-storied pagoda and main hall; and Maruoka Castle, built in 1576 and the oldest standing castle in Japan. Nuclear power stations stand along Wakasa Bay.
fukuoka-prefecture: Fukuoka Prefecture lies at the northernmost point of Kyūshū, on the Kanmon Straits, which connect the Tsushima Strait and the Seto Inland Sea across from Yamaguchi Prefecture on the island of Honshu. It extends south towards the Ariake Sea and borders Saga, Kumamoto and Ōita prefectures. The prefecture faces the sea on three sides, and it includes a number of small islands off the north coast. Fukuoka is the capital and the largest city on Kyūshū, and other major cities include Kitakyushu, Kurume and Ōmuta. The prefecture includes the former provinces of Chikugo, Chikuzen and Buzen.

The prefecture's religious history is old. Kōra taisha, Sumiyoshi-jinja and Hakozaki-gū are its chief Shinto shrines. The oldest of its Buddhist temples, Kanzeon-ji at Dazaifu, was founded in the 7th century by the emperor to honour his mother, and together with its Kaidan-in it was one of three places in Japan where Buddhist monks could be ordained.

Monks who had studied in China sailed back and founded temples in the heart of Hakata, now Fukuoka City. Eisai founded Shōfuku-ji, known as the oldest Zen temple in Japan, and Kūkai established Tocho-ji. Enni built Jōten-ji, and he is also credited with first bringing udon noodles to Japan. During the Tokugawa shogunate the daimyo Arima Toyōji was relocated to the region and moved his family temple to Kurume, where it became the Zen temple Bairin-ji.

The prefecture contains much of Kyūshū's industry, with automobiles, semiconductors and steel among its major products; the tire maker Bridgestone was founded there. Kyushu University is in Fukuoka. The Kyushu National Museum at Dazaifu covers the history of Kyūshū from prehistory to the Meiji era, with emphasis on its cultural exchange with China and Korea. The Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival is held each July, and the Genko Historical Museum displays arms and armour of the 13th-century Mongol invasions.
fulda: Fulda lies on the river Fulda in the German state of Hesse and is the administrative seat of the Fulda district. Since 1974 it has been included in the district as a city with special status. Its station is an interchange between local and long-distance services on the Hanover to Würzburg high-speed line, and the Roman Catholic Diocese of Fulda has its seat in the cathedral.

In 744 Saint Sturm, a disciple of Saint Boniface, founded the Benedictine monastery of Fulda as one of Boniface's outposts in the reorganisation of the church in Germany. Carolingian rulers and leading families supported it with large donations, and in 751 it was placed directly under the Papal See. Boniface was killed by the Frisians in 754 and his relics were brought to Fulda. Between 790 and 819 the abbey church was rebuilt on the model of Old St. Peter's Basilica in Rome. Rabanus Maurus was abbot from 822 to 842, and the abbey owned the Codex Fuldensis and works by Cicero and Bede. Its school became a centre of learning.

On Christmas day 1235 five boys died in a house fire, and local people accused the Jewish community of killing them for ritual purposes. Jews were tortured and 34 were killed after two confessed. Emperor Frederick II investigated and found them innocent. In the Counter-Reformation Prince-abbot Balthasar von Dernbach called in the Jesuits in 1571 and ordered his subjects, most of them Lutheran, to return to the Catholic faith or leave. He also ordered the Fulda witch trials, in which hundreds were arrested.

Fulda became a bishopric in 1752 and the prince-bishops ruled until Napoleon I dissolved the bishopric in 1802. The cathedral was remodelled in 1704–12 and the Stadtschloss in 1707–12 by Johann Dientzenhofer, which give the city its title of Baroque City. After 1814–15 most of the territory went to the Electorate of Hesse, which Prussia annexed in 1866.

From 1938 to 1943 a Nazi forced labour camp for Romani people stood at Fulda. In the Cold War the Fulda Gap, an old east-west invasion route, was presumed to be where a conventional war between NATO and Soviet forces would begin, and American cavalry regiments were stationed in the city until 1993. The crypt of the abbey church still holds the relics of Boniface.
fulgencio-batista: Fulgencio Batista y Zaldívar was born on 16 January 1901 in Veguita, in the municipality of Banes, Cuba, to parents who had fought in the Cuban War of Independence. He was of Spanish, African and Chinese descent, and possibly of some Taíno descent. His mother named him Rubén and gave him her surname, and he was legally Rubén Zaldívar until 1939. When he then tried to register as a presidential candidate, no birth certificate existed for Fulgencio Batista, and he had to pay the local judge 15,000 pesos.

Batista joined the Sergeants' Revolt of 1933, which overthrew Gerardo Machado. Contemporaries claimed he was drawn in mainly because he was the only sergeant with a car. He then became army chief of staff with the rank of colonel and controlled the armed forces behind a short-lived five-member presidency. In January 1934 he, conspiring with the United States envoy Sumner Welles, forced President Ramón Grau San Martín to resign, and he ruled through puppet presidents until he was elected president in 1940. He carried out social reforms and pro-union policies, and Cuba entered the Second World War on the side of the Allies on 9 December 1941.

After four years in the United States he returned, and on 10 March 1952, three months before an election in which he stood a distant third, he seized power with army backing and cancelled the vote. He suspended the 1940 constitution and revoked most political liberties, including the right to strike. Havana became a centre of gambling and prostitution run for the American Mafia, and United States companies owned large shares of Cuba's sugar lands, mines and utilities. After Fidel Castro's attack on the Moncada Barracks on 26 July 1953, Batista relied increasingly on police violence. Estimates of those killed range from hundreds to 20,000, a figure that is disputed.

From December 1956 to December 1958 Castro's 26th of July Movement waged guerrilla war against the government. Rebels under Che Guevara defeated Batista's forces at Santa Clara on New Year's Eve 1958, and on 1 January 1959 Batista fled to the Dominican Republic under Rafael Trujillo's protection. He later found asylum in Portugal, living on Madeira and in Estoril, and died of a heart attack in Marbella, Spain, on 6 August 1973.
furth: Fürth lies in the Middle Franconia region of Bavaria. Its centre is only seven km from that of Nuremberg, and it forms a continuous conurbation with Nuremberg, Erlangen and Schwabach. The historic centre stands to the east and south of the Rednitz and Pegnitz rivers, which join to form the Regnitz northwest of the Old Town. To the north lies the fertile market-gardening area called the Knoblauchsland, the garlic country. The name comes from the German word for ford, because the first settlements grew up around one.

Founded as a Franconian settlement in the mid-8th century, Fürth is first mentioned in a document of 1 November 1007, in which Emperor Heinrich II gave his property there to the newly created Bishopric of Bamberg. Market privileges were granted but later lost to Nuremberg under Heinrich III, and restored from 1062, by which time Nuremberg was already the more important town. In 1524, as part of the Reformation, Fürth became a Protestant town like Nuremberg, though ties with Bamberg meant there were always some Catholics.

In the Thirty Years War the town lost about half its population. When Croatian soldiers set fire to it in 1634 it burned for several days and was almost completely destroyed, and at the end of the war only 800 people lived there. Huguenots from France settled in 1685, and by 1700 restoration was complete and the population had risen to about 6,000. Until the end of the 18th century a representative of the Diocese of Bamberg administered it. Fürth passed to Bavaria in 1806 and from 1818 was a city responsible for its own administration.

Jews are mentioned in Fürth as early as 1440. In 1528 the Margrave of Ansbach, George the Pious, allowed two Jews, Perman and Uriel, to settle in return for high taxes, and the community grew. By the 17th century there was a Talmudic academy of considerable repute, a synagogue was built in 1617, and in 1653 the first Jewish hospital in Germany was founded. The position of Jews in Fürth earned it the name Franconian Jerusalem, a phrase based on an older reference meant as an insult. The Jewish Museum in Franconia, opened in 1999, occupies a house that goes back to the 17th century.

Fürth survived the Second World War with less damage than most German cities and has many historic buildings. The Protestant Church of St Michael, dating from about 1100, is the oldest, and the Rathaus, built in 1840–50, has a tower modelled on the Palazzo Vecchio in Florence. The toy industry remains a major employer, and the football club SpVgg Fürth has won the German championship three times.
fussen: Füssen lies in the district of Ostallgäu, one kilometre from the Austrian border, on the banks of the Lech River at 808 m above sea level. The mountains of the Ammergau Alps surround it, and at the 47th parallel north it is one of the southernmost towns in Germany. The Lech flows into the Forggensee, a man-made lake built to prevent flooding. The town is known for violin making and is the nearest transport hub for the castles of Neuschwanstein and Hohenschwangau.

The town was settled in Roman times on the Via Claudia Augusta, the road from northern Italy to Augusta Vindelicum, now Augsburg, the capital of the province of Raetia. Its first name, Foetes, comes from the Latin word for a gorge, probably the gorge of the Lech. In Late Antiquity a part of the Legio III Italica was stationed there to guard the trade route over the Alps.

Below the High Castle stands the Baroque complex of the former Benedictine monastery of St Mang, whose history goes back to the 9th century. Saint Mang, Magnus of Füssen, is the town's patron saint; he and his brother monk Theodor, from the Abbey of Saint Gall, are considered its founders. His bones were moved to the crypt of a church built in 850, and around 950 they all disappeared. The coat of arms, a triskeles alluding to the German word for feet, is based on a seal of the early 14th century.

The Treaty of Füssen, signed in 1745 between the Electorate of Bavaria and Habsburg Austria, ended Bavaria's part in the War of the Austrian Succession. In the 19th century the composer Richard Wagner came to Füssen by railway to visit King Ludwig II of Bavaria. Since the 1950s the town has been the southern end of the Romantic Road.

The High Castle houses a branch gallery of the Bavarian State Collections of Paintings, with late Gothic and Renaissance works. The crypt of St Mang's Basilica holds the oldest fresco in Germany, from about 980. The saint's feast day, 6 September, is marked by a Mass and a torchlight procession through the old town.
futurism: Futurism was founded in Milan in 1909 by the poet and art theorist Filippo Tommaso Marinetti, who first published his Manifesto of Futurism on 5 February 1909 in La gazzetta dell'Emilia; Le Figaro reproduced it on 20 February. He was soon joined by the painters Umberto Boccioni, Carlo Carrà, Giacomo Balla and Gino Severini and by the composer Luigi Russolo. Marinetti expressed a passionate loathing of everything old, especially political and artistic traditions. The Futurists admired speed, technology, youth, violence, the car, the airplane and the industrial city, and they were passionate Italian nationalists. They praised originality and dismissed art critics as useless.

The movement worked in every medium, including painting, sculpture, theatre, film, music, architecture, fashion and cuisine. Boccioni's sculpture Unique Forms of Continuity in Space (1913) and Russolo's The Art of Noises (1913) are among its works.

In architecture Antonio Sant'Elia drew La Città Nuova (1912 to 1914), a city meant to be an efficient, fast-paced machine, never built; he was killed in the First World War. Francesco Balilla Pratella joined in 1910 and wrote a Manifesto of Futurist Musicians. In literature the Futurists called their poetry parole in libertà, rejecting meter and syntax. Italian Futurist cinema affected the film industry from 1916 to 1919, and only 35 minutes of Anton Giulio Bragaglia's Thaïs (1917) survive.

Many Italian Futurists supported Fascism in the hope of modernising Italy. Marinetti founded the Futurist Political Party in early 1918, which was absorbed into Benito Mussolini's Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in 1919. He walked out of the 1920 Fascist congress, calling its later exaltation of existing institutions reactionary, but supported Italian Fascism until his death in 1944. After Fascism's triumph in 1922 the Futurists gained official acceptance and could carry out important work, especially in architecture. A second generation took up aeropittura, aeropainting, from 1926, launched by the 1929 manifesto Perspectives of Flight.

Parallel movements appeared in the Russian Empire, where Vladimir Mayakovsky, Velimir Khlebnikov and Kazimir Malevich took part; their Cubo-Futurism combined Cubism's forms with Futurist movement, but many Russian Futurists were ideological opposites of the Italian movement, embracing the emerging communist movement.

Futurism influenced Art Deco, Vorticism, Constructivism, Surrealism and Dada. As an organised movement it is regarded as extinct, having died out in 1944 with Marinetti's death. After the Second World War many Futurist artists struggled in their careers because of their association with a defeated regime. Marinetti's manifesto also declared contempt for women, though he later called Luisa, Marchesa Casati a Futurist.
fuzhou: Fuzhou lies between the Min River estuary to the south and the city of Ningde to the north; together the two make up the Mindong linguistic and cultural region. According to a geographical treatise published in the 9th century under the Tang dynasty, the Yuanhe Maps and Records of Prefectures and Counties, its name comes from Mount Fu, a mountain said to lie northwest of the city, combined with zhou, meaning settlement or prefecture. Fuzhou has a humid subtropical climate, with long, hot summers, short mild winters, and typhoons in late summer and early autumn.

Archaeology shows long settlement. Bone analysis links the ancient inhabitants of Xiying (7300–6500 BCE) to Austronesian peoples, and the Keqiutou culture (6500–5000 BCE) is the oldest known site of rice cultivation in Fujian. During the Warring States period the Chinese called the area Minyue. According to the historian Sima Qian, the surviving members of the royal family of Yue fled south after Yue fell to Chu in 306 BCE and settled among the local Yue people. In 282 CE, under the Jin dynasty, two artificial lakes and a canal system were built in Ye, and the core of modern Fuzhou grew around these water systems. The first large-scale migration of Chinese settlers to the south and southeast began in 308.

In 893 the warlord brothers Wang Chao and Wang Shenzhi captured Fuzhou in a rebellion against the Tang and took control of Fujian, and in 909 they proclaimed the Min Kingdom. Under the Song dynasty Fuzhou produced ten zhuangyuan, scholars who placed first in the imperial examinations, a large number for any city of the time. Between 1405 and 1433 Admiral Zheng He's fleets visited en route to the Indian Ocean, and at Changle he built a shrine to Tian-Fei and in 1431 erected a stele.

Lin Zexu, a native of Fuzhou, was appointed in 1839 to enforce the ban on the opium trade; the First Opium War followed, and the Treaty of Nanjing of 1842 made Fuzhou, then known to Westerners as Foochow, one of five treaty ports. Japanese forces took the city in 1938, and the People's Liberation Army occupied it with little resistance on 17 August 1949.

Fuzhou is the capital of Fujian. Besides Mandarin, most of its people speak Fuzhounese, the prestige form of Eastern Min. Mahayana Buddhism and Taoism are its traditional religions, and its cuisine is one of the four traditional styles of Fujian cuisine. Its arts include bodiless lacquerware, paper umbrellas and horn combs, called the Three Treasures. The Sanfang Qixiang, the Three Lanes and Seven Alleys, preserves ancient residential buildings from the late Jin dynasty, and Hualin Temple, built in 964, has a main hall known as the oldest surviving wooden building in south China.
fyodor-dostoevsky: Fyodor Dostoevsky was born in Moscow on 11 November (Old Style 30 October) 1821, the second child of Dr Mikhail Dostoevsky and Maria Nechayeva. He grew up in the grounds of the Mariinsky Hospital for the Poor, where his father worked, and met patients from the lower end of Russian society when playing in the hospital gardens. His nanny read him sagas, fairy tales and legends, and his mother taught him to read from the Bible. His parents also introduced him to Pushkin, Schiller, Goethe, Cervantes, Walter Scott and Homer.

Dostoevsky completed his first novel, Poor Folk, in May 1845. His friend Dmitry Grigorovich took the manuscript to the poet Nikolay Nekrasov, who showed it to the critic Vissarion Belinsky, and Belinsky called it Russia's first social novel. It appeared on 15 January 1846 and sold well. He soon wrote The Double. He also read the French socialists Fourier, Cabet, Proudhon and Saint-Simon, but his Russian Orthodox faith could not accord with Belinsky's atheism and scientific materialism, and he parted from Belinsky and his circle.

In 1849 he was arrested for belonging to the Petrashevsky Circle, which discussed banned books critical of Tsarist Russia. He was sentenced to death, but the sentence was commuted at the last moment. He spent four years in a Siberian hard labour camp, which inspired The House of the Dead, and then six years of compulsory military service in exile. Later he edited magazines of his own and wrote A Writer's Diary, travelled in Western Europe and developed a gambling addiction that brought financial hardship.

His major novels include Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot (1869), Demons (1872), The Adolescent (1875) and The Brothers Karamazov (1880). Notes from Underground, a novella of 1864, is considered one of the first works of existentialist literature. After his release from prison he put religious themes, especially those of Russian Orthodoxy, into his writing. His fiction takes up suicide, poverty, human manipulation and morality, and depicts the chaotic sociopolitical order of contemporary Russia.

Mikhail Bakhtin saw polyphony, the simultaneous presence of several narrative voices and perspectives, as an important element of his style and a major advance in the novel. Friedrich Nietzsche called him the only psychologist from whom he had something to learn, and Sigmund Freud ranked him second only to William Shakespeare among creative writers. He died on 9 February (Old Style 28 January) 1881 after a series of pulmonary hemorrhages, and asked that the parable of the Prodigal Son be read to his children.
